An constet de Virtutibus theologalibus Fide, Spe, Caritate tum in Deum cum in Proximum, necnon de Cardinalibus Prudentia, Iustitia, Temperantia, Fortitudine earumque adnexis, in gradu heroico, in casu et ad effectum de quo agitur.

NO. I — DEPOSITIONS OF THE WITNESSES

(A. - FROM THE ROMAN ORDINARY PROCESS, years 1913-1927)

p. 3

WITNESS I
Most Rev. Eminence GENNARO GRANITO DI BELMONTE

Scope in the process: From Sess. 5 of 7 April 1913 (cf. Proc. fol. 46) to Sess. 18 of 8 May 1913 (fol. 163v).

Name, surname, date and place of birth: Gennaro Granito di Belmonte, born on 10 April 1851 in Naples.

State and profession: Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, formerly Apostolic Nuncio in Brussels and Vienna.

Quality of the witness: Eyewitness.

Age of the witness when he met the Servant of God: 23 years.

Age of the Servant of God when the witness met her: 43 years.

Age of the witness at the time of the deposition: 62 years.

Length of acquaintance and its motivation: The witness, still a layman, came into contact with the Institute founded by the Servant of God in 1874, commissioned to paint a picture of St. Anne for the Sisters' chapel; from 1879, ordained a Priest, he was placed in charge of the house of the said religious in Naples and appointed their confessor. Hence his thorough knowledge of Gattorno, who found in the witness at once a wise and respectful confidant who followed and counseled her almost to the end of her life.

Observations on the witness, on the scope and on the content of the deposition: The qualification of the witness, the frequent and extensive relations he had with the Servant of God and the fact that she kept him informed about her ascetical-mystical phenomena classify this deposition among the most reliable and rich in content. The concrete and detailed information that characterizes it embraces both the secular and the religious life of Gattorno. Of this second period the witness illustrates the beginnings of the foundation of the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne and the fervent, fruitful activity that the Servant of God at once gave it in order to help all persons in need and abandoned whom Providence placed on her path; ample space is given to the analysis of the way in which Mother Gattorno carried out the office of Superior General, an office exercised in an enlightened manner until death. As to the virtues, after the admission that all were exercised to a heroic degree, the witness shows a vast knowledge of each. In the last interrogatories the themes of Gattorno's writings, of supernatural gifts and of mystical phenomena are explored in depth; then the subjects relating to death, to the reputation for holiness and miracles are treated, regarding which the witness, a highly qualified person, continues to maintain a wholly positive judgment.

Note of the Patron: The individual testimonies are generally reported in full; the omission of substantial parts will be explained, while the answers in which the witness declares he has nothing to say, or repeats concepts already known, are eliminated without justification.

Ad 2 interr., Proc. fol. 50v., testis respondit:

§ 1
Particulars of the witness.

My name is Gennaro Granito di Belmonte, son of the late Angelo, prince of Belmonte, and Donna Paolina Pignatelli. I was born in Naples on 10 April 1851. I was Apostolic Nuncio in Brussels and in Vienna and in the Consistory of 29 November 1911 I was created Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church.

§ 2
Scope of knowledge,
§ 3
The witness's great trust in the Servant of God,

Ad 7: In 1874-75, being still a layman, I busied myself with the fine arts and painted. I was asked by my mother, who belonged to a group of Ladies who, at the charge of Cardinal Riario Sforza, then Archbishop of Naples, took care to facilitate the new Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, to paint a St. Anne for their Chapel. On that occasion I met the Religious Daughters of St. Anne and their Foundress Sr. Anna Rosa Gattorno. In 1879 then, made a Priest, I was placed by Cardinal Sanfelice in charge of the House of the said Religious and appointed also their Confessor, whereby I came into greater contact with the said religious, and could know the Institute and the Foundress better, on the occasions when she came to Naples. Although she did not confess to me, she opened herself to me about the affairs of the Institute and also about matters concerning her spirit. From that time I was always in relation with the Servant of God, by word or by letter. Although knowing the great virtues of the Servant of God and facts which I had to hold to be prodigious, my admiration never went as far as enthusiasm, whether because of my natural character, or also because the Servant of God, communicating to me some of her interior things, almost enjoined on me not to manifest them to anyone, it being her lively desire to be heard in the prayer she constantly made to the Lord, to be humbled, to remain in obscurity and be despised. And she added that, given her said lively desire, she herself could not explain why she revealed to me the things she was telling me. Whether, as I said before, because of my character not prone to enthusiasm, or because of the said lively desire of the Servant of God, I kept very reserved, and so I did not come to know many things that I could have known by questioning. The Servant of God showed me such trust as to reveal to me exceptional facts, which I believe I alone know, and she herself sometimes added: «This I tell only you». The Religious now at the head of the Institute, such as Mother Carrega, Mother Speranza, and others now deceased, who were very much in contact with the Servant of God, and the Priest Tornatore Giovanni Battista, of the Lazarists, likewise now deceased (who I declare from now on seems to me to have let himself be carried a little too far by enthusiasm for the Servant of God, although a good connoisseur of ascetics and mystics), spoke to me of the Servant of God with great esteem and admiration, as of a saint. In the particular accounts the religious avoided that the revelation made to me by the Servant of God should become known, knowing well her humility and having received from her the order not to reveal to anyone anything about her that had seemed to them not ordinary. But all that I learned from others were things that had a little of the exterior, the more secret things I having known directly from the Servant of God. The correspondence of the Servant of God that I possessed, I handed over to the Daughters of St. Anne for the search that will be made of the writings. The Servant of God wrote, she told me, by God's order (and by me then well encouraged to continue in these writings) all that happened in her spirit, whether of revelations, anguish and trials, and from time to time she gave me a reading of them and handed me some fascicle to read, but with a most lively request not to communicate them to anyone.

§ 4
In the writings of the Servant of God nothing contrary to the Cause of beatification.

The showing me these writings afterwards was to justify some permissions she asked when I came: for [...] the reading [...] of these [...] [... knowledge] of what had preceded, and so I could regulate myself.

§ 5
Wrong title of the book of the Servant of God.

After the death of the Servant of God her Religious, having learned from me that I had had communication of these writings, wished to hand them all over to me. I reread them attentively to see whether there was anything contrary to the Cause of her Sanctification (and I saw nothing on my own account); and when I handed over the correspondence to the Religious I returned these too to them. As also I returned to them a manuscript of the Servant of God relating to the foundation of the Institute. I had exhorted the Servant of God to write the history of her foundation; but she, through continual fear of coming out of her shadow, seemed to me not very disposed to consent. Pressures from other persons were then added; among these from the Princess of Fitalia, a great admirer of the Servant of God and benefactress of her Institute. The Servant of God thus found herself obliged to yield. She set to work and handed a writing to the Princess of Fitalia. Who, assisted by Cardinal Guarino Archbishop of Messina and by Canon Pennino of the same Cathedral, both masters of the spirit, had it published. In the edition of the said manuscript, preceded by two letters of praise for the work addressed to the said Princess, they put on the title page the title, in my view unfortunately wrong: «Travagli e conforto dell'anima nel cammino della perfezione [... Dio]» (Labors and Comfort of the Soul on the Way of Perfection).

[...] described by a Servant [of God] and bore the approval of the ecclesiastical authority of Palermo. I said that the title was unfortunately wrong, because in the reading I recently made of the printed book, I found that it was nothing other than the true history of the foundation and development of the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, which the Servant of God had ingeniously wished to hide under figures, allegories and the like, so that the mission she had had in this matter of the foundation should not come to be known. I was able to ascertain with certainty what I have said, because I was perfectly acquainted with the facts reported in that book in allegorical form. Which facts were then confirmed to me by the Religious who were part of them, or in other ways had knowledge of them. The book with such a wrong title, in my view, provoked a measure of the ecclesiastical authority, by which the Religious Daughters of St. Anne were forbidden to keep and read the said book. This measure seemed to me and to others who are interested in the Cause of the Servant of God an obstacle to the success of the Cause itself, but I think that, in view of the explanations I have already presented to the competent authority, it will be revoked. Meanwhile I have obtained from the Holy Father permission to have the said book read by those Religious whom I should think suitable, so that they might have had part in, or knowledge of, the facts mentioned in the book, and who therefore could on occasion confirm, as they have confirmed to me, what I had already seen in the book. In my answers to the Interrogatories I declare that I shall keep to what I heard from the Servant of God or from other authoritative persons, specifying whether it was drawn from reading.

§ 6
The witness's esteem for the Servant of God.

Ad 8, Proc. fol. 59v.: I have always had and have at present for the Servant of God Rosa Gattorno great esteem and veneration for her exceptional virtues; and I should certainly be glad if I could see her canonized for the glory of the Lord and to see her virtues rewarded, as also for the credit that would redound to the Institute founded by her. I have then worked to have the present Cause of beatification introduced; however I do not promote it, and as to the outcome, I submit to what Holy Church will decide.

§ 7
Family and childhood of the Servant of God.

Ad 9: I know that the Servant of God was born in Genoa, but I do not know either the day, or the month, or the year of her birth. She belonged to a well-to-do and religious family. I know two of the brothers of the Servant of God, Federico and Francesco. The first, unfortunately very different from his sister from the point of view of religious sentiments, and for whose conversion the Servant of God prayed to the end of her life, indeed offered bodily penances to the Lord for the same purpose, and she treated him with the greatest affection and charity, hoping to win him also by way of the heart. For his part the brother always showed esteem for the virtues of his sister, having no difficulty in affirming it publicly. The other brother, Francesco, is a religious person, and has a regular family, composed entirely of most worthy persons.

§ 8
She practiced charity from the first years of life.

Ad 10: I can say nothing more about the childhood and youth of the Servant of God, except that from the first years she always showed herself charitable, taking part in those works in the City of Genoa that had as their purpose beneficence and the relief of neighbor. The Servant of God then alluded to me several times to the good spiritual direction which in childhood she had received.

Ad 11: I know that she united herself in marriage with Mr. Custo. I could not say whether there was kinship between them or other canonical impediments, nor how long the engagement lasted and when the marriage was celebrated.

p. 8

§ 9
A good wife and mother.

Ad 13: I have heard nothing to the contrary about the good relations between the Servant of God and her husband. I know for certain that she had two children from the marriage; of others I could not affirm it. The first, now deceased, was called Alessandro; the second, Carlotta, now Countess Barbiellini, is still living.

The Servant of God was solicitous for their education as long as she remained in the family. After her husband's death, having placed these two little children where they would be educated, she withdrew from the house to begin the work to which the Lord called her.

One thing in this regard made a singular impression on me in a favorable sense, and it is that the Servant of God never made the slightest mention to me of her husband, nor of the period of her married life.

Ad 14: After a few years the husband of the Servant of God died, and she, on so mournful an occasion, spared nothing for him, both from the religious point of view and from the temporal point of view. I know that he received the Sacraments of the Church and died as a good Christian.

This trial was borne by the Servant of God with sorrow, but together with signs of resignation. Of this I never had a direct account from the Servant of God, but only from other persons who knew her.

§ 10
Sufferings of the Servant of God because of her son Alessandro.

Ad 15: About thirty years ago one of the children of the Servant of God died, Alessandro, who, although attached to his mother, made her suffer much by his private conduct, and the greatest anguish of the Servant of God was to see him far from God, while a grave illness (consumption) brought him nearer day by day to the grave. The Servant of God spared nothing for his temporal health, and at the same time worked that he might return to God, and also for this purpose she offered herself to the Lord with bodily penances. She was heard by the Lord, because the son, sent to Naples for a climatic cure, grew worse and reached the point of death. Then he confessed, making it plain that he was glad to be able to give this consolation to his mother. The illness having given a little respite, he went to Piacenza, where he died with the last religious comforts. I could not say whether the Servant of God was present at his death, but this I know, that in her deep maternal sorrow she thanked the Lord for having heard her in what concerned the health of the soul of her son.

§ 11
Works of charity during widowhood.

Ad 16: After her husband's death the Servant of God gave herself with greater fervor to works of charity in the City of Genoa, and I have heard that in some of those works they would have wanted her as President, precisely because of the virtues with which they saw her adorned. She refused such presidency, and I have reason to believe that this happened both through her humility and modesty, and because perhaps from then she had conceived the plan of founding a special work for the spiritual and temporal relief of the poor.

§ 12
First steps toward the foundation of the Institute.

Ad 17: I do not know precisely when the Servant of God conceived the plan of founding an Institution for the good of neighbor, but certainly she devoted herself to such work after her husband's death. For this purpose she took counsel with her own Director, now deceased, and also with the Archbishop of Genoa who esteemed her much. And both the spiritual Director and the Archbishop encouraged her to carry out her plan. And although the desire of the Servant of God to carry it out as soon as possible was very lively, and for which purpose she saw the need to withdraw from her family and from the native City where she enjoyed many relations, she had to delay somewhat the beginning of the work she cherished.

§ 13
She founds the Institute at Piacenza.

Ad 18: To free herself from the said difficulties, the Servant of God resolved to leave Genoa, putting to heroic test her heart as daughter and mother, because, having learned of her plan, both her old mother and her tender children, with affectionate and repeated violence, begged her not to carry out her intentions. The Servant of God, feeling in her soul that the hour of the Lord's call had come, crushed by the material pain, left her native land and began her pilgrimage to settle at Piacenza, where the field of her apostolate was reserved for her.

It was reported to me, I do not remember by whom, that her old mother, as a last means to overcome her daughter's heart, said to her: «If you must leave the house, you will first have to pass over my body». I cannot affirm whether the mother carried out her threat or not, a threat that did not attain its aim, because the daughter in fact went away.

p. 10

Certainly in this period of time the Servant of God did not go to Rome.

Ad 19: I could not say why the Servant of God preferred the City of Piacenza for carrying out the work to which God called her. At Piacenza she had occasion to approach the Bishop, Mr. Giovanni Battista Tornatore, Priest of the mission, and some Lords and Ladies of the Aristocracy known for their piety and generosity, who showed themselves at once disposed to favor her in her projects. Nevertheless also in Piacenza there was no lack of difficulties for the work of the Servant of God, difficulties which she met also on the part of some of the local Clergy, who judged the foundation of new works inopportune.

§ 14
Recourse to prayer in difficulties.

To overcome these difficulties the Servant of God had recourse to prayer; and here I wish to note that, in all the time of her life, in the many times in which Ecclesiastics were for her and for her Institute a cause of displeasure and of very strong opposition, the Servant of God had as a maxim never to make known to others what might give occasion to lessen the reputation of those same Ecclesiastics, and I repeat again, her powerful means for succeeding in bringing remedies or in making the truth known was prayer.

I know that the Servant of God, before founding her Institute, fully obtained the consent of the local ecclesiastical authority and, with the few elements that at first joined her, began the cherished work.

§ 15
Title of the Institute.

Ad 20, Proc. fol. 69: I recall having heard that the first thought of the Servant of God was to work for the foundation of a new Institute of charity under the title of Daughters of Mary. I could not say why this title was from the beginning changed to the other, Daughters of St. Anne; to which title the appellation of nurses was commonly added, it having been in the mind of the Foundress an excellent means of charity for obtaining the salvation of many souls. Afterwards to this purpose was added also that of the education of youth, preferably the most abandoned. Little by little the charitable institution spread in Hospitals and Asylums, the Sisters being invited by the civil and municipal administrations.

After the due Ecclesiastical approvals the new work was inaugurated with the taking of the religious habit by some young women, of whom she was not one. The reason for this circumstance, if I do not misremember, was that she was still occupied in arranging the interests of her family, which consisted principally in dividing and securing to her children the whole family patrimony.

§ 16
The habit of the new religious.

With precision I could not determine the moment when the Servant of God herself put on the habit of her Institute, but I well remember being assured that it was after a short interval. As regards the choice of the form of the new habit I recall having heard from the Servant of God herself that she had seen St. Anne dressed in precisely that same habit which the Servant of God chose, and which her daughters still wear.

I recall having heard from Fr. Giovanni Battista Tornatore, who had acquaintance with and unlimited veneration for the Venerable Bernardo Maria Clausi, that the latter had encouraged the Servant of God in the foundation of the new Institute.

§ 17
First rule of the Institute.

Ad 21: With precision I could not determine the moment in which some rules for this new Institute were compiled and printed. It was then reported to me (a circumstance that I verified in the relative position which is found at the Sacred Congregation of Religious) that the said Rules were denounced to the Holy See, which, after the usual prudent examination, had the most severe orders intimated that all the copies of them be destroyed, with a severe injunction that the Author of them, if belonging to the Institute, be forever deprived of any office, and if an outsider be removed altogether from the Institute. The carrying out of these orders was entrusted first to the Archbishop of Genoa (because the Servant of God being a Genoese, it was thought she was under his jurisdiction), and then to the Bishop of Piacenza, to whom it was easy to come to know the author of the above-mentioned rules, and it was Fr. Giovanni Battista Tornatore.

He, in execution of the orders of the Holy See, was immediately removed from the Institute, in which later, with the consent of the Holy See, he was able to exercise his Ministry.

§ 18
Obedience of the Servant of God in the matter of the rules.

It is not known to me whether Tornatore had a charge directly from the Servant of God to compile the said rules, or whether this happened through the great part he took in the foundation of the Work. What I wish to bring out is that, in his measures and inquiries made by order of the Holy See, both the Archbishop of Genoa and the Bishop of Piacenza made to the Sacred Congregation the most flattering praises of the Servant of God, the former praising her virtues and the latter, also praising her virtues, brought out the prompt and generous obedience of the Servant of God in complying with the orders of the Holy See.

§ 19
Rule written by the Servant of God out of obedience and its approval.

Following what had happened, the Servant of God, with a willing mind, begged the Bishop of Piacenza himself to provide the Rules which were to guide the new Institute. The Bishop in his turn enjoined on the Servant of God to present to him a draft of those Rules which she would have wished to give to the new work for the formation and sanctification of her daughters. Not without intense repugnance the Servant of God obeyed, and when she presented her work to the Prelate, she had the consolation of seeing how, a short time after, the Bishop returned to her the Rules approved by him.

From the information I was able to draw from the Servant of God herself, at the moment she undertook out of obedience the compilation of the Rules, she felt herself as if guided by a supernatural help, so that without interruption in a short time she was able to write the draft of the Rules asked of her by the Bishop. I do not remember precisely the year in which the decree of praise was given to these same Rules, but I think I remember that on the occasion of the first twenty-fifth year of the foundation of the Institute, the Most Eminent Cardinal Verga, then Prefect of the Congregation of Bishops and Regulars and also Protector of the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, took care to give the Servant of God the welcome surprise, handing her the definitive decree of approval of the Institute.

In the said Institute there are simple vows, which are renewed every year. I know then that some of the Religious, after a long period of simple profession, may make perpetual vows, with the prior opinion of the local Ecclesiastical Authority and of the Superiors of the Institute.

Besides the three usual ones no other special vow is prescribed.

§ 20
The Servant of God first superior of the Institute.

Ad 22: It is known to me that the Servant of God was the first Superior of her Institute. I could not say whether this office was imposed on her by the Ecclesiastical Authorities, or by the very fact that she was the foundress and was in relation with it. This office was kept for her until death, notwithstanding that repeatedly she would have wished to be relieved of it so as to be more quietly recollected in exercises of piety.

§ 21
Oppositions and sufferings in the foundation.

In the development of the Institute, which took place very rapidly, there was no lack of observations made about the Foundress concerning the admission of candidates and the foundations of houses. The few inconveniences that occurred in this order of things never seemed to me a defect to be attributed to the Servant of God, but rather a consequence of the rapid esteem that the Institute acquired, whereby the charity of the Servant of God could not refuse the help that was asked of her for the good of neighbor. For her part the Servant of God used all the means of prudence necessary for the admission of the Religious, keeping to what had been laid down by the Holy See in the rules. It cannot be denied that in the number of her daughters, from time to time, there were some who did not correspond to their vocation, and in these cases the zeal of the Servant of God to make them mend their ways was remarkable, having not seldom had the consolation of winning them by her charity.

§ 22
A firm and prudent superior in the government of the Institute.

The Servant of God was always very firm in the oversight and direction of the Institute; and this firmness she not seldom had to exercise, with devout submission, with Ecclesiastics and with Bishops. The Servant of God, in taking measures and dispositions in the direction of her Institute, in the most difficult circumstances always turned to Jesus Christ, to St. Anne and to her holy Protectors, and did not carry out her steps and her measures except when she felt strongly assisted by supernatural helps. From this it followed that, when she was opposed by anyone whatever, especially by Bishops and other Ecclesiastical Authorities, after having made her submissive observations, she did not oppose the measures that were demanded by the others, these same having after some time to recognize that the measures taken by the Servant of God were just and prudent, and had to follow them. What I have now set forth I can affirm from personal experience, since in the many years in which I was in the direction of the Daughters of St. Anne in the House of Naples, it having happened that I wished to take measures or to oppose some of the dispositions given by the Servant of God, she never opposed my will while making me note that she did not agree with me. Time then, as I indicated above, proved the Servant of God right.

Proc. fol. 78v.: Continuing the same subject, I wish to observe that most of the time the judgment that I, or other Ecclesiastics too, formed on the dispositions given by the Foundress was a consequence of the ascendancy that some Sisters exercised over us, and to whom we more easily gave credence. I recall having heard it said several times, and I myself sometimes thought it, that the Foundress was a little obstinate, and also that she was very personal. I repeat what I have already mentioned above, that, looking at things dispassionately, this was due to the general knowledge she had of the things and persons of the Institute.

Here it is relevant to mention a fact which for many years was a cause of great tribulation for the same Foundress.

§ 23
Influence of Fr. Tornatore on the [...].

As I recalled at the beginning, Mr. Giovanni Battista Tornatore, Priest of the Mission, who had had a great part in the foundation of the Institute, habitually lived in the same Houses of the Institute, and often followed the Foundress and the other Sisters who went about visiting the Houses. He with much zeal worked for the right running of religious life, but also was often influenced and impressed by those Religious who were either reproved or punished by the Foundress, and often took their side against the very measures of the Servant of God. As is easy to understand, this dualism was a cause of tribulation for the Servant of God, who, with her habitual system, while she did not wish to oppose the said Ecclesiastic, in her mind felt well and noted the inconvenience that resulted from it in the discipline of the various Communities. Here too I can affirm that time gave full satisfaction to the Servant of God.

§ 24
Prudence of the Servant of God in the choice of superiors.

In the choice of persons destined for the various offices in the Communities, I absolutely exclude that she could have been guided by secondary ends, notwithstanding that sometimes the person chosen did not live up to her expectation.

The Servant of God was very solicitous in the oversight and visitation of the Houses of the Institute, going personally or sending visitors. In fact, to the distant Houses of South America and Africa she was never able to go personally, but, as I have said, she always provided indirectly. Not seldom the Servant of God assured me that she was guided by supernatural helps to go by preference to one House or another, it being verified that where she was thus guided, she found that her presence was really necessary. Likewise, under the same guidance she was dissuaded from going to some place, it being verified afterwards that some grave danger would have overtaken her. These facts were a subject of unlimited gratitude to Providence.

In confirmation of what I have said, I recall that once, having decided to go to a town in Sicily to visit her Houses, by a strong inspiration, at the moment almost of departure, she was dissuaded. She came to know afterwards that a plot had been formed there by people hostile to Religion to assault and harm the Servant of God. At the moment I do not remember the name of the town to which I have here alluded, but I am sure that in the course of the Process this detail can be completed.

§ 25
Charitable and watchful government.

As regards the temporal welfare of her subjects, she always gave measures that answered the purpose. I cannot deny that in several Houses inconveniences occurred on this point, but I absolutely exclude that this depended on negligence of the Servant of God, and I prove this by the fact that she took energetic measures when she was informed, and after having verified or caused to be verified the deplored inconveniences, which not seldom were exaggerated by Religious of little spirit.

She had great charity for her sick daughters, and showed it when she could personally attend them, giving at the same time the strictest dispositions to the Superiors of all the Houses of the Institute. Here too I must agree that she was not always met with a response by her subordinates, who nevertheless in due time did not go without severe reprimands and measures.

To answer the question whether the Servant of God was prompt in giving dispositions so that her little daughters who were in danger of life should receive the Holy Sacraments, I believe I have sufficiently answered when I said that she gave the Superiors the strictest orders for the spiritual and temporal good of the sick. In this connection I recall that when the Servant of God was in Naples, and a little celebration was being held in the Community on that occasion, a Religious died in that House, the gravity of whose illness, which had come upon her at that moment, the local Superior concealed from the Servant of God and from myself, who in the morning was there in that House; and this silence was in order not to disturb the celebration, and perhaps also because she did not see the imminence of the danger. The Servant of God was so indignant at it that she treated the guilty Superior in the harshest manner (who then died shortly after). I do not know whether the knowledge that measures were being taken against her had no part in that death. When the Servant of God was at the bedside of a dying daughter of hers, it sometimes happened that by extraordinary light she recognized that the conscience of the dying woman was not at peace, and with maternal charity made it known to her, it being found that the sick woman, confirming to her mother that she was right, provision was made by having recourse once more to confession.

§ 26
Development of the Institute.

Ad 23: I cannot give extensive information on the origin and truly prodigious development of the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, as regards time, because, as I mentioned at the beginning, it is only from the moment their House was opened in Naples that I began to take an interest in it. Already by that time many Houses of the said Institute had been founded in Italy and in the principal Cities, such as Piacenza, Ferrara, Genoa, Florence, Rome and others. The Generalate was in Piacenza and, invited by the Foundress, I stayed there for some time, observing and taking pleasure in the religious spirit that reigned there. Since that time there have been very many other foundations of Houses, both in southern Italy and also in South America and Africa.

As regards Africa, I recall that at the time of the Eritrean war the Foundress, moved by zeal and charity for the natives of the conquered places, placed the work of her daughters at the disposal of the competent authorities, and it was accepted. With the prior consent of the Holy See, the Servant of God immediately sent Religious to Massawa and Assab, obtaining first from the Holy See and then from the civil authorities that Religious men should accompany and care for the spiritual good of her daughters and of the natives.

The means indispensable for the maintenance of this grand edifice never failed her, because not seldom they came to her in a prodigious way. When Houses were opened at the request of private administrations, the necessary for their maintenance was agreed with these. The subsidies of benefactors, devoted to her person or attached to the work, were also abundant. However, as the needs were often grave and urgent, the Servant of God had recourse to Heaven; and she herself affirmed to me that she had been largely heard, finding multiplied in her drawers the few means she had, which were wholly insufficient for the need. To make precise how these cases of financial straits occurred, I shall mention the taxes which she was obliged to pay from one moment to the next to the government for the buildings owned by the Institute, as also the great constructions undertaken for the Generalate in Rome, for which she needed to dispose of sums that she did not have, and which at the given moment were found entirely paid.

As regards the financial relations of the subordinate houses, the Servant of God arranged that they could provide for themselves, as usual; those Houses that had a surplus sent it to the Servant of God, as Superior General, for the needs of the Generalate, of the Novitiate, and of other Houses which the Servant of God judged she ought to assist.

§ 27
Valid defense of justice.

Complaints were made by the Sisters on this point, saying that the local Superiors deprived their subordinates of what was necessary in order to make themselves acceptable to the Superior General; it is known to me that in a few Houses this inconvenience occurred, but it is also known to me with what severity the Foundress rebuked those Superiors, and this clearly says that the deplored inconvenience can never be attributed to the Servant of God.

Proc. fol. 88: In the visits which the Servant of God made to the Houses under her authority, her first thought was to inquire about the fulfillment of what the Rules prescribed concerning meditation and the other exercises of piety. From the good or less exact fulfillment of this duty she gathered, without mistake, the general course of discipline in those Houses, and she worked to bring remedies where there was need.

§ 28
Prudence in providing for the good running of the communities.

On these same occasions she was most strict in giving dispositions to the Superiors that they should prevent the frequent presence in the house of Confessors, Ecclesiastics and laymen without real necessity. Her deep veneration for Ecclesiastics and the charity she nourished for neighbor in general brought it about that in the measures which the Servant of God had to take in the circumstances mentioned they did not in any way offend the esteem and honor of others.

She was most diligent in the administration of the goods of the Institute and of other revenues of the Institute, but as regards goods (except those of Gargatano near Piacenza) there was little to administer, since it possessed no buildings apart from those for the habitation of the Sisters.

§ 29
Diligent administrator of the goods of the Institute.

In the books of administration the Servant of God abstained, however, for reasons of humility, from recording some revenues of prodigious origin. Wise reasons moved the Servant of God to entrust the administration of the properties of Gargatano to her son-in-law. First, because those properties were very badly managed by those to whom they had previously been entrusted, and so she thought that a relative would have shown greater honesty and that greater profit would have come from it for the Institute; the more so since until then the son-in-law, although he showed that he wished to draw economic profit from the physical condition of his wife, who was deaf-mute, had not up to then given any reason for believing him dishonest. Second, another reason which moved the Servant of God to the said act was the persuasion that she could keep him more closely united to herself and in dependence, and by continual contact through business could influence his morals. For it must be well noted that the Servant of God did not entrust to him the general mandate for the management of those goods, but left it well limited to ordinary and daily matters as regards contact with the government administration and with the tenant farmers.

§ 30
Prudence and fortitude toward the son-in-law.

Unfortunately the son-in-law did not respond to her trust; when, however, the Servant of God saw that the son-in-law no longer deserved her trust (and she came to know this from the fact that one day the son-in-law by surprise induced her to sign a blank sheet, which however had no consequence, thanks to the Servant of God's quickness), she provided at once by a notarial act of Dr. Monti of Rome, revoking any mandate to the said son-in-law.

What I have said and perhaps shall say concerning the son-in-law of the Servant of God shows of itself how much reserve it requires as regards publication, the son-in-law himself being still living, who could cause trouble both to the Religious Daughters of St. Anne and to me. I believe therefore that I may express my wish that this point not be published, in the certainty that it will be received as just.

§ 31
She never neglected her duties as a mother toward her children.

Ad 24: Having torn herself away from her family, the Servant of God never neglected her duties as a mother according to the flesh, and always concerned herself with her children, especially in what regarded morals. It must not be thought, however, that she let herself be so absorbed by these cares as to neglect even in the least her duties toward the Institute she had founded. Having procured a good education for her daughter (born unfortunately deaf-mute), so that she did not appear disagreeable even in conversation, she was glad, as at a providence of the Lord, to learn that a young man of the Roman aristocracy, Count Gaspare Barbiellini-Amidei, had taken an interest in her daughter and had asked for her hand in marriage. Even after the marriage the Servant of God continued to concern herself with her daughter in order to make less painful the unhappiness which nature had given her.

§ 32
Charity and utmost prudence toward her daughter.

At times she assisted her also with money; nor does it seem to me that she can be blamed for this, since it is to be noted that of the money that was given to her by benefactors, some was at times presented to her with this determined purpose, of using it for her particular charities. The Servant of God was, however, so delicate that she hesitated to give a small part to her daughter and son-in-law without having asked advice, and she asked me myself several times, and I always judged that it was well-ordered charity to help that unhappy daughter of hers, who was forced by her husband with violent means to have recourse to the Servant of God, all the more since I knew that these subsidies were offered to the Servant of God for works extraneous to the Institute. In this connection I recall that at times the little grandchildren went to the Servant of God telling how their father ill-treated their mother, who then, in her turn, came to report to the Servant of God the purpose of that ill-treatment, which was always money. Although the financial condition of this family was not such that they lacked necessities, the plan to economize their own patrimony was clearly seen, largely made up of the dowry which had come from her parents to his wife.

§ 33
Maternal solicitude for her little grandchildren.

The solicitude of the Servant of God extended also to the little grandchildren in their early age, having entrusted them to her Sisters for instruction and education. There was also the circumstance which made this easier, namely that the son-in-law's house was adjacent to those of the Sisters both in Rome and in Piacenza. Such adjacency of houses might perhaps be objected by someone against the Servant of God; yet as to this one in Rome I know that the construction was entrusted to the brothers of the Servant of God, who built both the one house and the other; the one belonging to the Sisters and the other the common property of the Gattorno brothers and of their nephew Gaspare Barbiellini; it can only be said that perhaps the Servant of God did not oppose it; but I would like the natural unhappiness of that poor daughter of the Servant of God to be well considered, and that moreover there was no internal communication.

To justify once more the conduct of the Servant of God regarding her son-in-law, I think it opportune to point out how he always showed himself in appearance most pious, to the point of frequently approaching the Sacraments, and was in reality always of correct morals.

§ 34
She never contracted debts against the rules of prudence.

Returning again a little to the administration, I must point out that no debts were ever made apart from the usual ones made with mortgages for the new buildings of the Institute. I must however add that the money obtained from the said debts the Servant of God saw to it was not used for other purposes, keeping it ready for the payment of the installments and meanwhile making it bear interest in public debt bonds; on the other hand, this system of administration was a shield against possible harassment by the state property authorities.

§ 35
Malcontents in the Institute and the innocence of the Servant of God.

Ad 25, Proc. fol. 96v.: In the Institute of the Servant of God there were, as moreover usually happens in many others, Religious who showed themselves discontented with how they were treated by the Superiors, and seeing that after making some appeals to the Servant of God they did not obtain the result they desired, they then turned directly to the Congregation of Bishops and Regulars, from which they provoked two Apostolic Visitations. Of the first I have only the news of the fact, and I do not know the particulars; certainly it had no result against the Servant of God, as is shown by the fact that shortly afterwards the decree of praise of the Institute was obtained, and then the definitive approval of the Rules. Of the second, which took place about 1893, I recall that Monsignor Domenico Serafini, now Assessor of the Holy Office, was named visitor. Also of this visitation the result was flattering for the Servant of God, who however had remained greatly afflicted because such an Apostolic visitation was a wound to the honor of her Institute. She showed herself, however, of strong and generous spirit in this contingency, and did not fail to make her own the sentiments of Jonah, saying: «If this storm has arisen on my account, put me, I beg you, aside; employ me in the humblest offices». These words she often repeated to the Sisters, and to me myself she expressed such sentiments several times.

§ 36
Humble deference of the Servant of God toward the Apostolic Visitor.

She always showed herself deferential to the Apostolic Visitor, although her humility did not allow her to declare the miraculous origin of some revenues, as I already mentioned at the last session.

The Servant of God died before the visitation was completed. The measures taken were communicated to her successor, and these measures were of little importance.

Recently, having had occasion to become acquainted with the file of this Apostolic Visitation, I found that the principal impression of the Visitor about the Servant of God was that the Servant of God had centralized too much the direction in herself. It is clear to me that the Servant of God did not fail to conform to the approved rules in what regarded her office of Superior General, always asking the opinion of her Council in the matters foreseen by the rules themselves; whose spirit, however, nobody could know better than she.

§ 37
She heroically practiced the virtues in general.

Ad 26: That the Servant of God always observed her religious and moral duties in the various states of her life from childhood, I can affirm with certainty, not only for that time in which I knew her personally, but also for the earlier time, from reports received. Bound by the Vows of obedience, poverty and chastity, she observed them with the greatest fidelity and scruple, requiring of her daughters also the most perfect observance.

The commitment she had for the observance of these three vows extended also, with great zeal, to the observance of all the rules, even the smallest; not only as regarded herself, but also her subjects.

§ 38
She heroically practiced the virtues in particular.

Ad 27: As to the virtues, both Theological and Cardinal, I can attest that she possessed them all and exercised them in an uncommon degree.

§ 39
Heroic faith.

As regards faith, she adhered with perfect attachment to all the truths revealed and proposed by the Church, and I do not doubt that she would have come to shed her blood for any of them. Such living faith moved her to take the initiative of sending her Sisters to Africa for the conversion of unbelievers and schismatics. This moved her to pray for the conversion of sinners and of unbelievers and schismatics, to pay with her person and with her blood for the faults of others, tormenting her body. This faith moved her still to declare herself unworthy of being so favored by Him.

The foundation of her Institute, dedicated to religious instruction, education, care of the sick, the care of abandoned girls, was by principle of faith. The thought of the presence of God dominated her to such a degree that she remained, I would say, absorbed, and to me myself she sometimes declared that especially after communion her union with God was very close, and sometimes when she went to confession, at the moment of absolution she no longer heard the words of the Priest, raised as if outside herself by the thought of God's goodness. And this last fact she told me to quiet her conscience, for fear of not having been present to herself for the effects to be obtained in the absolution.

§ 40
Eucharistic life.

Every day she received communion, and in order to receive it she submitted to any sacrifice it cost her. When traveling, even if she arrived at noon at her destination, she did not find herself to have broken the fast, and her first thought was to go and make her communion. For this purpose she interrupted, if necessary, the journey; if ill, she rose from bed only for this; and when in the last times, because of infirmity, she could no longer remain fasting, she sometimes availed herself of the permission to break it; yet such was her respect for the prescriptions of the Church in this regard that very few times did she avail herself of such privilege, and preferred to make the sacrifice of the fast in order to receive communion.

§ 41
Exercise of meditation and prayer.

Not only did she faithfully observe the rule of meditation, but she began it by herself in her room before the appointed time; and very often, during such exercise, she was lifted from her senses, as she herself declared to me.

I add that she did this exercise also at times during the day; indeed I can say that some days, which I would call privileged, she did nothing but this, and many nights too she spent sleepless in meditation. The preferred object in her meditations was the Passion of Our Lord, which so inflamed her spirit with love of her Beloved that she then raged against herself, scourging herself harshly, or stretching herself upon a great Cross which she had at Piacenza. As an ordinary thing, the night from Thursday to Friday she spent in meditation and penance. From the night of Holy Thursday through all of Friday she did the same, but moreover it is to be noted that she did not leave her room for all the twenty-four hours, not even to eat.

§ 42
Devotion to the Passion, to the Eternal Father and to the Eucharist.

Her favorite devotion being the Passion of Our Lord, she worked to spread it in her Institute, and it seems to me that the book she imposed as the text for meditation in her houses was the Sorrowful Year.

A special and characteristic devotion of the Servant of God was that to the Eternal Father, to whom she always turned with filial trust, and in the Institute devotion and a prayer to the Eternal Father is prescribed.

Ardent was her devotion to the Most Holy Sacrament, as already appears from what I have said about her communions. She paid Him visits as frequent as she could, and sought as she could to extend His cult in her Institute. When she had the opportunity, she heard a second Mass besides that of the Community.

During the thanksgiving she made after Communion, not seldom she was rapt from her senses, remaining motionless. When she foresaw that she would be rapt out of herself, she hurried to leave the Chapel and withdraw to her room.

In prayers in the Chapel it sometimes happened to her that she could no longer even pronounce the words, although mentally she followed them, and did violence to herself to pronounce them. The Servant of God was impressed by this, and sometimes spoke to me of it, expressing to me the fear that that exercise or practice of piety had no value for her, and I had to reassure her.

§ 43
A very special devotion to Jesus Crucified.

Proc. fol. 106: Particular also was the devotion of the Servant of God to the Crucified: to Him she had recourse in all her difficulties and anguishes, often having on her lips the words: «My Crucifix will see to it, will help me», etc. She jealously kept a wooden Christ almost fifty centimeters tall without the Cross, before whom she poured herself out, unburdening her heart in her room. Being, however, without the Cross, she kept it with a certain reserve; to me, because of the special benevolence she bore me, she gave it one evening to help me at a moment when my heart suffered some pain, almost as if she foresaw the comfort it would bring me, not failing to accompany it with her prayers. From her Crucifix the Servant of God had experienced great comforts and spiritual helps, especially in the most difficult moments for the Institute and in her interior struggles and those with demons, of which I shall speak further on.

Vaguely and confusedly I recall that the Servant of God assured that she had had sensible signs from her Crucifix in response to those prayers she made to it, and relative to the anguishes in which she found herself, making known to her beforehand the determined solution of certain facts painful to her and for which she had recourse. The events were then fully in conformity with what her Crucifix had expressed to her.

When someone had recourse to her, asking for the help of her prayers, she ordinarily answered: «I shall tell my Crucifix». In short, her Crucifix was for her the anchor for all the storms by which she was assailed. In a word, it was her all.

This Crucifix, all blackened by the kisses of the Servant of God, is now in veneration in the Generalate chapel of her Institute.

In general all that I have said so far I know by communication made to me by the Servant of God herself.

In confirmation of her devotion to the Crucifix, I learned from her Religious that she wore for a long time pressed to her breast like a hair-shirt a small metal Crucifix, which had penetrated into her flesh.

She was also devoted to the Holy Child, the Sacred Heart, the Most Precious Blood, but not in the characteristic way of the preceding ones.

§ 44
Fervent devotion to Our Lady.

Very special was the devotion of the Servant of God to the Most Holy Virgin; a devotion made more familiar to her by the daughterhood of Mary Most Holy in relation to St. Anne, whose daughters she and her Religious wished to be called. She cherished a small picture which had belonged to the Ven. Bernardo Maria Clausi, lent by Fr. Donadio, Postulator of the Cause of the said Venerable. Of this image, which has the title «Mater gratiae et misericordiae», the Servant of God had a large copy made to place on the High Altar of the new Church of her Institute in Via Merulana, which she wished dedicated to Her. Only after the death of the Servant of God could the said image return to the Minims, the Religious having however had an identical copy made, to place in their Chapel and continue through it the veneration of their venerated Mother.

In all the prayers she addressed to her God the Servant of God did not fail to join the intercession of the Most Holy Virgin. After God and the Most Holy Virgin came the special devotion to St. Anne. She promoted her cult, and wished her Institute named after her.

§ 45
Other particular devotions of the Servant of God.

She was also most devoted to St. Joseph, St. Francis of Assisi and St. Francis of Paola. These were the Saints to whom she principally turned with all trust and, I would say, familiarity, in her necessities.

On the devotion of the Servant of God to the Most Holy Virgin I return to speak, recalling that she nourished a special cult for her Immaculate Conception. For this she once went to Lourdes, had a facsimile of the miraculous Grotto made in the Church of her Institute in Via Merulana to spread the devotion. She commended herself in a special way to St. Michael, to whom she wished an altar dedicated in the Church of her Institute in Via Merulana. To these she had recourse particularly in her struggle with demons, and to St. Anne, St. Joseph and St. Francis of Assisi; these she wished as co-patrons of her Institute.

An affectionate cult she nourished also for her Guardian Angel, whom she always truly held as her guide, and especially on journeys.

§ 46
Veneration of the Pope, of Bishops and of priests out of faith.

Profound was always her veneration for the Supreme Pontiff, and her sentiments were revealed in her speaking with me and with her Religious. Toward Pius IX, however, to her veneration out of faith she joined still particular affection and devotion. She felt united to him by his virtue; to him she had turned to submit to him the idea of the foundation of her Institute, as to have from him the last word, which would have been decisive for her, holding it as the manifestation of the will of God; from him she had had approval for her idea; from him the comforting and prophetic words that her Institute would spread throughout the world with the swiftness of the flight of a dove.

The veneration she had for the Supreme Pontiff was shown also in that which she had toward his representatives, who shared in the Authority of God.

Full of respect and veneration she was likewise toward anyone who bore the priestly character.

Particular then was her veneration for her Confessors and also for her Directors, although from them she did not always receive satisfactory answers to her questions, as regards communications made to her by the Lord, on account of which her spirit remained in anguish; the Servant of God received these anguishes, however, as a trial from the Lord, and the sentiment of veneration for those who directed her was not at all weakened in her. After a long period of such anguishes the Servant of God welcomed, as a providential favor, the direction of Fr. Bernardino of Portogruaro, then Minister General of the Minors, in whom her spirit found satisfaction. This direction lasted very little for her; for the said Father, his office of Minister General having ended and he having been elected titular Bishop, withdrew from Rome to end his days elsewhere. The Servant of God suffered therefore (because of this veneration of hers toward any Ecclesiastic) when for the good running of the Houses, and to obviate some inconvenience that had occurred, she saw herself forced to take measures which could result in discredit to some Priest. Here I repeat that she took such measures with all delicacy and prudence, so that the honor of those Priests would not be injured.

§ 47
The idea of founding also an Institute of priests.

To provide her Institute definitively with a sure and permanent help, the Servant of God had conceived the idea of founding an Institute of Priests parallel to her Sisters, to provide them with Spiritual Directors, Confessors, Chaplains, etc. At first she cast her eye on the various Priests who already took an interest in and devotedly occupied themselves with her Institute, among whom also on me, who occupied myself with her Houses of Naples and the vicinity.

Proc. fol. 115: I, having come to an understanding with some Ecclesiastics of Naples who were well disposed toward the Institute of the Servant of God, there was formed at first among us a league by regular act at the Curia of Naples (having already received not only the consent but also the approval and blessing of the Most Eminent Archbishop). The purpose of this league was that we should work with prayer and with action to assist the said Institute, each however remaining in his own home. The desire and intention of the Servant of God (who was already content with this first step) was that a true and proper Religious Congregation should be founded.

To second the desires of the Servant of God, to which I adhered, I wished to ask counsel of the Holy Father Leo the Thirteenth, who however sent me back to my Archbishop. To him I presented a formal request for approval of the planned Congregation. But the Archbishop answered me: «Non expedire». Following such answer, persuaded that the will of God was that nothing should be done, I gave up occupying myself with it. The Servant of God, although obsequious to the answer of the Archbishop of Naples, did not seem to me convinced that she herself ought to renounce her project, and continued to pray for this purpose, hoping that in the future the Lord would hear her. And this desire of hers lasted until the end of her life without being comforted by any fact.

§ 48
Zeal for the house of God.

The zeal of the Servant of God for the House of the Lord, besides having to be inferred from all the things I have already said, is made manifest by the facts that the Churches of her Institute shone with cleanliness; by the fact that the Sisters busied themselves in providing all that was necessary not only for the cult, but also for the elegance of the cult; by the fact that many gave gifts to her Churches because they believed they were doing something pleasing also to the Superior; by the general upkeep of her Churches and Chapels, from which her solicitous care is gathered in choosing personnel fit for the office of Sacristan.

§ 49
Manifestations of firm hope and trust in God.

The Servant of God possessed in an eminent degree also the virtue of Hope. In all her life, all her work was always directed to pleasing God in this life, and then to possessing Him forever in the other.

This Hope she also infused in her Religious while she was forming them, to whom she always pointed to Paradise as the ultimate goal. In herself, however, she had no trust whatever, but it was all placed in the Blood and the merits of Jesus.

§ 50
Exercise of the virtue of hope in trials.

Not only was she resigned in all the trials she had to suffer, which moreover were continual, but she received them with generosity of soul, acknowledged them as deserved by her unworthiness; I do not know whether she ever prayed that they be lightened, but she always showed herself in this perfectly conformed to the will of God, convinced that the trials came to her because of her demerits; the stronger such trials were, the more she raged against herself with penances, seeking to appease the Lord. In these circumstances of trials, she sometimes wrote to me, and more often spoke to me in person, asking to be allowed to use her harsh penances, that is, the discipline to blood.

Knowing that this harmed her physically, being in continual fasts and the other penances which she also continually made, I was reluctant to satisfy her, but her thirst to suffer was so great, and she knew so well how to manifest it, that I saw myself forced to yield in part.

§ 51
Detachment from temporal things.

From temporal things she was perfectly detached, and her heart never ran after money. For the needs of the Institute, however, she did not hesitate to go begging and, made strong by her unlimited trust in the Lord, she faced all the humiliations that are met in such circumstances. God, however, largely compensated the humiliations she had in the said collections, providing for her very often more than the urgent need.

Although she made use of men, her exclusive trust was however in God, considering them only as ministers of His providence, spiritual or temporal.

§ 52
Heroic and firm trust in God.

When the local Superiors of any of her Houses laid their difficulties before her, she directed them straightaway to the Lord, seeking to infuse in them the most unlimited trust in Him. I remember well that in the first times of her foundation in Naples her Religious, worn out by the fatigue of assisting the sick day and night, and increasing in number to provide for the ever greater requests for assistance, often recommended themselves to the Servant of God that she should provide them with lodging more suited to their Religious Life, and also to hygiene; for it must be well noted that at first in Naples they had no house of their own, but lived in rented quarters. The habitual answer of the Servant of God was constantly this: «Have trust in God: He will provide for us». The Servant of God changed rented quarters five times, always having present in her thought the idea of having a house of her own. The small providence had never failed her House of Naples, and finally, the Servant of God having a small sum available, the Lord inspired a benefactor to add the rest to make their settlement definitive, with a house of their own and a garden.

To the sick and to all who turned to her, finding themselves in anguish, she always pointed to her God.

§ 53
Charity toward God: far from faults, even slight ones.

Most ardent was her love for God, whom she always guarded with every solicitude against displeasing, even by the lightest fault. Sometimes she confided to me that she found herself embarrassed in searching for faults to accuse to the Confessor. Out of her charity she expiated with harsh penances her presumed faults and those of others, so that the anger of the Lord might be calmed.

In conversing with her I always had to note her great love for God, although she did nothing to manifest it to me, being always reserved in her words, in her behavior, in every act of hers. This reserve of hers was constant with everyone, and she made her hiddenness a continual object of her prayer, as she told me, so that no one could have known what flame of charity burned in her heart if he had not known the continuity of her acts and the results of her works.

Her charity toward God moved her to prompt correction also of the defects of her Religious.

She did not spare measures necessary to avoid inconveniences, even if they were painful to her heart. Charity toward God made her afflicted when she came to know of grave faults of others.

Charity moved her to knock constantly at the Heart of God for her son and for the brother whom she knew to be far from God, as I have already reported.

§ 54
Her spiritual instructions, proof of her charity.

Her charity toward God moved her in the conferences to her Religious, when she instructed them on prayer, she exhorted them to regular discipline, interpreting successively all the points of the rule. In a word, God was the One who occupied her whole heart. God, however, to His faithful Servant who loved Him so much, made her heart ever more ardent toward Him. And she herself told me that it seemed to her at times that her heart swelled and her ribs dilated, and she felt constrained to pray the Lord to lessen somewhat the effects of those ardors toward Him. Ordinarily in the Servant of God nothing extraordinary was seen, as I have already said. Only when she came out of her room after those extraordinary recollections in it for reason of prayer or penances, I had occasion to notice her, and with me the other Religious, pale in the face and swollen to such a degree, also in the hands, that she could not hold, for some short time, even the pen to write.

§ 55
Charity toward neighbor.

To the charity of God so ardent in her heart there corresponded, as a perfect reflection, charity for neighbor. Proof of it is the foundation of her Institute, wholly devoted to the care of neighbor, indeed having as a means of sanctification the care of neighbor, bodily and moral.

I now remember a little episode which was reported to me by the Religious themselves. The Servant of God having arrived on the occasion of her visits at a hospital run by her daughters, and no comfortable place being found to let her rest, she set herself to assist a dying woman, and stayed at her bedside until death. When that poor woman had died, the body was removed, and the Servant of God, not minding that she had died of plague, and not asking that even the linen be changed, lay down in the same bed and slept there.

§ 56
Spiritual and temporal works of charity.

Proc. fol. 125: It sometimes happened that, having known by supernatural light that some of her Religious were not wholly at peace with God, in the admonitions and corrections she gave them she did not expose them to the disesteem of others, but gave them privately, opening their eyes to their spiritual state with much charity and generally with happy result. Concerning these supernatural lights which the Servant of God received about the spiritual state of her Religious, I can add that sometimes there was found one who, to the maternal corrections and exhortations of the Servant of God, answered by denying being at fault. The subsequent facts however always showed that the Servant of God had not been deceived by her own imagination, since it happened that the Religious who had denied the facts charged to her by the Servant of God committed some excess which fully justified what the Servant of God had said to her.

She prayed much for sinners and, as I have already said, mortified herself with harsh penances. To whoever asked her for prayers, having trust in her, she did not refuse them.

The Servant of God took a personal interest that at the door of the Houses of the Institute in which she was, care should be taken to give alms to the poor who presented themselves.

From the offenses that others had done her, she did not feel touched; she received them for love of the Lord; it is therefore not even the case to ask whether she forgave them.

§ 57
Charity toward the souls in purgatory and the dead.

Most devoted to the souls in Purgatory, she aided them with her prayers, with penances, and also with Mass offerings.

When one of her Religious died, she was at once informed of it by a sort of star, more or less large, more or less luminous, according as the deceased was a Superior or a subject, more in need of suffrages or less. Some of these had expressly asked the Servant of God for her suffrages. She told her Sisters that a Religious had died, and the official announcement from the houses of the deceased followed the words of the Servant of God. Then the customary suffrages introduced by the Servant of God were performed by the Communities.

At times the Servant of God, at a certain point, saw as it were black, frightful spots, and her spirit was led to recognize in them the approaching appearance of some scourge, and especially epidemics. She herself spoke to me about this at times, before any news was had of the facts that justified her forecasts. To these forecasts of hers I never gave great weight, and only afterwards was I surprised by the coincidence of the facts with them. When the Servant of God had these forecasts, she worked with prayers and penances to avert the scourges of the Lord. When, however, the chastisement of the Lord came down notwithstanding her prayers, she sent her Religious to assist those struck by the disease, and as far as she could, sought to satisfy the many requests of the Municipalities for their lazarettos and for other assistance to the sick. It need not be said with what zeal she encouraged her Sisters to the exercise of such charity!

§ 58
Kindness and courtesy, expression of her great charity.

Finally, as a complement to her charity, I shall say that the Servant of God never failed in the forms of kindness and courtesy that are due on the occasion of visits by outsiders, and also with her subordinates. When, however, in her conversations during visits the talk became vain or frivolous, it was seen that she remained absorbed in higher thoughts and became a stranger to the conversation.

To the question whether the Servant of God always made useful use of her time, I can answer only affirmatively; indeed she led a most laborious life.

Not only in the affairs of the Institute did the Servant of God follow the rules approved for her Institute, asking the opinion of her council, but I remember well that often she asked mine too.

§ 59
Heroic in the exercise of prudence and justice.

Prudence was also seen in the happy effects of the measures she took. In dealing with the civil authorities she always showed herself prudent and firm. In her zeal for the good of souls she never let herself be carried away by excessive ardor. She never violated justice. I remember well, from a report received, that she was accused and dragged into court by a Priest, as if she had violated the contracts made between her and him, with the due authorizations, relating to a work of charity for which the Servant of God had been invited to provide the assistance of her daughters. The Servant of God came out of that Process, however, in full triumph, both on the civil side and on the part of the Ecclesiastical Authority, which at first had given credence to the Priest.

With her there was no acceptance of persons, and she did not tolerate this defect in her Religious.

§ 60
Fortitude and temperance in difficult occasions.

To those who took an interest in her Institute, to those who did her good, both spiritual and temporal, she showed a most lively gratitude.

In the punishments and reproofs to her Sisters she never showed anger or was carried away by indignation, but always by the good of their souls.

By temperament the Servant of God, as I knew her, was neither lively nor phlegmatic, but calm, with that calm joined to resolution and firmness. This firmness was always put to the test through so many difficulties of her life, but these were the cause of this virtue of hers shining all the more, being perfected. Her firmness and her prudence were put to a hard test before a highly placed Ecclesiastical person.

It is my absolute wish that what I am about to narrate remain under the most reserved secrecy possible.

The personage to whom I alluded was Cardinal Verga, Prefect of Bishops and Regulars, and Protector of the Institute. He had done much good to the Institute. The Servant of God showed herself most grateful to him. Unfortunately it happened that he felt inclined to preferences toward a young Religious endowed with fine natural qualities. Whereas at first the Cardinal was in perfect agreement with Mother Gattorno, from whom he received communications even of intimate and spiritual matters (for the Servant of God then held him as a providence sent to her by the Lord), the Cardinal's preferences toward that Religious to whom I have alluded above reached such a point that he gave credence to her in everything she told him, even though it was in opposition to what was asserted to him by the Mother.

§ 61
An episode, example of the heroic prudence of the Servant of God.

Proc. fol. 133v.: The Servant of God groaned in her heart, for she perceived that the preferences to which the Cardinal felt inclined were not moved by the spirit of God, and also because the fact gave occasion to unedifying admiration on the part of her Religious, it being too manifest. It is not to be said that the Servant of God saw in the said fact anything grave in itself, but she feared the consequences that might result for those two souls and for her whole Community. The religious in question belonged to the Secretariat of the Servant of God herself: she had a great part in the matters of singing for the Church, and was active in everything. Given these circumstances, I think that the Servant of God did not judge it opportune to take radical measures, such as the transfer of the Religious, which would have brought shame upon the Cardinal and made people believe, or at least suspect, grave matters which really did not exist. The Servant of God did not fail, however, to make the Religious in question understand that her conduct could not please the Lord, nor her, and she took an attitude of such marked reserve toward the Cardinal, in the presence of other Religious, in everything concerning this fact, as to make her whole Community see clearly how much she disapproved of it. Neither the observations of the Servant of God to the Religious, however, nor all her demeanor availed to make the matter cease; on the contrary, it seemed to the Religious that she was the object of unjust observations, and for this reason too she sought greater protection from the Cardinal. The anguishes of the Servant of God relating to this fact are manifest to me because she herself spoke to me of them, asking my advice. That the Servant of God, not discerning in that fact, so painful to her, the spirit of the Lord, did not oppose without reason, is evident from the fact that that Religious, not long after, left the Institute.

p. 34

I wish, however, to point out, for the honor of that poor Religious, that even after leaving the Institute she kept a conduct always regular and keeps it still in the married state she embraced. There followed upon this fact also an Apostolic visitation, but I do not know what relations of cause or effect there may be between this and the visitation.

§ 62
She loved and diligently practiced chastity.

She was a jealous guardian of the virtue of Chastity. When she heard of facts contrary to this virtue, there came from her mouth words that clearly showed all her inner and profound horror. It need not be said, then, how much she inculcated it on her Religious, how solicitous she was to remove from her Communities everything that might even remotely offend it; and the promptness she had, when she noticed anything contrary, in taking energetic measures, and if necessary, even expelling from the Institute whoever it might be. Her love for this virtue reached such a point that she strictly forbade her Sisters to allow doctors to touch her body in case of any illness. The doctors therefore had to limit themselves to feeling her pulse, and when she was at times swollen, and the need of further examination was evident, they had to go away, abandoning themselves to conjectures. And her illnesses were indeed frequent. The causes were well known to her most of the time, coming from the harsh government she exercised over herself. It need not be said in what way she tolerated her infirmities; even then her spirit did not detach itself from mortification; although knowing that her sufferings would have been relieved by some medicine or food, she did not have recourse to them, and if offered, did not make use of them. Habitually the Servant of God took neither meat, nor broth, nor milk. Her food was legumes, eggs, salt cod or other ordinary fish and herbs with oil, which at times she sought to make less tasty. A Religious related that, having wished one day to taste a remnant of a dish of the Servant of God, her mouth was left all embittered; the life of the Servant of God as regards food was in short a continual and harsh Lent.

The quantity of her food was most limited. In the morning, a simple black and bitter coffee. Other details will be told by other witnesses.

§ 63
Spirit of evangelical poverty.

The poverty of the Servant of God was not limited to the observance of the simple vow, but she carried it to the point of suffering from it. The bed, which for the greater part of the nights was only for show, and when it served her, she used it for a few hours (she used it habitually only when she felt exhausted by her penances), consisted of a simple sack of corn husks, without mattress. This bed, which served her so rarely, the Servant of God took care to leave unmade in the morning.

§ 64
Diabolical apparitions.

Almost every night the Servant of God was molested by apparitions of demons. They presented themselves to her in various monstrous and ugly forms; at times they pulled the bedclothes off her bed; they leaned on the bars of the bed itself; they knocked at the door, at the window, made threats to her; if she did not heed them, they tried to frighten her, calling her damned, and at times threatened to throw her out of the window. The habitual answer of the Servant of God was recourse to her Crucifix or to the harshest penances. From this she received relief for her spirit; the demons disappeared at the moment, and the Servant of God, however, remained exhausted of strength. Such molestations lasted a great part of the night.
