I heard from her Religious that very often they heard the noises in the room of the Servant of God, and sometimes the Sister who was assigned to her person, and who slept near her room, on hearing those noises approached the door of the room to ask whether she had called or needed anything.

Having a horror of singularity that might attract the admiration of anyone, the Servant of God could not show herself poorer in her clothes than the others, but in these she conformed perfectly to the way of dressing of her Religious. She inculcated this virtue on her daughters, and as she had no acceptance of persons for any quality, so neither had she it for social standing, nor did she permit other local Superiors to have it.

§ 65
Obedient to God and to superiors.

Obedience: A spirit so united to the Lord, so scornful of self and of the things of the earth, it is no wonder that it was also united to the will of her Superiors, first the Pope, then the Bishops, and her spiritual Directors. In the lines of conduct which God directly traced for her in her interior communications, the Servant of God stopped when the authority of Superiors or spiritual Directors showed itself contrary. In these cases the Servant of God felt the duty, especially when it was a matter of the affairs of the Institute, to set forth candidly and with submission her observations, leaving however free the will of the Superior. The subsequent facts, I note here, always came to prove the Servant of God right, when her ideas had not been willingly adhered to. Her obedience extended also to small things. I recall that on the occasion of a grave illness of hers I searched in my mind for what I could suggest to her to relieve her. None of the many things I thought of, and which I indicated to the Servant of God, such as broth, milk, etc., met with her adherence, because they clashed with her habitual system of most mortified diet, and I did not insist, because I recognized that this was true. After the illness, however, the Servant of God confessed to me that she understood then that a little milk would have done her good, and that if I had commanded it of her, then indeed she would have taken it. This fact demonstrates the spirit of mortification and of constant obedience in her.

§ 66
Practice of humility and love of hiddenness.

Of the humility of the Servant of God it suffices to recall what I declared about her love of hiddenness. If someone pointed out to her that by her special qualities she could do this or that thing, the Servant of God felt all confused and declared that she was good for nothing, a she-donkey, fit only for the vilest offices. When she knew that honors were being prepared for her by her Religious or by the administrations by which they had been called, the Servant of God felt, in her humility, the need to avoid them. While on the other hand she worked to celebrate and honor others, above all when they were deserving of the Institute.

§ 67
In service of the sick in the lowliest tasks.

Proc. fol. 143v.: It was reported to me that the Servant of God, going at times to the Hospitals, served the sick even in the lowliest and humblest tasks. To her Religious she then inculcated, as all virtues, also the love of this one, humility.

Questioned on the origin of the photograph reproduced by the Postulator in his articles, I declare that I do not know its origin. I know from my own knowledge the most absolute and decided repugnance of the Servant of God to being photographed. Because of the good relations that bound me to the Institute, in vacation time, passing through Rome and staying in their house, I asked to be able to take photographs of groups of Sisters with the cameras I carried with me. She allowed it for the Sisters, but I never managed to take a photograph of her, not even by surprise. As a general rule, moreover, she never permitted her Daughters to be photographed, except those leaving for America, or in some other exceptional circumstance.

In all the virtues the Servant of God always went on growing until death.

§ 68
Heroic in the exercise of the virtues in general.

Ad 28: I do not doubt the heroism of the Theological virtues of the Servant of God, and of her Cardinal virtues, as well as of mortification, humility, chastity, poverty, obedience. This heroism is manifestly proved by the grave difficulties generously overcome by the Servant of God, by the extraordinary harshness of her penances, in which she evidently showed the desire to be wholly a victim of her God, as it might please Him. It is proved by her ardent love and effort to hide herself, by having governed with happy result her whole very numerous Institute to the end of her life. On the matter of hiddenness I recall having noticed in the Servant of God the effort she made to hide herself from the eyes of all. It is proved still by her never having given way in her fervor, not even in the times of aridity of spirit which it also pleased the Lord to send her; in a word, her heroism is proved by all that I have narrated.

§ 69
She practiced the virtues and penance without exaggeration.

Ad 29: It does not seem to me that it can in any way be doubted that the Servant of God sinned by excess in the exercise of her virtues. If I were to observe any excess in the Servant of God, it would be that of her penances, and I pointed it out to her myself at times, telling her to think of her obligation to preserve her health for her Institute. The Servant of God, however, answered me that her penances did not prevent her from attending to her duties and discharging them. And the facts have shown that she was quite right, since she always attended to and discharged her office perfectly, and ended her days at an advanced age.

§ 70
Supernatural gifts: visions, ecstasies.

Ad 30: I have already said how the Servant of God knew the interior of her Daughters, and the spiritual needs of some of her Houses, by supernatural lights.

It now comes to my mind that I heard from a Religious, the present Superior at Florence, that, being Superior in I do not know which other House, in order to receive the Servant of God worthily, who was going to visit that House, without saying a word to anyone, she contracted some small debts. When the Servant of God had arrived and visited the House, before leaving she said to the Superior: «It was really worth making debts for this!». The Religious was astounded because of the secret she had kept with everyone.

The Servant of God also had from her Lord, from the Most Holy Virgin and from the Saints sensible communications, as regards her spirit, in response to graces she asked or to doubts in which she found herself concerning her spirit and her Institute.

The Servant of God sometimes remained, and more often after Communion, rapt out of her senses, so as not to notice all that surrounded her; yet nothing showed outwardly.

In the sensible communications of which I have spoken, the Lord, the Virgin and the Saints appeared to her personally, and the Lord permitted also that there appear to her visibly her daughter, Sr. Anna of the Savior, who died in the odor of sanctity, to whom the Servant of God had turned as intermediary with Him, and she brought her the answer.

When the Servant of God spoke to me at times of these facts, I absolutely exclude that she did so out of ostentation or vainglory.

Of some of her Religious the Servant of God had a particular esteem for their union with God, and I am persuaded that these, in their turn, will have had exceptional knowledge of the value of the spirit of the Servant of God, and among these I could cite Sr. Anna Maria Teresa Patti, Superior in a House at Palermo, Sr. Anna Serafina, Sacristan in the Church of the Mother House.

§ 71
Recourse to prayer to obtain healings.

Ad 31: Of miracles worked by the Servant of God in her lifetime, I know none. I recall, however, that she, when asked for prayers to obtain healings, prayed, and gave some oil which she called the oil of the Eternal Father, toward whom, as I have already said, she nourished special devotion. And the sick many times were healed.

Ad 32: Besides what I have already said about the writings of the Servant of God, I know nothing else, except that there exist many letters, of which a good number addressed to me, and the rest to other persons, especially of her Institute. To her distant daughters, and when she knew that some of them, because of anguish of spirit, needed particular assistance, the Servant of God wrote in her own hand. All these letters and the other writings have been gathered in the Mother House for the search that will be made by the Sacred Congregation of Rites.

§ 72
Spiritual and apostolic value of the writings of the Servant of God.

As regards the writings of the Servant of God, those that attract my attention in a special way are those of which I spoke in my first deposition, for which I myself encouraged her. They are like her diary, interrupted only when her journeys and visits to the Houses prevented her from continuing it. As they have attracted my attention, so I believe that they deserve to attract the attention of the Tribunal of the S. Congregation of Rites. For me they have a real value of truth because of the serious, frank, unexalted and simple character of the Servant of God, and as confirmed by the partial knowledge of the facts that I had. I say partial because the diary dates from a time earlier than that in which I knew the Servant of God, and because I myself was not continually in contact with her, having in this time knowledge only from the reading of her writings.

On the occasion of the publication of the book of the Servant of God with the title «Travagli e conforti, etc.» [«Labors and Consolations»], the Most Eminent Cardinal Guarino and Canon Pennino noted, with wonder, that the Servant of God had not divided her work into chapters or with chronological dates. This is for me a confirmation of what I asserted in the first session, namely that in that book it was not a question of a history of a soul or of a direction for a soul. Her history, instead, is found in this diary of hers, in which in fact the chronological division is then found.

I mentioned earlier the trustworthiness of this diary of hers also because of the simplicity of her character. In the contact I had with the Servant of God, I became persuaded that she was completely alien to any artifice, to hiding second intentions, and I always knew her frank, upright, loyal.

§ 73
The gift of the stigmata.

Ad 33, Proc. fol. 153v.: Reading the writings of the Servant of God I understood the allusions which she herself sometimes made to me, in a vague way, to the gift of the Stigmata which the Lord had granted her. This gift was in some way confirmed to me by a Religious, to whom the following fact happened, which I already knew from the writings of the Servant of God. This Religious, having to leave for the Missions of America, was greatly afflicted, although disposed to do the will of God, because she feared she did not have the qualities sufficient to discharge the offices to which she would be assigned there. The Servant of God, who did not intend to oblige the Religious (as no other) to go to the Missions, wished to comfort her Religious and give her confirmation of the will of God. «Well then — she said to her one day, on which she was favored with the gift of the Stigmata — I shall give you a memento». With this she gave her her hand. The Religious, at the touch of the hand of the Servant of God, felt in her own a most lively pain and in the same act felt herself wholly revived inwardly and comforted to make that journey, persuaded that it was the will of God. She is Sr. A. Camilla Valentini, Assistant General, who in America afterward did immense good.

§ 74
Death and funeral of the Servant of God.

The death of the Servant of God occurred in May of nineteen hundred; but I do not know the particulars, being then at the Nunciature of Belgium.

When I had occasion to speak with the Sisters, who communicated to me some detail which I do not now remember about the death of the Servant of God, I do not recall that they told me anything extraordinary. Only this I know: that the Sister assigned to the person of the Servant of God, before the others charged with caring for the body of the same Servant of God, took care to remove from the waist of the Servant of God the chain which for so many years had constantly girded her. The said Religious found it all embedded in the flesh. One can imagine how much the Servant of God had to suffer from it, being in general in her illnesses swollen from anemia, which I would say was her natural state.

When the Servant of God had too much to suffer from this chain, feeling herself fail, on any pretext she withdrew to her room and did not take it off; only once in her life, I believe, had she loosened it. I must note that already before I knew her the Servant of God had girded herself with that chain.

Sr. Anna Serafina took care to remove the said chain, without the other Sisters seeing her girded, because she knew well the love of the Servant of God for hiddenness, for which she had received an order not to manifest her extraordinary things to anyone.

p. 41

Ad 35: The Servant of God, after the funeral held in their Church in Via Merulana, was buried in the mortuary Chapel of the Institute at Campo Verano and placed at the entrance door, with an epigraph inscribed on it, which I do not now remember.

Ad 36: I do not know that on the occasion of the funeral and at the tomb of the Servant of God there was ever any sign of cult, and I believe that, if there had been, I would have known.

Ad 37: Once I was at the Sepulcher of the Servant of God. I know that other persons, benefactors of the Institute and acquaintances of the Servant of God, went to the same Sepulcher, but I do not know whether to offer suffrage or to commend themselves to the Servant of God. Naturally her Religious go there frequently, have Masses celebrated in her suffrage at the Altar of the little mortuary Chapel and commend themselves also to her intercession.

§ 75
Venerated in life and after death.

Ad 38: In the circle in which she lived and in her relations, the Servant of God was esteemed by me, and was esteemed by others, as a woman of extraordinary virtue, and this esteem has been preserved after death until today, spreading ever more. And this esteem, I must note, was not produced by any artifice. I note further that of the persons who esteemed the Servant of God, there were not and are not only those who are easy to esteem and to believe, but also very serious and authoritative persons. I for my part judge the virtue of the Servant of God to be that of a Saint, and I hope that this judgment of mine will be confirmed by God with miracles of the first order through the intercession of His Servant.

Ad 39: Of persons opposed to the Process of Beatification of the Servant of God I know only one high dignitary well known to this Tribunal.

§ 76
Permanent fame of sanctity.

Ad 40: Of miracles and graces of the Servant of God after death nothing is known to me personally. I have however heard them spoken of many times by her Religious, who gave me the details, which I do not now remember. Having asked them whether they had provided themselves with medical certificates, I had in reply that in the most important cases they had been able to obtain only the diagnoses, the doctors refusing to declare that the cure was beyond the forces of nature. Moreover, some of these favored persons are still living. quod Servae Dei mortua sit ab intestato,

§ 77
The Servant of God did not die «ab intestato».

Respondit: It is not true. Indeed it is known to me that several months before her death she made a regular will by the hand of the Notary Tommaso Monti here in Rome. I know further that as a prudential measure, and at an unsuspected time, the Servant of God had been divesting herself of the title to property of several Houses of the Institute.

WITNESS II
Sr. ANNA FABIANA ORSI

Scope in the process: From Sess. 198 of 13 May 1913 (fol. 168v) to Sess. 283 of 28 May 1913 (fol. 248).

Name, surname, date and place of birth: Veronica Orsi, born about 1846 at Albareto, district of Borgotaro.

State and profession: Religious in the Institute of the «Daughters of St. Anne», mistress of novices.

Quality of the witness: Eyewitness.

Age of the witness when she met the Servant of God: 29 years.

Age of the Servant of God when the witness met her: 44 years.

Age of the witness at the time of the deposition: 67 years.

Length of acquaintance and its motivation: From 1875, the date of her entrance into the Institute founded by the Servant of God, until the latter's death (1900), the witness was in continual contact with Gattorno, for a total of 25 years.

Observations on the witness, on the scope and on the content of the deposition: The witness's effort to answer all the questions fully is remarkable, even those for which her knowledge is indirect; consequently in the latter the witness reports generic information, learned from other persons. For this reason the answers to the questions from no. 9 to no. 21 are omitted.

Once her direct knowledge comes into play in the interrogatories, the characteristic depth is at once noticed: it suffices to read the reconstruction of how Gattorno carried out the role of Superior General, displaying among other things a truly maternal solicitude for all her daughters. As regards the fulfillment of duties, the witness is persuaded that the Servant of God faithfully respected her commitments as daughter, wife, widow and religious. In the examination of the individual virtues the deposition is further enriched, exhibiting detailed proofs that justify the judgment of heroism that accompanies them all; the proofs concerning the supernatural gifts, the writings, the events before, during and after death, and the proofs of a fame of sanctity always in force also deserve due emphasis.

The witness concludes her precious contribution to the Cause by confirming and enriching the content of numerous articles.

Ad 2 interr., Proc. fol. 171v., testis respondit:

§ 78
General particulars of the witness.

My name in Religion is Anna Fabiana Orsi; in the world I was called Veronica.

I was born at Albareto, district of Borgotaro, about the year 1846 (I do not remember the date precisely), of the late Angelo and Domenica Mussi.

I entered religion in 1875 and two years later made the profession of temporary vows, and after some time of perpetual vows. For eight years I have held the office of Mistress of novices.

I was for one year portress of this house, and for fifteen years Superior of the assistant Sisters of the Clinic in Via Garibaldi.

§ 79
Scope of knowledge.

Ad 7: Before entering Religion I had already heard of Mother Gattorno, but I did not know her until I entered Religion, she herself having received me in the House of Piacenza.

All that I shall depose will not be for having read it in some writing of the Servant of God, or in printed matter about her, but for having heard it from other consisters of mine, or because known to me personally.

Ad 8: I feel lively affection, veneration and devotion for my Foundress. Certainly I should be very glad if she were canonized by Holy Church, for the greater glory of God and also for the luster of our Institute, and also because it would be an encouragement for us Sisters to follow her in her virtues. For the rest, however, I adhere to whatever Holy Church shall decide in this regard.

Ad 22: I know that the Servant of God was always Superior General of her Institute, and this against her will.

§ 80
She did not like being superior, out of sentiments of humility.

From the time I entered among her Daughters I noticed that the Servant of God was not willingly in that office of Superior General, and not because of the great deal to do, but out of a sentiment of humility. In this office, as far as I was able to know, the Servant of God was exemplary, and I noticed no defect in the fulfillment of the inherent duties.

I have heard it said that the Servant of God at the beginning of the foundation of her Institute was much criticized by ill-disposed persons because she received very young personnel, but it seems to me quite unjustly.

§ 81
Balanced, prudent, watchful government.

The Servant of God occupied herself with solicitude about disciplinary observance and for this reason not only watched over the house where she resided, but also visited the others with zeal. At times she wrote not only to the Superiors, but also to simple Religious, as she did also to me a couple of times; exhorting, encouraging, comforting. If she noticed any lapse in observance, she made herself heard, yet she was not harsh, although she did not yield.

Although it is not its place, I shall now tell a fact that comes to my mind. One day the Servant of God came to me when I was Superior of the surgical Clinic in Via Garibaldi (now passed to the Polyclinic), urgently asking me for the Sister who kept the accounts of the clinic, and telling me that she had to take her away from me. Not knowing how I could make up for that Sister, I pleaded as effectively as I could that she leave her to me. She not wishing, however, to yield to my entreaties, I brought in the Secretary General, Sr. Anna Celsa, and then the Servant of God: «Very well, I shall yield — she said to me — but know that within three or four days you will lose her. Make no fuss; when you have lost her, come to me». We were in Holy Week, on the Tuesday or Wednesday of Holy Week, and on Easter Sunday I no longer found her in the house, she having left the Institute. I cannot imagine that the Servant of God knew by other ways the state of mind of that Religious, except by supernatural way. It must be well noted also that the said Religious had given me no displeasure and no sign of the lost vocation. She seemed on the contrary very pious.

Once, the Servant of God having sent some Religious to Africa, immediately afterward she sent a telegram to the Superior of her Religious, saying to her: «Send me back at once the Religious who has black hair and black eyes whom I have just sent you: I do not remember her name: I made a mistake in sending her to you». The local Superior had noticed nothing abnormal in that Religious; she put herself on guard to discover something and found her of somewhat light behavior with the soldiers. She sent her back to Italy, but unfortunately here, having continued in her lightness, she left the Institute. This fact I learned from the Religious who accompanied her, who returned to Africa, Sr. Ernestina Lepri, present Superior at Pontremoli.

§ 82
Absence of personal preferences in government.

The Servant of God, in assigning to offices, sought the aptitude of the Sisters and paid no heed to qualities not related to the office. She had no preferences for any natural gift or quality, or for riches which one might hope would come to the Community through someone. Her intention was directed to God.

§ 83
Care for the spiritual and material good of the religious and of other persons.

Proc. fol. 181v.: The Servant of God was not only solicitous for the spiritual good of her Religious, but also took every care that nothing necessary should be lacking to them, and wished that the other local Superiors too should watch over this point. She was especially tender toward the sick, having them cared for as well as she could, and in the conferences she gave us she strongly recommended the care of the sick Sisters, and likewise recommended them to the local Superiors. When they then grew worse, and I myself noticed it, she was solicitous that they be provided with religious comforts. And such solicitude she required equally of the local Superiors for their subjects.

Ad 23: The Servant of God did not spread her Institute by sending her Sisters here and there uninvited, and did not seek other new houses, but only, if invited, agreed, if she had personnel available.

The solicitude of the Servant of God for spiritual and temporal things was not limited to her Religious, but extended also to all who were entrusted to the care of her Sisters: to the sick, that they might be comforted and provided with the Sacraments in case of need; to the girls received for education, for their religious and civil instruction; that nothing necessary should be lacking to anyone.

§ 84
She never neglected her duties as a mother.

Ad 24: The Servant of God, having left the world, devoted herself wholly to her Institute, not however in such a way as to forget completely her daughter, who, living in a house adjoining this one, came frequently to the Servant of God. In these circumstances the Religious showed every solicitude in a thousand attentions toward the poor deaf-mute daughter, and also toward her brother Federico, who also came on some rare occasions. These attentions displeased the Servant of God, who therefore reproved them, so that they found themselves obliged to do behind the back of the Servant of God herself what they wished to do for the relatives of their mother.

p. 46

§ 85
The Apostolic Visitation, a source of afflictions for the Servant of God.

Ad 25: I know that an Apostolic visitation took place in our Institute (I know of only one), made by Monsignor Serafini, by whom I was called. I do not know the reason for that visitation; I know and remember that at that time the Servant of God was very afflicted, but I do not know whether for this reason. I recall likewise that the Servant of God gave no instruction on how to behave and speak with the Visitor (at least to me she certainly gave no instruction), and forbade the Secretaries to give me too any instruction on the matter, and I think that this prohibition applied to all. I do not know whether any measures were taken concerning this Apostolic visitation. I believe that the Visitor remained content, as the Secretaries told me.

§ 86
She exemplarily observed her duties.

Ad 26: I am persuaded that the Servant of God observed the commandments of God and the precepts of the Church with diligence, also before I knew her, and was faithful to her duties as daughter, wife, widow and finally Religious. This persuasion I formed from the exemplariness of her life in the time that I knew her, from the exhortations full of conviction which she made to us, for it is well to know that almost every Sunday she convoked all the Religious to instruct and exhort them about their religious duties, about the duties of how to conduct themselves with the sick, in short in everything she thought opportune for them. So I myself verified in that year in which I was portress of this House. And in this time I noted the exemplariness of the observance of the rules by the Servant of God, thus giving herself the example of what she taught us. Also with Circulars she exhorted or corrected the Sisters of the various Houses about religious observance.

§ 87
A most lively faith and the practice of it.

Ad 27: The faith of the Servant of God extended to all that the Church teaches, and was most lively, as can be gathered not only from the instructions and exhortations she gave to the Sisters, but above all from the love she had for suffering.

One day, having come to this House to her, I do not know whether the solicitude of other persons to lighten her Cross was being spoken of, but this I well remember, that she said to me: «I would not wish anyone to touch this Cross which I bear». Never have I heard from the Servant of God, and never have I known as reported to me by others, that she complained of her Cross or lamented persons who made her suffer.

§ 88
Ready to give her blood for the faith.

Her faith can be gathered also from the desire which I heard she expressed to give her blood for the same faith. Her faith is manifested still by the prayers which she made or had her Religious make for the conversion of unbelievers and sinners; and by having welcomed with great pleasure the occasion to send her Religious to America and Africa for the unbelievers and non-Catholics, and for the spiritual good of the Eritrean colony.

Her faith is shown by the foundation of her Institute for the care of the sick and for the instruction of youth, and especially of the poor class, which she recommended in a particular way.

§ 89
Devotions of the Servant of God, expression of her great faith.

Great was her devotion to the Most Holy Sacrament. In Church she was seen motionless, and no noise succeeded in distracting her during any exercise of piety. She received communion every day and prolonged her acts of thanksgiving at length. The Servant of God could do this because she heard Mass in the Chapel on the first floor together with her Secretaries, and did not go down to the Church of St. Anne together with the whole Community, perhaps because she was always suffering in health.

Communion was so dear to her that never any day did she wish to omit it, neither by reason of any illness, however grave, nor because of the hardships of travel, in which she preferred to remain fasting until after twelve so as not to deprive herself of Holy Communion.

Devoted to the Most Holy Trinity, she was so in a special way to the Eternal Father, and established the month of January to be honored in a special way by her Religious, to whom likewise she prescribed a prayer to be said every day.

§ 90
A very particular devotion to the Passion of the Lord.

She loved the Crucifix tenderly. In her words and in her letters there were unfailingly these: «My Crucifix [...]».

A Crucifix she wore over her heart, adhering to the flesh; I have heard it said that she wore it five years, and that it penetrated into her flesh, as I heard from several Sisters and among others from Sr. Serafina, assigned to the Servant of God. This Crucifix she took off, although it greatly displeased her, before taking to bed for her last illness.

As a consequence of her love for the Crucifix, she had likewise devotion to the Passion of Our Lord, and prescribed various exercises of piety to her Religious for this.

On Fridays, in memory of the Passion of our Lord, she stayed withdrawn in her room, in prayer, and at Piacenza I know that she suspended herself on a wooden Cross which the Sisters do not know how she could have brought into the room, so large was it. In this room, where she had this Cross (it stood immediately beneath the ceiling), she allowed no one to enter; and the Religious entered it only after her death. On the arms of the Cross there were two chains, by which one could suspend oneself; at its foot there was a support for climbing up. Having mounted and bound herself to the Cross, she let herself hang suspended. So at least suppose the Religious who saw those contrivances. In a special way then the Servant of God stayed withdrawn in her room on the days of Thursday and Friday of Holy Week. Habitually the Servant of God ate very little, always meatless, but on those days, when she stayed withdrawn in her room as I have said, she ate nothing.

At Piacenza, when she came down after the harsh penances from her attic cell, at times feeling exhausted, she went to rest a little on the bed of one of her Religious, because her own bed was full of instruments of penance.

Proc. fol. 190v.: During the thanksgiving after Holy Communion, and some time before it, the Servant of God was so concentrated in herself that she did not even answer if someone approached to speak to her.

§ 91
Devotion to Our Lady.

She was most devoted to Mary Immaculate, inculcated devotion to her on us, and wished that when we went to the sick our first greeting should be this: «Praised be Jesus and Mary Immaculate».

I know that once the Servant of God went to Lourdes. She had a most special devotion to Mary Mater Gratiae, to whom she had the Church of this House consecrated.

Once, while she was at Piacenza, the Servant of God having fallen gravely ill, the Most Holy Virgin appeared to her in a dream asking her for the erection of the said Church. So, among others, Sr. A. Serafina told me. As from childhood she was most devoted to Our Lady, and consecrated to her the direction of her daughters, to her Religious she gave at the beginning the name of Handmaids.

She also venerated greatly the mystery of the birth of Our Lord, and to me too, when I was Superior of the House in Via Garibaldi, she inculcated that I should have the three Masses of Christmas midnight said.

To all of us she recommended devotion to Our Lady and inculcated that the month of May be kept with much piety, and in this Church of ours in Via Merulana she also sought the Preacher for each evening.

Among her devotions that to St. Michael the Archangel stood out.

§ 92
Devotion to the saints: St. Michael, St. Joseph, St. Anne…

His feast is preceded by a triduum in this House. In this Church of ours she had an altar erected to him.

St. Joseph too held a particular place in her heart, and we also have a prayer for him, prescribed to us by the Servant of God in the common prayers, as also the month of March is consecrated by us to him.

It is not to be said how devoted she was to St. Anne, after whom she named her Institute, and she wished her Religious to bear before their particular name the common one of Anna. She inculcated devotion to her on us; at the striking of every hour we are obliged to greet St. Anne with these words: «Blessed be the glorious Our Mother St. Anne, mother of the Immaculate». And on the twenty-sixth of every month we have a special prayer to this Saint; as likewise one to be said every day; and all this was prescribed to us by the Servant of God.

Also by the Servant of God we have been prescribed fasting on the vigil of the said Saint and abstinence on all Wednesdays of the month consecrated to her, which is the month of July. In this month prayers and pious practices in her honor are prescribed to us.

We have likewise prescribed by the Servant of God, like all the rest narrated above, a prayer to St. Francis of Assisi, to be recited every day.

I had forgotten to say that the Servant of God wished that the month of March to St. Joseph be kept by us with special pious practices.

p. 50

She exhorted us to the acquisition of numerous indulgences. In the holy year (1900) she wished that all the Sisters should perform the practices necessary for gaining the Holy jubilee.

I now remember that I forgot, in speaking of her solicitude for the spiritual good of us, her Religious, that to the Professed and Novices she inculcated saying frequent ejaculatory prayers, prayers, and making spiritual communions; and to engage us better, she wished that account be rendered to her in writing.

In that year in which I was portress in this House, she inculcated the said practices on me also.

§ 93
Veneration of the Word of God, of priests, of the Holy Father.

She listened with much pleasure to the word of God; she saw to it that it was preached to her Religious by good and learned Ecclesiastics. She prescribed ten days of annual Spiritual exercises to her Religious.

I never heard nor learned from others that the Servant of God used scriptural words in a less reverent way.

She had great reverence and veneration for the Supreme Pontiff, the Bishops, and any Ecclesiastical authority, as was revealed by the way in which she inculcated on us also reverence and submission to the Church.

As I said at the last session, the Servant of God was deferential and respectful toward the Apostolic Visitor; and at that time, having come to visit me while I was in Via Garibaldi, she told me that she desired to resign from her office of Superior General (she did not tell me the reason, however), but that her daughters did not permit her.

For Pius IX she had a veneration as for a Saint, and exhorted her Religious, after his death, to commend themselves to him. To him she was indebted for the counsel which the Servant of God had asked of him and for which she had therefore come to Rome from Genoa, and which he gave her, to found her Institute. The Supreme Pontiff, to the hesitations of the Servant of God, who found herself embarrassed by having two children and an old mother, replied: «If you do not found it you will find yourself repentant». He predicted to her also that her Institute would spread throughout the whole world, as swiftly as the flight of a dove.

The Servant of God prayed for the Pope; and likewise inculcated on her daughters that they should pray, and we have a special daily prayer prescribed by her. She prayed and had us pray for the whole Church. She wished likewise that special prayer be made for the Clergy.

We have always had in our Houses one ordinary Confessor, and the extraordinary ones. The Servant of God confessed to the one of the Community. She exhorted us all to deference and obedience to the Confessors.

Respect and reverence the Servant of God wished to be shown to all Priests, but she would never have permitted any familiarity, and watched over this.

The Servant of God was a lover of the decorum of the House of the Lord, and wished the Churches and Chapels of the Institute to be kept very well and adorned.

§ 94
Firm hope and trust in God.

Hope: The soul of the Servant of God was turned to Heaven; and I never heard from her mouth, nor heard it said by others, that she spoke any word of mistrust in this regard. At times she also said to me: «Everything is obtained from God: have trust in God and nothing will be lacking to you».

In her tribulations her refuge was prayer; her hope, however, wholly placed in the Wounds and the merits of Jesus Crucified. Tribulations she received from God with great humility and gratitude, as a great good.

§ 95
Detachment from honors and riches.

Her heart was wholly alien to honors; she even suffered at being called Mother General and did not want the title of Mother General to be put in letters addressed to her. When her daughters, receiving her in their Houses, honored her with acts of homage, I did not notice in her face any sign of satisfaction; on the contrary she was seen to be quite indifferent.

Likewise her heart did not run after riches, and I never saw her discouraged, nor heard it said that anyone ever saw her discouraged for lack of money, as happened at times at the beginning of the foundation of her Institute, in which at times even necessities were lacking. In financial straits, however, she had help come to her in a providential way. In these straits the Servant of God made special prayers and ordered others to her Sisters. When she had special needs, at Piacenza she shut herself in her attic room destined for penances, and there did violence to the Lord. Likewise here in Rome in her needs, of whatever kind they were, she had the habit of shutting herself in her room to pray and do penances.

This trust of hers in God she did not keep for herself alone, but transfused it also into her Religious, and also into other afflicted and troubled persons.

§ 96
Charity toward God: distance from sin.

Proc. fol. 199: The charity of the Servant of God M. Gattorno toward the Lord was great. As far as I know she was most diligent in everything, and I never noticed in her the slightest defect; which certainly did not happen without her watching over herself. It was seen that her heart was always intent on the Lord whether she spoke with us or did any other thing. And this not only did I notice every time I saw her, but also my other Consisters. She exhorted us all to be most exact in everything and to abstain from the slightest fault. She was ready, once she knew the opportunity, to correct us even of simple defects. Once a Consister failed in reverence toward another older one. The Servant of God immediately imposed on the guilty one to kiss the feet of all those present. Few were the outward effects of her charity toward God, being an enemy of outward show; against which she exhorted us all to guard well. Yet she could not hide her lively love for God when she spoke.

I remember at this moment that I forgot, in speaking of the Apostolic visitation, that the Servant of God learned from the Crucifix, a year before it happened, of the Apostolic visitation, that she would have many sorrows, but that she must always remain strong. This Sr. Anna Serafina, Sacristan in this House, told me. Speaking to us of the Lord, her words were fiery, and penetrated our hearts, and inflamed us with love of God, to which she exhorted us frequently.

Her heart felt great love for the Heart of Jesus, to which she prescribed to us to recite every day the little chaplet.

§ 97
Charity toward neighbor: the Institute, a work of charity.

She had so much charity for neighbor. Her Institute was founded principally for the sick at home, then for girls in danger, for the poorest, then for hospitals, for orphans, for women prisoners, in short for every sort of misery.

In doing temporal good to neighbor, the Servant of God wished to reach her principal end of saving souls. When she was invited and had personnel available, she did not look at the economic conditions proposed to her, but sent her daughters at once, with prior agreement with the Bishops, trusting for the rest in providence. When she sent her daughters to Florence, she sent them lacking everything, and when they came to Rome accompanied by the Servant of God, they were so ill-provided that they had to make do sleeping on the floor, as Sr. Anna Crocifissa Fiocchi, at present Superior at Siena, told me. The Servant of God slept on two chairs.

§ 98
Delicate charity toward the religious.

Finding her Sisters afflicted or preoccupied, she at once comforted and consoled them. At her words anxiety, sadness, doubt vanished, and we all remained serene. This I know, not only from my personal experience, but also because it was reported to me by other consisters.

Her solicitude to console her Religious extended to any kind of tribulation; and I know that sometimes she gave some Religious money to have Masses celebrated in suffrage for the souls of their dear ones. She exhorted us all to mutual charity, and if despite her observations she saw that some dissension persisted between Consisters, she assigned them to other houses, and so separated them.

I never heard that the Servant of God complained of anyone. Not even on one occasion when three of our Consisters, who were in a hospital entrusted to us, refused to remain any longer subject to our Foundress and, having changed habit, continued to remain in that hospital, not even then, I say, did the Servant of God complain. Her words followed upon the facts, and she exhorted us all not to bear rancor against whoever had offended and persecuted us, and to continue, if possible, to do them good.

§ 99
Charity extended to all without envy.

She did not want her daughters, and to this she exhorted them, to bear envy toward other Institutes which had an aim similar to ours, and she inculcated on us that we should pray that God would make them prosper, saying that none of this should matter to us, provided God be glorified.

Her charity extended still to the poor dead, and we have prescribed by the Servant of God some daily prayers for them.

When the Servant of God sent us to care for the sick at home, she exhorted us to take care to comfort the family of the sick person.

§ 100
Generous alms without expecting anything in return. Charitable in making corrections.

She gave many alms to the poor, in clothing (as at Piacenza), in bread, in soup, and also in money, especially in winter. For them she also worked. From when she was a laywoman, and then as a Religious, she went begging for the poor, for the sick, and to be able to send the obolus to the H. Father. For the Peter's pence she once went begging with a certain Sr. Anna Crocifissa Fiocchi, as she herself reported to me. Until she was prevented by the government of her Institute, which had expanded very rapidly, she did not spare herself in going herself to care for the sick, for whom I know she felt great inclination.

The Servant of God did not want anything ever to be expected in compensation for the service rendered to the sick, not even a cup of coffee; she permitted only a glass of water to be taken.

Once in Genoa a Consister received a closed envelope from the sick person's family to take to the Superior. The Superior, having opened the envelope and found money in it, had it carried back by the same Sister to the sender; so the said consister, whose name I do not now remember, told me.

Here in Rome once it happened that a gentleman, in whose house our consisters were caring for a sick person, insisted much with them that they accept at least a cup of coffee. They refusing, that Gentleman telephoned for permission to the Servant of God, whom he said he knew, but received from her a refusal.

When the Servant of God corrected her Religious, she never raised her voice, and woe to that Superior who threatened her subjects; she wanted them to be calm when they had to reprove.

I never knew that any Religious was left badly impressed or irritated by the corrections of the Servant of God, and it seems to me I can affirm with full certainty that she knew well how to regulate her words of correction according to the character of those to whom they were addressed.

§ 102
Practice of prudence in no common degree.

The Servant of God was a woman of government, therefore very prudent. She placed before the dispatch of affairs, especially the graver ones, prayer and counsel. She wanted the local Superiors too to regulate themselves in everything with great prudence, and how much she inculcated it appears also from the Circulars.

p. 55

Even in her ardent zeal for the good of souls she did not abandon the rules of prudence. The bearing of the Servant of God had nothing artificial or affected, but was simple and unconstrained, and she wanted her Religious too to be without affectation, as is written in our constitutions.

I now recall having heard a Superior reproved once because she had been too hasty in accepting Postulants; in this she wanted great caution to be used.

I do not know that the Servant of God ever denied others what she owed them, nor that she failed through prodigality.

I have heard it said that from girlhood she was submissive and reverent toward her parents. When later she was a Religious, great was her submission and reverence to any authority. And to her Religious too she inculcated this virtue.

I do not know that the Servant of God ever exceeded in reproofs to her Sisters, and the greatest penance was to keep herself very reserved and serious with those whom she intended to punish.

§ 103
Strong in physical and moral tribulations. Calm and amiable character.

Proc. fol. 207v.: The Servant of God showed her fortitude in tribulations of every kind, as in illnesses and in the great difficulties which she had to overcome in the foundation of her Institute and in the government of it, as I have heard said by several of my Consisters, whose names I do not now recall.

The Servant of God was very often suffering in body, and although she tried to conceal it, she did not always succeed in hiding it from her daughters, who attentively observed her.

The character of the Servant of God was grave, calm, but not jovial; of habitually smiling aspect, she was amiable in her gravity.

To all of us she inculcated, and especially to the Superiors, fortitude and constancy in tribulations and temptations.

§ 104
Interior and exterior mortification.

I believe that the Servant of God practiced interior mortification, but of this I have only inductive arguments, that is, from her exterior mortification. This exterior mortification she showed in the bearing of her eyes, of her whole person, in food, in rest, and in the other most harsh penances which she performed.

When she corrected, I never noticed in that year in which I was here, and never heard others note, that the Servant of God made an uproar in corrections, but she was always calm. Not only did I not hear this said, but on the contrary I heard from other consisters the opposite, that is, that she was always calm.

§ 105
Mortified in eating and in sleeping.

The ordinary food of the Servant of God was potatoes, and these in small quantity. Not totally excluded from her diet, however, were milk, eggs, butter and fish. Everything was cooked in oil. Meat was absolutely excluded from her diet, and likewise wine, contenting herself with water alone.

I know that she slept little, and on a straw pallet, without mattress, and that in the pillow there was a rather thick chain arranged in the form of a circle, on which she laid her head.

§ 106
Use of particular instruments of penance.

Sr. Anna Serafina told me (let it be well noted that the said Religious had the special charge of attending the Servant of God) that she removed from the side of the venerated Mother, a day before she expired, to relieve her pains, she being all swollen, a little iron chain, three fingers wide, which girded her all round and had sunk into the flesh. The present Mother General, Sr. Anna Benedetta, showed me the said chain in the first days after the death of the Servant of God, and I observed that there were still clots of blood.

The same Sr. Anna Serafina told me that after the death of the Servant of God she washed with water and vinegar the wound which the Crucifix, which the Servant of God wore closely adhering to her breast for five years, had formed on her.

Besides the Fridays, of which I spoke at another session, on all occasions of tribulations, and as often as she felt the need of special graces, she withdrew for whole days into her room, and we all Religious believed that in that time she did penances and prayed.

§ 107
She loved chastity and used the necessary means to preserve it.

The Servant of God was most jealous of the virtue of Chastity. Not only did she insert in our Rules some precautions to guard this beautiful virtue, but also by word of mouth she effectively exhorted us to use all the necessary means to preserve it intact. These means and precautions were never to separate from one another when engaged in the care of the sick, never to give the hand to persons of the other sex, never to be alone in the parlor, flight from idleness, prayer, etc. She recommended then to the Superiors that, if they saw anyone somewhat light, they should tell her directly at once. Often she repeated these things to us by word of mouth. Never have I heard, nor heard said by others, that the Servant of God ever spoke of her married state and of things relating to it.

So great was the care of the Servant of God to guard this virtue that in her illnesses she never let herself be touched by the doctors. Once, when I was in Via Garibaldi, she told me she was not feeling well, and when I replied that it seemed to me necessary that she be carefully examined by some doctor, she retorted: «That never».

§ 108
She loved poverty and practiced it constantly.

Not only did the Servant of God observe the vow of poverty, but she also practiced its virtue in the strictest way. Her habit (of which she had only one), conformable to poverty and simplicity, was like that of the others. The present Mother General and Sr. Anna Celsa, General Secretary, told me that they sometimes tried to replace the old habit of the Servant of God with some new one, but did not succeed, she holding the old one very dear. I myself never noticed on her a new habit. Very poor was the room of the Servant of God here in Rome, and I imagine it was the same at Piacenza, if not more so. The furniture consisted of an iron bed, as I have already said, a night table, a kneeler of unvarnished wood, with the white straw seat where she rested her knees, just as is seen in so many Churches of Rome, a small whitish table with an ordinary Crucifix on it, and a little picture of Our Lady of Sorrows, so it seems to me, I am not sure, a chair, and I recall nothing else.

She recommended to us also so much the spirit of poverty and detachment from everything, as she first gave us the example, and as all of us noticed.

§ 109
Obedience to superiors.

Strictly observant of the smallest rules of her Institute, she required from all of us the most exact observance. She inculcated on us highly obedience to Superiors, first to the Pope, then to the Bishops, and to any authority, and admitted no word of discussion, as I myself heard, when she exhorted to the practice of this virtue of obedience.

§ 110
Subject to all out of humility.

Profoundly humble, as I have already said, she did not want to be called Mother General or Foundress, not only in the addresses of letters, but not even by word of mouth. She never spoke of anything that might bring her some honor, even slight, and some vain satisfaction. So, as far as I know. Although of a different opinion, she yielded to me in that circumstance of which I have already told, in which she asked me for a Sister who then left three or four days later. I still recall having heard that of some Religious of very good spirit she sometimes asked counsel, besides those which she asked by rule of the Assistants. Among these Sisters of good spirit, of whom she asked counsel, there was the infirmarian, and she obeyed her, not only in illnesses, but also in other affairs concerning the Institute. This I learned from other Consisters, whose names I do not recall; it was, however, the general report. Unaware of her virtues, she considered herself a great sinner and asked to be helped with prayers on account of her sins, as I myself heard, and said she did not deserve favors from the Lord. This virtue too she warmly recommended to us. She told us that our Institute was the last among all and that we should be well content to belong to it.

Being asked, I can answer nothing about the photograph which is seen at the beginning of the Articles proposed by the Postulator. Before it I had never seen any photograph of her. I know that she was averse to letting her other Religious be photographed, except in groups of the various Houses, and I believe she permitted a photograph only in extraordinary circumstances. Finally I am persuaded that the Servant of God constantly persevered in the practice of the said virtues until death, and I am likewise persuaded that she went on always growing. This was the impression I received of her when at the end of her life I had occasion sometimes to approach her.

§ 111
She practiced all the virtues in a heroic degree.

Ad 28: Having understood the declaration of the heroism of virtues, it seems to me I can affirm without hesitation that the Servant of God practiced all the virtues in a heroic degree, and that in the practice of them she never exceeded, but kept the just way proper to virtue.

§ 112
The supernatural gifts.

Ad 30, Proc. fol. 217: I have already told that fact, surprising to me, that the Servant of God, while she was Superior at the Clinic in Via Garibaldi, predicted to me that the Religious she had asked of me would leave me, as in fact happened. I recall further that some years later, when I was Superior in Via Garibaldi, I had formed in my mind the intention of asking the Servant of God to relieve me of the office of Superior. I had not, however, expressed this thought to anyone, nor that I felt uneasy in that office. While I was in this intention, the Servant of God came one day and, having me called to the carriage, from which she did not descend, forestalled me at once with these words: «One must stay in that post in which God has placed us. Most willingly I too would leave mine, but it is fitting that I remain in it, because such is the will of God».

It seems to me I heard it said by other Consisters that the Servant of God knew the interior of the hearts of her Religious, but I could say nothing, because I recall it only vaguely.

I have heard it said, I do not remember by whom, that the Servant of God, in composing the Rules, was inspired by the Lord.

Sr. Anna Serafina told me further that Our Lord spoke to the Servant of God several times.

Ad 31: When I was Superior in Via Garibaldi, I once fell gravely ill, to such a degree that one evening the doctors said that I would not see the following morning, as the consisters reported to me afterward. I recall indeed that I felt my breath failing; the following morning, on the contrary, I felt improved. Then the Servant of God arrived and reproved the Consisters for not having informed her. She came to me in my room, gave me some relics to kiss, laid them on the diseased part and said to me: «Be at peace, for you will suffer no more from this illness». After a few days I left my bed and up to now I have suffered no more from that ailment.

I have heard of other healings worked by the Servant of God, but I recall them too confusedly.

Ad 32: I do not know that the Servant of God wrote pamphlets or books, but I know that she wrote various prayers.

§ 113
Writings of the Servant of God.

I now recall having heard it said that there exists a book written by the Servant of God, and that, it seems to me, it bore this title, or something similar: «Conforti e pene di un'anima afflitta» [Comforts and sorrows of an afflicted soul]. This book I saw many years ago, but then it was withdrawn by the Superiors without saying why and I saw it no more. In this book there is always talk of my Crucifix, but to me it seemed very confused, because without distinction of chapters and dates. I, however, read only two or three pages of it, not having time available.

Of the two letters or so which the Servant of God wrote to me (I was then in Sicily, in an asylum, caring for the poor sick), I do not know what became of them; perhaps I have mislaid them, I did not destroy them, and I cannot find them any more, to my regret. In one of them I remember well that she comforted me and exhorted me to confidence in God and that, if I abandoned myself to the Dear Crucifix, He would certainly not fail to comfort me; of the content of the second I recall nothing more. She also wrote to me on the back of a little picture of the Child Jesus, exhorting me to have the three Masses celebrated on Christmas night, and she sent me the money too. I add further that in writing, the Servant of God was most skilled.

From the present Superior General I know that all the letters that could be found have been requested. I do not know them, but I am convinced that they are nothing other than a mirror of the whole soul, of the Lord, of the venerated mother.

Ad 33: I do not know that the Servant of God prophesied the time of her own death. However a most singular fact occurred close to it. On a feast day (I do not remember well which), but close to her last illness, she called to her side to have recreation with them (a thing she had never done before) all the professed, not only of this Generalate House, but also of the other Houses of Rome and its surroundings. In this recreation she gave us many admonitions, which she judged most suitable for us. I recall in particular that she recommended to us the care of the poor, and that she repeated to the portress of this house what she was accustomed to say to her: «When you have no more money for the poor, tell me».

§ 114
Fortitude in illness and holy death.

Long before her death the Servant of God was suffering in health. She sat in a chair when her strength did not permit her to go about the house. I do not recall up to which day she could go to the Chapel; the Thursday, however, before the Sunday on which she died, she was still up. She occupied herself with her Institute always until the last. She omitted Communion no day. Every time I saw her, in the last days of her life, I never found her discouraged, but found her on the contrary always cheerful in spirit, and always solicitous for her little daughters. On the night of the Saturday preceding her death she grew worse and the Chaplain was called at once, Fr. Vincenzo da Alatri, Capuchin, still our Chaplain. He, or a Paulist, a certain Fr. Agostino, I think, Donadio, who came frequently to visit her during the illness, and also before, administered to her the last Sacraments. I know no other details of her death.

On the said Saturday I, who was in Via Garibaldi, had had relatively good news about the health of the Servant of God, and on Sunday morning I received the news of her death.

§ 115
Manifestations of devotion toward the Servant of God after death.

Ad 34: Having learned of the death of the venerated mother, I came at once to see her, and found her as if she were sleeping. I noticed that they had rosaries and other objects of piety touch her body, and this was done by lay women who had come to see her. After lunch, as far as I remember, perhaps by reason of the internal ailment (it seems she had an intestinal tumor) and also because of the heat, the Servant of God having died on the sixth day of May of 1900, the body began to corrupt, and then access was forbidden to the many who were arriving to see her.

Before the said prohibition I know that many lay people came to see her, and gave signs of veneration toward her, having objects of piety touch her body. This I heard from my consisters, because, as soon as I had visited the body of the Servant of God, I had to return to my House, which I could not leave for long hours.

It seems to me that on Monday the body was carried to our Church and that on Tuesday the funeral was held. The Church was crowded with people, the greater part lay people.

Ad 35: On the very day of the funeral the body of the Servant of God was taken to the Cemetery; it was placed first in a tomb of our Institute, in the quadriporticus, and after I do not know how long a time, it was placed in another tomb likewise of our Institute, precisely over the entrance door of the Chapel.

Ad 36: It is not known to me, nor have I ever heard of acts of undue cult paid to the Servant of God, neither at the tomb nor elsewhere.

Ad 37: I and my other consisters go from time to time to the tomb of our venerated mother; there we pray for her, and to her

p. 62

prayers we commend ourselves. The other Consisters too who come from afar to Rome all express the desire to visit her tomb, and they too commend themselves to her; and I add finally that I for my part invoke her sometimes every day.

§ 116
Reputation for holiness.

Ad 38: During her life the Servant of God enjoyed among her daughters the reputation of a Saint, and I too have always esteemed her such, and also now. This opinion lasted and still lasts among my Consisters, and we hope that one day she will be raised to the honor of the altars.

Ad 39: Such a reputation for holiness did not arise, nor was it confirmed, by any artifice, but was and is a thing wholly spontaneous. I know of no persons opposed to the reputation for holiness of the Servant of God, nor to the Process of her sanctification.

§ 117
Many spoke of graces received.

Ad 40: I have heard it said, but I do not recall particulars, that Religious and lay persons who commended themselves after her death to the Servant of God, to obtain graces, obtained them. I recall in particular that in Spain, I think in Barcelona, where our Sisters are, lay persons who asked for the photograph of the Servant of God commended themselves to her and obtained the graces they asked for.

. Et expleto examine super Interrogatoriis, deventum est ad examen super Articulis, super quibus Reverenda Testis

Respondit: As to the Articles, my knowledge does not extend to all that is contained in them; however, reading them in part and in part having them read to me, I found nothing contrary to my ideas, and nothing exaggerated. Up to article sixty-four I refer to what I have deposed, knowing no more.

Concerning article 64: I recall that it was told to me by I know not which Consisters that Pope Pius IX, after the refusal of approval of the Constitutions, having had the Servant of God come to him, comforted her, was generous to her with counsel, and, in blessing her with her daughters, dismissed her saying: «We wish that the regulation be drawn up by you alone. The Lord will help you; keep your spirit firm».

p. 63

As to the 85th: I recall having seen her myself too, after Communion, instead of staying long on her knees in thanksgiving, flee from the Chapel and hide in the secrecy of her room, without saying the reason for her flight.

§ 118
Penances for the conversion of sinners.

As to the 94th, I confirm that the Servant of God often made honorable amends for the transgressions of sinners, and that on the days of carnival she shut herself in her room for several hours, and often the whole day. And she exhorted us to penances in the last days of carnival, and we have, on the last two days, fasting. We also have, I think, the exposition of Jesus in the Blessed Sacrament on those days.

Of the 95th I confirm having heard it said that the Servant of God said: «There is no softer bed than the Cross. This wood contains every delight». When she wrote to her daughters she added at the end: «I leave you in my dear Crucifix».

§ 119
Devotion to the Passion: recourse to prayer.

As to the 102nd, I confirm that the Servant of God often recommended to her daughters prayer as the only means to overcome temptations, to obtain graces and as the true road that leads to eternal life.

As to the 105th, regarding the words attributed to the Servant of God: «If I saw the Institute without tribulation I would fear that it was not the work of God», it seems to me I too heard them from the mouth of the Servant of God. Besides, those words were conformable to her spirit; and I confirm that she never departed from her habitual serenity in any tribulation of hers.

§ 120
Serene and smiling in speech.

As to the 109th, it does not seem to me exact to say that the Servant of God was always cheerful and jovial. I never saw her cheerful; I saw her always serene in speech and smiling. If in this sense the words cheerful and jovial are taken, I admit it; otherwise no.

The words «She was inwardly convinced that the higher the degree of confidence one has in God, the more provident his mercy becomes» correspond perfectly to the concept she wrote to me in one of her letters.

Art. 119: I have heard it said, by I do not remember which consisters, that the Servant of God spoke for long hours before the Tabernacle, and when she could not by day, she took a great part from the scant rest of the night, so as to give vent with fervent prayers to the affections of her heart.

Art. 120: I confirm that the daily pasture of the Servant of God was meditating on the Passion, which I infer from her discourses and from her having prescribed to us, as a book of meditation, «L'anno doloroso» [The sorrowful year], written by a Capuchin Fr., a book which we must use every day, except Monday and Saturday.

Art. 121: I have heard it said, by I do not remember which consister, that the Servant of God, meditating on the Passion, was abstracted from the senses.

Art. 126: I confirm that the Servant of God felt an ineffable sorrow at the offense to God, and that she made the sign of the cross on hearing a blasphemy, and that she always recommended to her daughters to pray for the conversion of sinners.

Art. 127: The words «Never tell lies, but let truth always be on your lips, and you will live secure in the heart of St. Anne our mother», written to Sr. Anna Camisia, I heard from the venerated mother, said to all of us in public.

I confirm art. 138, for having heard it in part from the other Consisters, and as to her wanting us her daughters to be victims of charity for neighbor, for having heard it from her own mouth.

Art. 140: The thoughts on charity expressed to Sr. A. Canisia are conformable to the spirit of the venerated mother.

§ 122
Help to the needy and submission to authorities.

Art. 141: I am myself a witness that the Servant of God helped the needy who were reluctant to beg, contriving with holy art not to humiliate them, as I am also a witness that she excused the faults of others with her charity.

Art. 147: I have heard it said by the Servant of God herself that she never undertook any work, however holy, without the permission of the Archbishop or Bishop of the Diocese in which it was to be done, and did not per-

p. 65

mit us to go to care for the sick without at least a note from the Pastor.

Art. 153: Concerning the words written to Sr. Anna Giovanna Bixio, reported in this article, I confirm them, as heard by me myself from the Servant of God in various exhortations to us her daughters.

§ 123
Living model of the rules of the Institute.

Art. 161, Proc. fol. 234: I confirm having heard it said that all her daughters, in the 33 years that she lived the life of the community, admired her as a living model of the rule, since they could not surprise her transgressing any part, however small, or departing in any act from the common way of living.

Art. 163: I do not remember well in what circumstance, once, among others, the Servant of God showed herself quite resolved to leave the office of General. Then those who were beside her, as Assistants and Secretaries, informed all the Superiors of the various Houses, making known to them at the same time that there would be no other means to make the Servant of God desist from resigning than for all the Superiors to unite, begging her to remain in that office. All the Superiors then spontaneously addressed to the Servant of God a petition to this end, and she then desisted from her purpose.

§ 124
Evangelical fortitude in contradictions.

Art. 173: I recall that when I was still a laywoman, the Servant of God and her nascent Institute were attacked with calumnies. A young woman, who had left our Institute, told me, still a laywoman, that the Servant of God took girls away from their relatives, and that her parents and brothers would send the Servant of God to prison if she did not decide to let her return home. She who said this to me is now dead. Her name was Rosa, I do not recall the surname. A sister of hers remained in the Institute, likewise now dead, Sr. A. Filomena. Threats were made to her by relatives to make her leave, but she resisted until death. To all these attacks the Servant of God resisted courageously, and went forward on her way, always calm and serene.

Art. 175: The Servant of God did not yield at the premature death of many of her daughters at the beginning of the Institute, nor at the scarcity of means of that time.

p. 66

Art. 180: I know this particular from having heard it from several consisters; I do not now remember the name well.

Having been left a widow, the Servant of God had to resort to borrowing from some friend a habit more suitable to her condition in order to present herself, I do not know where she had been invited; a sign this that she had stripped herself of everything. And the fact mentioned corresponds precisely to what is written in article 181.

Art. 182: In the time that I was here as portress, I noticed that the Servant of God slept little.

Art. 188: I recall that the Servant of God, having arrived at the Hospital of Cento and not having found a bedroom for herself, went quietly to take a place in a bed from which they had just removed the corpse of a person.

§ 125
Prudent and strong in forgiving.

Art. 190: In a certain house of our Institute there was a sister somewhat too attached to the local Superior. The Servant of God, to cut off this pernicious affection, had the Sister come to Rome, assigning her to the house in Vicolo del Piombo. After some days the Superior of this latter house came with the said sister to the Generalate House to greet the Servant of God. After both had spoken with her, on taking leave the Sister kissed the Servant of God, who let herself be kissed but said to her still: «See that it is not the kiss of Judas». In fact, on the return, the Superior had not yet reached Piazza Venezia when the said sister had fled, leaving her Superior all alone in the street. (Because of this fact this poor Superior, some time after, fell ill and died; she was called Sr. Anna Angela Gallinaro).

Whether the Servant of God knew it by supernatural means or not, the fact is that although she foresaw the grave sorrows the Sister would bring her, she did not refuse her kiss. This fact I know from the very mouth of Sister Gallinaro.

Art. 191: Not only when dealing with lay persons, but also with us her daughters, the Servant of God kept her eyes either turned to heaven or lowered. She advised us her daughters never to lose our habitual recollection and never to laugh in the presence of men.

p. 67

Art. 193: She had no attachment to her own opinion, and constantly submitted to the judgment of others.

§ 126
Heroic humility.

Art. 194: She reputed herself the most abject woman on this earth and the most unworthy sinner; and if she had done anything good, she was wont to say: «God has done everything».

Art. 196: I had no occasion to hear from the mouth of the Servant of God the words reported in this article. They are, however, conformable to her spirit, and she desired that this virtue of humility be practiced. She exhorted us likewise to humble ourselves in our falls, without losing courage, in accord with article 200.

Art. 202: She was wont to say more continually to us her daughters that to reach Heaven it was necessary to pass by the way of humility.

§ 127
Love and practice of poverty and charity.

Art. 213: Penetrated by the sublime virtue of poverty, she wanted her daughters to strip themselves of all that is dearest to them, whether to please the Lord more, or for love of this virtue.

I recall that love of poverty led her to reprove Sr. A. Vincenza, her Secretary, if she saw that she had wasted ink or blotting sand, or other little things; and in general she reproved all, though gently, if she saw us little scrupulous in the observance of this virtue.

Art. 222: I confirm that she was wont often to repeat: «Love one another all with one heart» up to the words «by means of your Superior», because I heard them myself.

Art. 227: From more than one Consister I have heard it said that the Servant of God, speaking one day with one of the Sisters attached to the Council, suddenly exclaimed: «America, America, how much you make me suffer». It was learned afterward, after some time, that a Consister on that day had apostatized from the Cloister.

Remarkable is that the Servant of God said those words suddenly, and in such a way as to impress the listener.

I now recall the following fact. When I was in Via Garibaldi, one day I ardently desired that the Servant of God come to my house, having something to say to her, and behold almost at once she arrives, and the first words she addresses to me are these: «Why did you make me come? How did you manage to make me come?». I was surprised and did not know what to answer.

I recall still the following fact: Sr. Anna Lucia, whose surname I do not recall, who is now Superior in our house at Barletta, felt pain in her side and, trusting in the Servant of God, one day asked her to make a sign of the cross on the diseased part, that she might be healed. The Servant of God looked her in the face, saying: «I make you the sign of the cross, but of this ailment you will not be healed». And so in fact it has happened; for she still suffers from that ailment. This fact I learned from the Sister herself.

Art. 230: Sr. Anna Maria Vittoria told me that when she was a pupil in our house at Messina, the following fact occurred:

The Superior of that house, Sr. Anna Gonzaga, had adorned the Altar and the sacred Ciborium, and lit the lamps before it, although the Blessed Sacrament was not there. The Servant of God, arrived at that House, went at once to the Chapel, as was always her custom on arriving at a house, even before greeting the Sisters. Coming out of there, after having prayed, she turned to the Superior and said to her: «Sr. Anna Gonzaga, how is it that you do not have the Sacrament?».

Ad Art. 235, Proc. fol. 243: I heard narrated to me, by I know not which Consisters, that Sr. Eulalia Amedei, cook in the house at Piacenza, having gone one day to ask the Servant of God for the money needed to buy the coal that had run out, received as answer: «It is not true; look better and you will find enough». Sr. Eulalia, returning to the store, found in fact a large heap of coal, where before there was nothing.

Art. 256: It seems to me I heard from Sr. Anna Serafina that the Servant of God had said that the day of her death would be the most beautiful day of her life.

In the last days of her life I found her always smiling, as in the rest of her life, almost as if she had no special sufferings.

It was also told to me by Sr. Anna Serafina that a few days before dying, the Servant of God exclaimed: «I have finished suffering: the Institute, I hope, will triumph».

Art. 257: It was told by all, of this house, that her death occurred while the bell of our Church was ringing festively for the solemn functions in honor of Mary Mater Gratiae, that is, of the dedication of our Church consecrated to Mary Mater Gratiae on 6 May 1900.

Art. 259: There were two coffins for her body, one of zinc and the inner one of wood. On the latter were written the following words at the foot of a Cross: «Rosa Gattorno, Foundress, and Mother General of the Institute Daughters of St. Anne. Rome, 6 May 1900».

Art. 260: I remember that at the transport of the body to Campo Verano very many people took part.

Art. 271: Of the fact recalled in this article I recall only that Sr. Amante La Barbera, present Superior at Florence, had a tumor under the breast threatening cancer and that she was suddenly healed.

Art. 278: Sr. A. Rebecca, now deceased, reduced to extremes by a gastric ulcer which had long tormented her, all the means of science exhausted, had recourse to the intercession of the Servant of God and was suddenly healed. This fact must have occurred at Torre Maggiore or at St. Mary of Capua.

WITNESS III
Sr. ANNA GIUSEPPINA TORNATORE

Scope in the process: From Sess. 29[...] of 29 May 1913 (fol. 253) to Sess. 448 of 6 November 1913 (fol. 372).

Name, surname, date and place of birth: Maddalena Tornatore, born 12 March 1856 at Dolceacqua (Imperia).

State and profession: Religious in the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, formerly Superior, music teacher.

p. 70

Quality of the witness: Eyewitness.

Age of the witness when she knew the Servant of God: 14 years.

Age of the Servant of God when the witness knew her: 39 years.

Age of the witness at the time of the deposition: 57 years.

Duration of the acquaintance and its motivation: The witness knew the Servant of God at Piacenza in 1870 and, after some years, having entered the Institute founded by her, maintained an intimate familiarity until her death (1900). The witness is very good and also very naive.

Observations on the witness, on the scope and on the content of the deposition: The contribution of the present witness is to be considered very relevant, being founded on an extensive and thorough knowledge.
