This is evident from the detailed answers on the childhood and youth of the Servant of God — the witness, among other things, had occasion to know her mother — and on the intense effort, by then a widow, aimed at giving an outlet to her apostolic zeal; in those moments, prelude to the foundation of a new religious work, Gattorno gave proof of knowing how to face and happily resolve obstacles.

The birth of the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, which took place at Piacenza, is a subject which the witness shows she knows in detail, as the development due to the enlightened action of the Foundress is also well known to her. The exposition of the individual virtues — theological, cardinal and the evangelical counsels — is another theme treated with great care, and the wealth of detail constitutes valid proof on the heroic exercise of the virtues. The treatment of the supernatural gifts, of the writings, of the last illness, of the death, as well as of the reputation for holiness and for miracles, is valuable, because she is an de visu witness.

Ad 2 interr., Proc. fol. 255v., testis respondit:

§ 128
General particulars of the witness.

My name is Anna Giuseppina Tornatore, in the world Maddalena. I was born in Dolceacqua, Diocese of Ventimiglia, of the late Andrea and Anna Maria Dall'Orto, I think on 12 March 1856. I entered this Institute in October 1876, received the veil at Genoa, after some days was transferred to Piacenza, where I made the Novitiate; I did not complete the twelve whole months of Novitiate, and made the profession of simple vows and, after about nine years, that of perpetual vows. Generally I was employed in teaching music. For some months I was Superior at Piacenza; almost three years at Cercola, Province of Naples; almost a year at Agrigento, from where I was called by the Servant of God for reasons of health.

Ad 6: I come to depose because regularly summoned, and no human motive moved me to present myself. No one has instructed me about the deposition I shall make.

§ 129
Scope of knowledge and esteem for the Servant of God.

Ad 7: I knew the Servant of God at Piacenza, being there in passing around 1870. At that time I came to Rome to become a nun among the Sisters of St. Mary in the Garden at the Four Corners; I remained, however, in that Monastery simply as a boarder for about a year. Here I saw the Servant of God again, she having come to visit me, and then, returning to my country, I passed through Piacenza, where once more I saw the Servant of God, who said to me: «See that St. Anne does not want you in our Institute». Having then become a religious, I had occasion to be many times in contact with the Servant of God, especially at Piacenza and in Rome, where I remained almost always.

I have read various obituaries of the Servant of God, and a little biography, which precedes our prayers in a book printed in Brazil for the use of our Consisters.

In my deposition I shall disregard these readings, but shall adhere exclusively to what I myself have seen and heard.

Ad 8: I have great esteem and veneration for the Servant of God; I often commend myself to her; willingly would I see her canonized, and I hope that it may so please the Lord for his glory and for the honor of the Institute, but I shall say nothing moved by this hope or desires, but for the truth, as I have sworn.

§ 130
Childhood and first education in the family.

Ad 9: I do not recall the precise date of the birth of the Servant of God. She was born in Genoa of well-to-do parents, whose names were Francesco Gattorno and Adelaide. I knew personally Signora Adelaide, who was a woman of much prayer. At Baptism she was given the name of Rosa. She had two brothers, Federico and Francesco, and two sisters, Giustina and Elisa; this last I knew personally, as also the two brothers still living: Federico, who seems to me of very good heart, I have heard it said, to my regret, that he belongs to freemasonry; the other, Francesco, I do not know whether he is a practicing Christian.

Ad 10: From conversations with the Servant of God and with her relatives I formed the conviction that she completed her education in the family in a Christian manner. I learned likewise that she was much loved, especially by her mother, whom, when she had grown somewhat, being the firstborn, she helped in the various household tasks. From relatives I learned that she was good and submissive, and I was able to infer from the whole that she was of judicious disposition and not given to play.

I recall this particular of her childhood, told to me by the Servant of God herself. She could not tolerate coffee with milk. Her father, fearing it was a little caprice of hers, obliged her one morning to take it; but shortly after the poor little one, who had nevertheless obeyed, having gone to Church, was seized by a fainting fit.

She was of lively wit; she knew music, a little French, and was skilled in singing. She was also very comely.

§ 131
Marriage of the Servant of God and children had.

Ad 11: I know that the Servant of God united herself in marriage (I think urged by relatives) with a certain Mr. Custo, I believe, a banker; as I also believe Gattorno's father was a banker. After the engagement the Servant of God was faithful to Mr. Custo, and much more after the marriage, as I learned from relatives.

Ad 12: I know no particulars, the Servant of God never having spoken to me of her marriage nor of her married life.

Ad 13: The Servant of God had three children, two boys and a little girl. One died small, the other died at about 35 years; the daughter survives, who, when still in the cradle, a blow of air made lose speech and hearing; so at least the daughter herself told me.

At first she educated her children in a Christian way in the family; then, having become a widow, she placed the daughter in an Institute for deaf-mutes in Milan. It seems to me that she then likewise placed the son in various Institutes successively; and I do not know precisely whether she also carried out part of the education in the family, having once seen the young son with a Priest, who to me had the look of being the Tutor.

§ 132
Death of the husband and solicitous care of the children.

Ad 14: The Servant of God lived in marriage a short time, the husband having died as a result of a fall, in which his chest struck violently against something. I know no particulars.

Ad 15: She loved her children and, as a wholly spiritual woman, desired that they be good, and when the son gave himself to an irregular life, I noticed that she suffered not a little from it.

In the son's last illness, the Servant of God took great pains that he receive the Sacraments. She had him attended by her Sisters; she herself went from Rome to Piacenza, assisted him to the end, and had the consolation of seeing him die as a good Christian. I was then in Rome, and therefore these things I heard said here.

§ 133
Meeting of the Servant of God with St. Francis of Camporosso.

Ad 16, Proc. fol. 263v.: I recall having heard from the Servant of God that she once, among other times, having gone to the Venerable Francis of Camporosso, who was then in Genoa, he showed himself apprehensive for the grave tribulations to which she would be subjected in the future and which he saw in spirit. It seems to me he predicted something to her, adding: «Take courage, my daughter, I will pray for you». This happened when the Servant of God was meditating in her heart the foundation of the Institute.

I have heard it said, I do not remember by whom, that the Servant of God, having become a widow, went to care for the sick of the Pammatone Hospital, with other Ladies, called Ladies of Mercy, of whom she, it seems to me, was the Directress or President.

I recall still, I do not know from whom I heard it, that, caring for the said sick, she at times licked their sores. This, however, I recall confusedly.

§ 134
Beginning of the new Institute and family contrasts.

Ad 17: I do not know when the Servant of God conceived the idea of founding the Institute, nor why she chose Piacenza as its cradle.

The first care of the nine companions whom she associated with herself was that, it seems to me, of caring for the sick women at home. Then with the said companions she turned to gathering little orphans and girls in danger.

To leave her family, her children especially, and her mother, in order to found the Institute, the Servant of God had to overcome gravest oppositions and difficulties; since no one was content to be abandoned by her, loving her very, very much. This I learned, among others, from the deaf-mute daughter herself.

I do not remember well from whom I also heard that the mother of the Servant of God opposed her leaving so decidedly that she threw herself stretched out on the threshold of the house to prevent her leaving at the moment of departure, and that the Servant of God did not hesitate to step over her body.

§ 135
In the foundation she took counsel from the Holy Father.

Ad 18: In keeping with what the Servant of God herself once told me, that she never did her own will, before taking the final decision for the foundation of our Institute she wished to come to Rome to hear the counsel of the Vicar of Christ himself. She chose as companion on the journey a Lady of Genoa (whose name I do not recall, though the Servant of God told it to me), who already, I believe, was her companion in the works of mercy carried out in Genoa.

On the journey she had much to suffer and, arrived in Rome, her only refreshment was some cold potatoes, the stomach of the Servant of God refusing anything fatty. This I know from the Servant of God herself. I know that the H. Father received her very lovingly, that he encouraged her in the planned foundation, and I no longer recall precisely the words he said to her. I know further that from then on the H. Father held her in great affection, that on some occasion he presented her with some fruit, and the Servant of God still kept a pear, or more, as a keepsake, in spirit.

Ad 19: The Servant of God, having left the audience of the Supreme Pontiff with a mind resolved on the foundation, went, it seems to me, directly to Piacenza, where she rented, or bought, the Dal Verme house.

§ 136
She began the Institute in Piacenza: name of the Institute.

At first she did not wear the religious habit, wishing above all to settle the family affairs, but she clothed nine companions. Of these I recall only the name of Sr. Anna Rosa Podestà, and I do not know whether Sr. Anna Bixio belonged to those first nine. I do not know whom she made use of nor on whom she relied at first for the foundation of the Institute; I do not even know whether the first of all was my paternal uncle, the Priest Giovanni Battista Tornatore, of the Lazarists. He told me that the Servant of God had gone to him to obtain his counsel and support. I know that at Piacenza my said uncle was called the Saint. (It was he who determined my father and the Bishop of Ventimiglia, Monsignor Biale, to cede me to this our Institute, whereas neither I nor my father wished it. Indeed I had already taken the veil as a Sister of St. Mary in the Garden at Ventimiglia itself and was determined to remain in that Institute. The esteem, however, of a man of God which my uncle enjoyed was a reason for making it believed that such was the will of God, and it was yielded.)

Ad 20: To our Consisters there was given first the name of Daughters of the Immaculate, and then that of Daughters of St. Anne. The reason for the first title was the devotion of the Servant of God to the Most Holy Virgin Immaculate. I do not know the reason for the change.

The habit also underwent a change. The veil at the beginning was not as thick as the present one, but was the so-called little veil, which women of middle and upper Italy ordinarily wear. Here in Rome it is little used. In seventy, when I passed through Piacenza, they still wore their hair long. I cannot determine when the prescription to cut it came.

The Servant of God, some months after the first clothing, took the veil herself too with others, among them Sr. Anna Giuseppa Troni, present Superior of Piacenza. I do not know whether she had yet settled all family matters; to her daughter certainly the dowry was assigned afterwards.

§ 137
Fr. Tornatore and the rules of the Institute.

Ad 21: Since my uncle the Priest Tornatore helped the Servant of God greatly, he wrote the first rules, which I do not know; so I heard from him himself. I always believed that the second ones too had been drawn up by him, but recently I heard from my Consisters that they were composed by the Servant of God. Approval was given to these latter, and I recall when Cardinal Verga brought the approval and handed it to Mother Gattorno in the presence of other Sisters, on the twenty-fifth anniversary of the foundation of the Institute or of the taking of the religious habit by the Servant of God. In the rules we have prescribed the usual vows of chastity, poverty and obedience, temporary for ten years or more, according to the dispositions of the Superiors, and then perpetual.

§ 138
Elected Superior general, she remained so until death.

Ad 22: The Servant of God remained in the general direction of her Institute until death.

Once there was fear that the Servant of God wished to leave that direction; and we all protested, at least those of us who were nearest. We were then living in the Vicolo Margana. I do not believe the Servant of God coveted this office at all, and I remember well that neither by word of mouth nor even in the addresses of letters did she wish to be called Foundress or General. For the admission of Postulants the Servant of God required that those recommended by reliable persons be presented, besides the usual certificates of good conduct, etc.

§ 139
She governed the Institute with great solicitude, though very ill.

The Servant of God was most diligent in visiting her houses, and set out on the journey although ill and with her legs swollen to such a degree that the skin folded over her shoes (so it seemed to me at times, she herself showing them to me). When the Servant of God showed me the swelling of her legs, I never received the impression that she did it to display her spirit of mortification, nor to be pitied, but I always interpreted it as an act of benevolence toward me.

In these visits she showed herself solicitous for regular observance; she sought to see everything, to know everything, and when afterward some inconvenience had occurred because the Sisters had not warned her, she went so far as to punish the Sisters themselves, as happened at Sampierdarena; where those Sisters did not give notice of the not very regular conduct of their Superior, who later left the Institute. At the end of the visit she took the appropriate measures.

Proc. fol. 272v.: I recall that despite grave sufferings, the Servant of God visited the houses of Sicily no fewer than twice. It must be noted that near death (and I believe the Servant of God no longer felt or understood), the doctor palpated her abdomen and it was very swollen (that swelling she had had for many years already) and he ascertained that it was a tumor which, as he said, the Servant of God had perhaps carried for twenty years. And in all this time she never abstained from the labors of visiting the houses nor from carrying out her other duties.

§ 140
Great activity despite her illnesses.

Not even in the last years of her life do I remember that she always stayed in Rome. Perhaps in the last 3 years she refrained from visiting those houses where she saw the greater need. And when she was absolutely prevented, she appointed a visitatrix. I could not say, and it is not known to me, that she let herself be influenced in her government by antipathies or sympathies or other human motive.

She was very jealous for regular observance, especially as regards the practices of piety. She was also greatly concerned that necessities not be lacking to anyone, and above all she was solicitous for the Sisters who were sick and weak in health. And I recall that the Mistress of Novices at Piacenza received a good scolding from the Servant of God because she forgot a sick Novice of hers, and did not bear in mind that the infirmarian had at certain hours gone out of the house. Also to me, weak in health, she showed many considerations and attentions.

When at Piacenza we had orphan girls or girls in danger, she herself sometimes went to care for them, when she knew them to be ill. A certain Sr. A. Beatrice of the house at Piacenza told me that when she was still a pupil in that house she fell gravely ill with typhus and that the Servant of God spent long hours at her bedside and at times whole nights. Except in the last years, when we showed greater consideration for the Servant of God, if any of us religious felt ill in the night, with filial freedom, if we called the Servant of God, who slept in a little room where after her death so many instruments of penance were found, she ran at once and assisted us.

§ 141
Maternal care for the sick; poverty and trust in the Lord.

It is not to be said how solicitous she was, then, that the gravely ill receive the Sacraments. And I recall vaguely having heard it said that, a Consister of ours having died at Naples without Sacraments through the lack of foresight of the local Superior, the latter was gravely reproved by the Servant of God.

At the beginning of the foundation of the Institute, grave were the economic straits in which our Consisters found themselves. But Providence never failed to send what was necessary, as I learned from the consisters.

Also in opening the first various houses of the Institute, in some of them they were without furniture and kitchen utensils; but some who had been present told that then above all they rejoiced greatly in spirit.

§ 142
Prudence and fortitude in the very rapid development of the Institute.

Ad 23: Very rapid was the development of the Institute because of the many and insistent requests for houses that came from every side. And on the other hand many subjects asked to take the veil. This, which is admirable, is that at the beginning of the Institute the Servant of God did not wait until they had completed the year of Novitiate, being pressed by the continual requests for houses. But having need of them she sent them where it was urgent; and some of these, who did not complete the Novitiate of one year, made a splendid success, such as Sr. Anna Fabiana Orsi and Sr. A. Celsa Speranza.

Admirable still that, pressed by urgent needs, the Servant of God sent as teachers Religious who scarcely knew how to read and write, and nevertheless they afterwards made an excellent success. This I heard from various consisters, and it seems to me I myself also verified that one sent as teacher knew very little. Of the following fact, however, I am myself a witness. I was teaching the first elements of music to a certain Sr. Anna Damasina Trocheis, now deceased. The Servant of God suddenly had need of a music teacher in the house of Aci Sant'Antonio of Catania. Without hesitation she took her from me and sent her. This poor little one was so scant in music that at the beginning she had to write to me for clarifications. But the fact is that she made an excellent success and always passed for a music teacher.

§ 143
Correspondence with the communities. Financial accounts.

The Servant of God was in continual correspondence with her houses, from whose Superiors she required frequent reports on the running of the house. She herself then wrote many letters, especially to the Superiors of America, because they were too far away.

If in some house some inconvenience occurred on the part of some Consisters and the local Superior did not notice, the Consister who noticed, according to the rules, should warn the local Superior; and, should the inconvenience be chargeable to the local Superior, the Servant of God wanted to be informed of it at once by the subjects, writing to her even without a stamp.

Every six months they had and have to send to the mother general the financial account, as they also had to send the surpluses. I have heard it said, I do not remember by whom (certainly not by the more important persons of the Institute), that some Superior, to enter more deeply into the mind of the Servant of God or to please her more, imposed on herself and on her community small sacrifices (such as, for example, withholding on some rare day the fruit, or one dish of the two which we have as food, besides the soup and the fruit), in order to be able to send some surplus to the Servant of God. I do not even recall which superiors it concerned. I hold it for certain that the Servant of God knew nothing. The revenues of the Institute from the beginning were alms, especially from the families of the sick whom we went to care for. It is forbidden to us to receive anything, except a glass of water and nothing else, in the houses of the sick. These are perfectly free to send or not to our houses what they think fit, as alms; but in their own houses nothing at all may be received.

In some cities, such as Palermo, Naples, Genoa, from the beginning some committees of Gentlemen and Ladies were formed, or rather simply lists of donors, to whom our Sisters then go to collect the sums subscribed.

§ 144
She never forgot her duties as mother toward her children.

Ad 24: Having given herself to her Institute, the Servant of God did not forget her two children. Her deaf-mute daughter having left, after her education was completed, the College in Milan, where she had been placed, the Servant of God took her with herself, and we Religious held her very dear. She was no disturbance to our life, being of very good character, and she was also very pious and often made Holy Communion.

§ 145
Marriage of her deaf-mute daughter.

The daughter being very comely and having no desire at all to become a religious, it was a worry for the Servant of God; and it was therefore with great pleasure to her that the hand of her daughter was asked by Count Gaspare Amidei-Barbiellini, with whom she had met in a conversation here in Rome. The daughter, even after marriage, could not detach herself from her mother; and at Piacenza, as here in Rome, she bought a little land adjoining our houses, and there built a house for herself.

Here in Rome, before building a house for herself, she lived in rented accommodation in some house, provided she stayed in Rome when her mother was there, and thus could visit her. And at Piacenza, before the house they bought was restored, for a very short time it seems to me they lived with her husband in a room of our house, but completely separate from the Community, and it also seems to me that for some time she took an apartment for rent. This always with the aim of not separating from her mother. The daughter's house, which was built in Rome adjoining ours, was built with the expenses shared with the brother or brothers of the mother.

Of the things of the Institute the Servant of God gave nothing to her children.

§ 146
She never gave her children things belonging to the Institute.

If she made some gift to her daughter, and if she paid some bill for which the son-in-law sent her daughter to ask, she did this with money which some Lady gave her that she might use it not for the needs of the Institute. I believe that Princess Fitalia above all, who was intimate with the Servant of God, as I have heard said, gave her much money for purposes foreign to the Institute and that she might use it for things of her own will. The son-in-law Barbiellini pleased me because he often made Communion; it did not please me, however, that he pushed his wife to go and ask the Servant of God.

§ 147
Prudence of the Servant of God toward her son-in-law on the administration of Gargatano.

Proc. fol. 281v.: The Servant of God, being unable herself to go nor to send her Sisters to preside over the works needed by the estate of Gargatano, donated to the Sisters by the Marquises Caracciolo of Piacenza, gave this charge to her son-in-law Barbiellini for a little time. I do not know what happened, but it was plainly seen that the Servant of God was not satisfied with him, because I heard him say himself: «But let them look at the accounts, let them see the books, let them verify them, etc.». The fact is that the Servant of God took away from him that office too. It seems to me that in entrusting the oversight of the said estate Father Tornatore also had influence. Fr. Tornatore, who assisted the Servant of God with his counsels, ceased to assist her a little before the Chapter presided over by Cardinal Alimonda. I infer then that Fr. Tornatore had influence precisely because he assisted the Servant of God with his counsel and had been confessor of the daughter when she was still unmarried. She used to say of Fr. Tornatore that he was very good. I add also that this superintendence of that estate was greatly desired by Barbiellini and his wife. And I recall that on that day when they came out of the study of the Servant of God after Barbiellini had received such charge, they showed themselves very content.

To act in her stead in the superintendence of the construction of this generalate house, the Servant of God charged her brother Francesco. I recall that brother Federico also took a little interest in it.

Concerning Barbiellini I believe I must add that he had no vices of any kind, such as tobacco, wine, or infidelity to his marriage bed. The deaf-mute, however, had a curious way of reasoning to support the claims her husband had against her mother. She said (and this reasoning I heard made several times by her husband) that her husband, having left for her sake the position he had here in Rome in I do not know which bank, the Servant of God would have the duty to indemnify him for the loss suffered by giving him a way to earn by another road.

§ 148
Education of the little grandchildren.

I was very much in relation with the deaf-mute and her whole family because I received from the Servant of God the charge of giving a little schooling to her little granddaughter Maria, whom I taught music and a little Italian and a little French. I also taught some small things to the other little grandchildren Camillo, Annina, Federico and Emilietta. I began to occupy myself with these grandchildren about 1882, and continued until 1896-97. For this teaching the grandchildren came to our house, but more frequently I went to them. Their house being adjoining, both here and at Piacenza (indeed at Piacenza there was also an internal communication at the end of a corridor, a communication now closed), I was ordinarily permitted by the Servant of God to go there alone.

§ 149
Apostolic visitations and prudent attitude of the foundress.

Ad 25: I recall that our Institute had two Apostolic visitations; I do not know the reasons. The first Visitor was Monsignor Cavicchioni; the second was Monsignor Serafini. As far as I know, Monsignor Cavicchioni visited only our Sisters in Rome; Monsignor Serafini, on the contrary, went elsewhere also. When Serafini came to Piacenza, I was away on holiday and, to my great pleasure, was not questioned.

On these occasions of visitations I noticed that the Servant of God was grieved, and I believe it was because of these visitations. It is in no way known to me, nor have I reason to believe, that the Servant of God did not show herself very deferential to the Visitor, nor that she gave or had given to the Sisters instructions on how to answer the Visitors.

Ad 26: I am persuaded, from her later life and from the love and esteem the relatives had for her, that the Servant of God observed the Precepts of God and of the Church, the duties of her state, not only in religion, but also before being a religious. Having become a religious, then, she always observed the Rules of the Institute and was always solicitous that her religious observe them exactly.

§ 150
She practiced all the virtues heroically.

Ad 27: I am convinced that the Servant of God practiced the Theological and Cardinal virtues, humility, poverty, obedience and chastity. Lively was always, so I am persuaded, the faith in the Servant of God; and I am likewise persuaded that for each of the truths of our faith she would have let herself be killed rather than deny them. This faith of hers showed itself in the contentment she displayed when she sent her daughters to teach catechism, or when she knew they were sent by other local Superiors; also in the joy she showed when she had news of some conversion wrought by her daughters who cared for the sick; in the great contentment she showed in sending her daughters to America, to Africa; and in the courage she infused into the Sisters who had to depart for those distant regions.

Not only did she watch that books or other equivocal printed matter not enter our houses, but not even indifferent newspapers. Not even good newspapers are read in our houses, and this makes me believe that it depended on the desire of the Servant of God, in order to maintain more firmly the religious spirit.

§ 151
Spirit of prayer and recollection of the Servant of God.

Proc. fol. 290v.: The Servant of God prayed much. The thanksgiving she made after Communion was with the utmost recollection; she could not be disturbed at that time, and no one dared to speak to her. It seems to me indeed that one of the consisters tried at that time to ask her something, and that she did not answer. She prayed especially at night. This is my persuasion, and also that of other Sisters. Sr. Anna Serafina Foglia, then, assured me of it, telling me she had seen her as if absorbed in God. To me myself the Servant of God said one day that she began her meditation about three in the morning. Sr. Anna Camilla Valentini told me that she had heard from the Servant of God that, while she was still a laywoman and sleeping above the room of her brother Federico, the brother heard much noise one night, so that he questioned his sister the following morning, asking her what she had done. From that night the Servant of God no longer let herself be heard by her brother.

§ 152
Particular devotions, expression of faith.

In the parlor it was seen that the Servant of God went unwillingly, and in her a very reserved and recollected bearing was noted. She nourished a special devotion to the Most Holy Trinity, as can be gathered from the prayer made by the Servant of God which is read on the back of her image distributed after her death. Five little prayers she composed to the Eternal Father, and we recite them throughout the month of January, which we consecrate to Him by the prescription of the venerated mother herself. Not only did she inculcate this devotion on us, but also on her deaf-mute daughter, to whom, I recall, in her mother's last illness, she addressed these words: «Mama, Eternal Father»; and, having gone out of her room, she herself turned to the Eternal Father, exclaiming: «Oh! Eternal Father», in the act of invoking his help.

For nothing in the world did the Servant of God omit Communion. Even when traveling and arriving at a very late hour at the end of her journey, she had kept herself fasting in order to be able to make Holy Communion.

In the last years of her life she had permission to take something before Communion, but I do not know how much she made use of it. I recall that at times she received Communion at about two in the morning, on occasion of illness, no longer being able to remain fasting. On these occasions many times it was administered to her by the Priest Emmanuelli Francesco, now Bishop in Sardinia.

She made visits to the Most Blessed Sacrament, and in all her prayers I noticed her recollected.

Most devoted to the Holy Child, she wished that on Christmas night the three Masses be celebrated; and in this Generalate House, although in the first Christmas when they came here everything was topsy-turvy, she wished that they be celebrated all the same. Christmas is, by prescription of the Servant of God, prepared by a novena.

§ 153
Extraordinary phenomena: the Crucifix and the Servant of God.

A characteristic devotion of the Servant of God was that of the Crucifix. She named it often and always closed her letters with the words: «My dear Crucifix».

Sr. Anna Camilla told me, at my question, that the Crucifix, which she wore hanging at her side, as we others do, spoke to the Servant of God several times.

Sr. A. Camilla Valentini told me further that Sr. Anna Serafina Foglia also heard the voice of the Crucifix while it was speaking to the Servant of God. Questioned by me, Sr. Serafina would neither confirm nor deny it to me.

Sr. A. Camilla Valentini told me she had heard from the Servant of God that one night, while she was praying with greater fervor before the Crucifix (at that time she was still in the world), it detached itself from the Cross and went toward the Servant of God.

p. 84

I do not know whether the same Sr. Camilla also told me that the said Crucifix, reattached to the Cross, detached itself another time. Certainly I recall, however, that Sr. A. Serafina Foglia told me that while the Servant of God was praying before Him, it detached itself another time, and that the Servant of God, doubting that she knew how to nail it well, had this operation done by a smith; but in vain, since Christ detached himself yet another time! This Crucifix is kept in the room of the Servant of God at Piacenza. In the same room there is also kept another small Crucifix which, as Sr. A. Camilla Valentini told me, the Servant of God wore for five years closely adhering to her breast, I believe to her side, and which, having formed a wound on her, she removed by order of Our Lord. The same Valentini added to me that on that Crucifix there are still seen traces of skin remaining there from its close adhesion to the breast of the Servant of God.

In the same room there is also found a thick rough wooden Cross, formed as if of two beams. This is hung on the wall and on its arms it bears I do not know what apparatus, but evidently for putting the arms in. It is the supposition of all those who have seen it (I, however, have not seen it) that the Servant of God hung herself on that Cross, and, suspended, recited the Rosary with a large rosary which is found hanging on the same Cross. Sr. A. Serafina Foglia told me that the Servant of God recited the entire Rosary in that room.

§ 154
Penances and spirit of mortification.

In the bed of that room, made of only a straw mattress, another wooden Cross was found, about 15 centimeters wide, which took up roughly the whole bed. On the pillow there was a chain going round in the form of a crown. It is said that the Servant of God lay on it to rest. It is certain that the Servant of God ordinarily in the morning came out of that room very weary and tired. In the last years of her life, being swollen in body, she reserved another room for herself, where she rested at night in a bed likewise without mattress. I do not know, however, whether the reason for no longer resting in that first room of hers was the increased swelling of her body, or a prohibition of the Confessor, or another reason. Until the end, however, she shut herself in there during the day, as I myself saw sometimes. Into that room she never wished anyone to enter, not even Sr. A. Serafina Foglia, although she had asked it of her as a favor. She admitted there only her little granddaughter Maria while she was small, and who certainly did not yet understand anything.

On the evening of Holy Thursday she shut herself in that room of penance and until Holy Saturday did not come out of it. There she remained without eating, and on Holy Saturday she came out at the hour of making Communion. She did the same when she was in Rome on those days. In the last years, however, I do not know whether three or four of her life, she no longer remained fasting, but took something and admitted also some Sister.

As I said, on those days of Holy Week no one could enter her room, neither in Rome nor at Piacenza. An exception was made, however, for Sr. A. Camilla Valentini, it seems to me in 1888, when she, having come from America, was already preparing to return there.

§ 155
The wounds of the Lord.

She knew so effectively how to beg the Servant of God to let her enter her room on Good Friday that the Servant of God could not resist and said to her: «Wait until Sr. Benedetta (Carrega) and Sr. A. Celsa (Speranza) have gone out and then come in». I entered, so Valentini told me, and found the Servant of God stretched on the bed, suffering greatly, in a state to move one to pity, as in a kind of agony. I noticed on her forehead certain marks like red points; I wished to feel her pulse, which I found very abnormal, and the hand had an extraordinary heat, things absolutely beyond the natural. I thought then that she had the stigmata, and said to the Mother: «But on the feet too it is so, O Mother!»; she having signed yes to me, I resumed: «But then what wonder that she needs poultices?». Sr. Serafina Foglia then told me she had seen something glitter in the middle of the hands of the Servant of God, and that, having begged her to let her touch that shining thing, the Servant of God answered her: «No, no, for I would hurt you». I do not know whether this happened when Sr. A. Serafina (who was assigned to the Servant of God) kept the night vigils in the last four months of the mother's life.

Sr. A. Camilla Valentini also told me that she had learned from the Servant of God, I do not know at what time, that she had had the stigmata for 28 years and that at first they were visible, but that having then asked the Lord to hide them from her, they remained invisible.

§ 156
Meditation on the Passion of the Lord and other expressions of devotion.

Proc. fol. 300: By prescription of the Servant of God we must make every day the meditation on the Passion of Our Lord, except Monday, on which we make it on the Eternal Maxims, and Saturday, which is reserved to Our Lady.

It seems to me that it was to Sr. Anna Camilla that she said: «I could not live without suffering». To Sr. A. Serafina Foglia too she said: «How beautiful is suffering». I recall in general having heard myself also from the mouth of the Servant of God expressions of her love of suffering.

Sr. Serafina Foglia told me that the Servant of God exclaimed: «Lord, even a hundred years at the bottom of a bed for your work».

The venerated Mother prescribed to us the month to the S. Heart of Jesus and the little chaplet of the S. Heart every day. She prescribed that we prepare with Novenas for the principal feasts of Our Lady, and in a particular way for the Immaculate, and the month of May, consecrated to Her.

She went on pilgrimage to Lourdes, but a most tender devotion she had for the Mater Gratiae, to whom she wished the Church of this House consecrated. In about '85 or '86 the Servant of God had a grave peritonitis, for which the doctor feared for her life. In that illness she had such spasmodic pains that she clung to the consister who was near, and for some days lay in a stupor without taking food. To me myself it made a great impression to see her in the moments of sharper pains: the alteration of her eyes, which I would liken to the eyes of dead fish. While by the doctor and by us her life was feared for, suddenly one day we find her sensibly improved. I remember that the Secretary, now Mother General, called me to tell me she was as if out of danger, and in five or six days she returned to her normal state.

After this fact I heard it said that the Servant of God had obtained the grace from Mary Mater Gratiae, whom we venerated in our Church at Piacenza. The Servant of God wished that she be crowned, and Monsignor Scalabrini, Bishop of Piacenza, performed this ceremony. When this church was later consecrated here in Rome, then that image was transferred here.

§ 157
Reverence toward priests and preachers.

I never heard that the Servant of God spoke with little reverence of Priests and Preachers. I recall indeed this fact: a certain Father, in giving us the Exercises, spoke to us very inopportunely. He was, for example, capable of insinuating to us in his sermons that the Superiors loved very much to have vocations from noble families, and that for this reason they were too lax about other requisites of spirit; he urged making appeals, complaints to the Congregations against the Superiors, and this always in the sermons; and other similar things. The Servant of God limited herself to dispensing silence to prevent us from concentrating on what the preacher had said, and to reporting it to Cardinal Verga, our Protector and Prefect of the Regulars.

The last part I know because Cardinal Verga often came among us, and stayed to converse familiarly with us.

Toward the Pope she was full of reverence. Of Pius IX, moreover, she spoke not only with reverence, but with great affection.

Most deferential was the Servant of God toward all Ecclesiastical dignitaries and toward any other Priest.

§ 158
Prudence toward a Cardinal.

Proc. fol. 312v.: At first the Superior permitted us to go and visit the Cardinal Protector, even at his house, and Sr. A. Francesca Chifenti, who was the one who had become fond of the Cardinal, went with much pleasure. The Cardinal himself, then, invited us. To go to him it was natural that Sr. Anna Francesca look for some companion, and habitually either I, or Sr. Anna Michelina Negri, or both together were chosen. When Sr. Francesca's attachment was noticed, the Mother General urged us to refuse to accompany (at least so she did with me) Sr. Anna Francesca to the Cardinal, in order thus indirectly to compel her not to go. Before arriving at this reserved conduct, things had gone so far that on the occasion when the Cardinal went to our house at Naples, Sr. Anna Francesca went too. After, however, the change of conduct of the venerated mother toward the Cardinal, he began to thin out his visits and Mother Gattorno then removed Sr. Anna Francesca from the secretariat. Then, sent to Naples for I do not know what operation, she left her there. She, however, decided, I do not recall after how long, to leave the Institute. I know that afterward she married and led the life of a good Christian.

She was very zealous for the decorum of the house of God. She wanted the churches and chapels of the Institute to be well adorned and provided with sacred furnishings, and spared no expense for this. One day, having found dust in the Church, she reproved the Sacristan.

p. 88

§ 159
Hope founded on the merits and mercy of the Lord.

Hope: The Servant of God toiled in her life for Paradise and hoped to attain it, and this hope was founded on the merits, on the goodness and the mercy of God.

Her heart was not attached to any material thing of this earth, nor to comforts. In her room she never wanted an armchair, not even at the last, when it would have been very comfortable for her. She never used a fan to cool herself, and in the midday hours of summer, about eleven, in the last months of her life, I went to fan her a little, and I used a piece of cardboard which she herself handed me.

In winter she never wished to use fingerless gloves, nor did I ever notice that she put glycerine on her hands.

All the confidence of the venerated Mother was in God, and God answered this filial confidence by always showing himself a father to her. Sr. Camilla Valentini told me that once, having come from America with a certain sum of money (about six thousand lire) to provide herself in Europe with school supplies, when she was about to make the purchases, she found that the Servant of God had spent it all for other urgent needs. Then, embarrassed, turning to the Servant of God, she said to her simply: «Have confidence in God». And God did not fail to provide for her. In fact then Taborga, with whom Sr. Camilla had traveled from America to Europe, later Archbishop of Sucre, wrote to Sr. Camilla from Spain, offering himself for anything in which he could serve her. Then Sr. Camilla answered him that he should provide this and that (all the more since they had to be in the Spanish language), that she would then think of reimbursing him the money on the return from America. But when all the things arrived at their destination, she found that everything had been generously paid by Taborga himself.

§ 160
In tribulation she always sought to accept the will of God.

Proc. fol. 320v.: In tribulations and anguish of spirit, in her infirmities and in all that happened to her of contrary, the Servant of God was wholly conformed to the supreme Will, and was wont to say: «All is little for God», «How beautiful is suffering», and other similar expressions. She felt tribulations, however, strongly, above all because she was habitually sickly. Once when an administrator, instead of paying the merchants who had given goods to the house, made false receipts for about ten thousand lire, when the Servant of God learned of this fraud, she was greatly grieved, and said: «This really should not have been!». This happened during her last illness and, notwithstanding that this sorrow came upon the already not slight pains of her body, I do not remember having noticed in her any sign of impatience or alteration, the slightest. Naturally, however, she had to dismiss this administrator or kind of bailiff.

It never came to my mind that the confidence of the Servant of God was excessive; rather, although she sometimes undertook works with scanty means, she was seen very soon helped by the Lord, and I never heard that other sisters or even persons outside the Institute charged the Servant of God with being imprudent or excessive in her confidence. I must also add that she sought to infuse her confidence into us her daughters, and exhorted us all to hope and trust in the Lord.

§ 161
Flight from sin: most exact in observing the rule.

For her charity toward God I must say that I noticed in her no act that could be called sin; and she was most exact in the observance of the rules. In the first times when I was in the Institute at Piacenza, I remember always finding her in the morning in the Chapel when I entered; and the Consisters told me that at the beginning of the Institute the Servant of God herself made and explained to her daughters the meditation.

How severe a judge she was of herself can be inferred from the following fact: once I, in the morning, before Communion, had broken silence with a Consister about things not urgent. Before making Communion, I thought it fitting to ask the Servant of God whether I might receive, and she answered me: «For this morning it is better that you abstain».

Her very great care was that we always make our meditation well, and even in the last times of her life she gathered us in this house, upstairs in the Novitiate, together with the Novices; she questioned us on the points of the meditation, how we observed its rules, and explained to us further the way to make it better. Then she gave us other conferences on the points which she thought more opportune for us.

p. 90

§ 162
She worked much for the poor; charity with the sick.

Her great charity was toward the poor. In free times she worked little shawls; she gave bread every Saturday to the poor and, on special occasions, such as Christmas and Easter, she also gave sausages, macaroni and other things. Before being a religious she went to care for the sick at the Pammatone hospital. Having become a religious, she gathered poor little orphans and to maintain them went begging herself. She deprived herself even of rest to work for the poor.

I have heard it said also that once she cared for a leprous woman, and that she herself contracted the disease. This Sr. Camilla Valentini told me. The mother herself, then, told me that, the leprosy contracted, it left something like scales in the sheets.

The already principal purpose of the Institute was the care of the sick; and then every other work for the good of neighbor. Her love for neighbor made her take good care of the sick. And she was so delicate in caring that I myself would have wished to have some small illness in order to be cared for by her. She exhorted us also to care well for the sick, to do good to their souls, and showed herself all joyful on learning that some conversion of these sick was wrought.

§ 163
Extraordinary charity toward the religious.

Great was her charity toward us; when we were not in full observance of the rule, she also inspired fear in us, but she was all amiable when we had nothing to reproach ourselves with. She wanted the Superiors to treat the Sisters very well, especially if sick.

On some feasts she had something extra passed to us at table, or during recreation she herself distributed sweets and thus gave a quite special tone of cheerfulness to the Feast.

Her authority as Superior General was not felt to weigh upon us; she was unconstrained, and I remember also that once she began to play with us others. In general she let nothing exceptional or extraordinary show through in herself, and was very averse to singularities.

§ 164
Prudence and justice in the government of the Institute.

Proc. fol. 328: From all that she did, I infer that the Servant of God was always prudent, especially in the government of her Institute. The houses in general were founded at the invitation of local authorities, except the principal ones, such as Naples, Genoa, Sampierdarena, which were founded on the initiative of the Servant of God, always with the consent of the Ordinary.

p. 91

I also noticed the prudence of the Servant of God in adapting her counsels and warnings according to the characters, the qualities and the office of the persons to whom she gave them.

It seems to me I need not hesitate to say that the Servant of God also practiced the virtue of justice. I do not know, in fact, that she ever failed against this virtue, and even in distributing offices to the Sisters I cannot say that she ever let herself be induced by human motives.

§ 165
Fortitude in corrections: balance and serenity.

Before very many difficulties the Servant of God showed herself generously strong. And even in her office, having at times to correct, it seems to me that she overcame the repugnance she must have had, and with strong constancy scrupulously fulfilled her office of Mother General, and after her death some letters were found to which she had reserved to reply.

She was of lively and energetic character, and I never noted that she let herself be carried away by a passion of anger or other in speaking and acting.

Most temperate I always knew the Servant of God. Setting aside this, that she took neither broth nor meat, because they harmed her stomach, she was nevertheless in the rest very frugal. Her ordinary food was potatoes, onions, vegetables and ordinary fish, in general what the Secretary or the mother cook provided for her.

§ 166
Spirit of mortification.

Sometimes, not knowing what to give her, they fried her an egg, but she did not eat it willingly. When she felt her strength failing, she herself at times asked for an egg yolk, and I never noticed that she took two. I vaguely recall that for I know not what ailment egg yolks did her much good; and then they were given to her. She was induced only in her last illness to use milk.

When I entered the Institute I saw that they prepared for her a small cup of chocolate in the morning, but it was very little; then I saw that in the following years she took only coffee without sugar in the morning and so remained until dinner.

I noticed that, although to us Sisters she sometimes had sweets passed, and she herself distributed some to us at times in recreation, saying: «Taste how good it is», toward the end she ordinarily never took any.

p. 92

In the last years she was induced, by order of the doctor, to drink wine, something she had not done before.

I noticed that the pasta served to the Servant of God was very ordinary, and when she was ill they gave her pasta in water with a little cheese.

Often, out of a certain devotion I had to the Servant of God, I took her leftovers and ate them; and I never found in these anything indelicate.

The furnishing of her room was poor. Her bed was without mattress; the little table she had was of ordinary wood; I recall that there was also another little table in her room where she kept the Crucifix, and that too was ordinary; two or three chairs, on one of which toward the end of her life a kind of cushion was fitted to the back. To make known how much the Servant of God suffered physically, I must say that when I first saw her she was very thin and slender; but when I entered the Institute she had already begun to swell. The swelling went on always increasing until it made her monstrous in her last illness, as is seen in the photograph taken of her after death.

I recall that in the morning, in the last times, we heard her make efforts to vomit and she brought up nothing but water. And she took nothing because she reserved herself afterwards to make Communion.

I know that even before she spent very bad nights and the consisters heard her give great sighs, so as to provoke the question, from those Consisters who slept near her room, whether she felt ill.

I believe that the Servant of God also suffered from liver trouble. This I infer because she could not lie on either side. Notwithstanding all these disorders of her body, she always showed herself patient.

§ 167
She lived and died as a truly poor woman.

Poverty: In dress she had nothing singular. The bodice, or upper part of the habit, she sometimes mended herself, giving it the necessary stitches. Princess Fitalia once gave her a little black shawl, and this she wore to the end although all tattered, rather than have another bought.

Mother Carrega, her Secretary, kept her aprons or other things for her, because she feared the Servant of God would give them to the other Sisters, as in fact to me too, I recall, she gave an apron. In short, this I can declare, that she held poverty very dear and exhorted us all to practice it. I recall that in a conference she even reproved the use of white handkerchiefs, so that all then used colored handkerchiefs to blow our noses. Seeing the virtue of poverty practiced so exactly by the Servant of God, we other Sisters too abstained from things which, besides, would have been lawful, such as the use of fingerless gloves, of the fan, at least in her presence, etc.

§ 168
Singular love of chastity.

She was most jealous of the virtue of Chastity. She did not want to be touched in any way and for this reason never wished to be examined by the doctors, to whom she scarcely permitted them to feel her pulse. I do not know whether two days before, and I do not know whether even the Servant of God at that moment understood, the doctor was finally able to palpate her. Such was the ruin of the body of the Servant of God that the doctor declared she was a corpse already two days before dying. I recall that two days before dying an enema was given her, which came out of her mouth.

She was most modest in her eyes and at the same time unconstrained. How rigorous she was on this point, and rightly, can be seen from the following fact. A consister was recalled from America because in the hospital she had entered into a relationship with I know not whom. When she came before the mother, she threw herself on her knees, but the mother gave her a severe glance and went on (the meeting had taken place in a corridor). Then the poor religious began to implore, calling her: «Mother, mother», but the mother paid no heed and did not turn. I myself was witness of that scene, harrowing for me, but which shows the fortitude and the love of the Servant of God for this beautiful virtue.

In regard to this virtue I have already related the fact that happened in the hospital of Sampierdarena. The Servant of God having prescribed in the Constitutions that they denounce to the Superior if they saw a Sister a little light on the occasion of caring for the sick, so as to give room to the tongues of the malicious, I asked the Servant of God to be dispensed from this obligation, but she would not dispense me from the said obligation.

As to obedience, I have already said that the Servant of God had declared she had never done her own will.

p. 94

§ 169
Sentiments of sincere and profound humility.

As to humility, I add to what I said in other sessions: she never allowed us to kiss her hands, and to me she always seemed very humble. I never heard that she attributed to herself anything good; of herself she always said that she had done nothing and that the little that appeared of her was all the work of God.

Regarding herself, indeed, I recall that she used abasing expressions.

Proc. fol. 337: Before going further, several things have come to my mind which I shall now relate.

§ 170
She avoided honors with particular care.

In the early years the Servant of God never wanted her name day to be celebrated, as indeed she loved no demonstration and wanted none in any circumstance. One year Cardinal Berardi, Protector of the Institute, was present at Piacenza on the occasion of her name day, and he wished a small demonstration to be made, and had me and other Consisters learn some compositions to recite before the mother. At the hour when the little celebration was to take place the Servant of God did not let herself be found. I do not know whether the Cardinal Protector reproached her. We all believed, however, that he really made observations to her about it, because in the evening that small demonstration which previously could not be made was held, and the Servant of God had to resign herself to listen to the compositions in her honor. I said resign herself, because the attitude which the Servant of God assumed in that hour was truly that of a resigned person.

Cardinal Berardi esteemed the Servant of God greatly, and was fond of her, as of the whole Institute. He had also arranged to give a hundred thousand lire for the purchase of a house, but, overtaken by death caused by a sudden pernicious fever, he could not carry out his plan.

§ 171
She persevered unto death in the uncommon practice of the virtues.

And now, continuing, I must say that in the exercise of all the above-mentioned virtues the Servant of God persevered unto death. I could not say whether and how much she grew in the virtues, but it is evidently certain that she grew in patience, her physical pains having increased.

Sr. Serafina Foglia, who attended her continually at night in the last four months of her life, told me that the Servant of God at night prayed much and remained absorbed in God, especially after Communion.

Ad 28: The Servant of God certainly practiced the above-mentioned virtues in an uncommon way, and not only so, but also above the other Consisters, though virtuous; she had made the habit of virtue and practiced it in a natural, spontaneous way. And if one must argue from her penances, one must also say that her love of God was in a heroic degree. And I could not say anything else about the heroism of her virtues.

Ad 29: I do not believe that the penances with which the Servant of God afflicted herself rendered her incapable or less fit for the fulfillment of her office as Mother General, since the facts showed precisely the contrary, she having fulfilled her duties to the very end.

§ 173
Supernatural gifts.

Ad 30: The Servant of God was endowed with supernatural gifts. A certain Sr. Anna Brigida, who until now has been at Barletta and at present is here in passing on her way I know not where, told me that one day, while the Servant of God was speaking with a certain Sr. Gironima (whose surname I do not remember, as I do not remember Sr. Brigida's, but who at present, I believe, is in a house in Sicily), she was overcome by a kind of sleep and then, rousing herself suddenly, said to Sr. Gironima: «Leave at once and go to such and such a House (now I do not remember the name even of this one) because there is a Sister who is about to leave the Institute». Sr. Gironima hastened and found it as the Servant of God had told her.

Sr. Camilla Valentini told me that when the Servant of God was at the Vicolo del Piombo, she (who had recently come from America to return there afterward) slept in the next room, and that one night she heard the Servant of God sigh strongly, and commend herself to the Lord, saying: «For charity's sake, Lord, do not permit this» and other similar expressions. Sr. Camilla then got out of bed and went to peer through the keyhole, through which she saw that the Servant of God was prostrate on the ground. Then Sr. Camilla asked the Mother whether she felt ill. The Servant of God fell silent, and for some moments nothing more was heard. But then she began again to hear the same anguished sighs as before and the same invocations to the Lord. Sr. Camilla got up again from bed, ran to peer through the keyhole, which this time she found stopped up, and knocked at the door, asking the Servant of God insistently to open to her, because she was not persuaded that she felt well. The Servant of God, at Sr. Camilla's lively insistence, had to yield, but first said to her: «Wait a little»; and after a little, having opened, Sr. Camilla was able to enter and found the Mother on the bed, worn out. Asked what she felt, the Servant of God revealed to her that a consister who was in America was betraying the Institute. (It seems to me that that Sister of whom the Servant of God spoke was called Sr. Stimmatina.) Sr. Camilla, seeing the Servant of God so prostrate, called Mother Carrega and Fr. Tornatore, who was also at the Vicolo del Piombo, in the same house, that he might give her Communion. Some time later the Servant of God received a letter from Monsignor Bosque, Bishop of La Paz, who informed her that on such a day, at such an hour, such a sister had left the Institute. Sr. Camilla then added that, having compared the day and the hour, she found that the time indicated by the Bishop corresponded precisely to that of that night in which the Servant of God, amid agitations, supplicated the Lord.

Ad 31: Besides what I have already said, I must add that I and many of my Consisters (I do not know whether all) had great trust in the prayers of the Servant of God, and turned to her in every need.

§ 174
The Servant of God as writer.

Ad 32: I know that the Servant of God wrote various prayers and also a book, which was afterward withdrawn from circulation. I no longer remember the title of this book, and I read a little of it, but nothing remained impressed on me. Of the prayers, the one to the Eternal Father is found in our Manual, and the one to the Most Holy Trinity is found on the back of her memorial pictures printed after her death. She dictated to me in French a prayer to the Most Holy Sacrament, and another, likewise in French, to Our Lady. I shall search to see whether I still keep them.

She wrote several letters to me, but partly I destroyed them, and those that remained to me I afterward handed to Sr. Anna Celsa Speranza. I could never notice in her writings anything that was not befitting the religious spirit.

I add further that on some occasions, such as Christmas, Easter, and name days, she was wont to write maxims and exhortations on the back of some pictures, and these too, which I possessed, I handed to Sr. Celsa Speranza.

§ 175
Last illness and holy death.

Ad 33: The worsening of the physical state of the Servant of God began at Genoa or at Sampierdarena, several months before her death. She then resolved to return to Rome, and the doctor thought it fitting to accompany her, fearing for the journey, having observed that the heart and the pulse were not regular. I noticed that in all this time, notwithstanding her sufferings, she never allowed herself to omit Mass on Friday, except in the last month. She had ups and downs in these months, but the doctor said she was always grave.

On the Thursday before her death, which took place on a Sunday, the sixth of May 1900, the peritonitis developed which was to be the fatal blow.

And now I shall go on to speak of her last illness.

We were accustomed to see her ill, and at times for twenty-four hours she had scarcely given a sign of life, and therefore not even in this last illness, right up to the very end, when the doctor took away all hope, had we believed that she would die. We prayed, however, very much in this house and in all the others of the Institute. Until Friday morning she made Holy Communion. I am not sure whether she made it on Saturday too.

On Saturday evening, seeing her worsened, and her words already scarcely understood, Fr. Vincenzo da Alatri, Capuchin, Confessor of the Community, and Fr. Agostino Donadio of the Minims, asked the Servant of God: «Mother, do you wish to receive Extreme Unction?». And she answered: «So be it», and I did not know that she said other words. And so she was given the Holy Oil.

On the following morning, Feast of the Dedication of Our Church, about nine, she rendered her soul to God.

Particulars I did not see, because the previous evening I had felt ill, and I stayed that day and several others in bed. I saw the Sisters weeping.

Ad 34: I learned that after a few hours the corpse of the Servant of God began to corrupt, and they had to put it promptly in the coffin and withdraw it from the sight of the others.

p. 98

I was told further that after being placed in the coffin, the gas emanating from the corpse had raised the lid of the coffin, and that a hole was then made in it to give the gas free exit; and so great was its pressure that a kind of whistle was heard as it came out.

It seems to me that the coffins were two, one of wood, outer, and the other of zinc.

Our Consisters from various Houses, even distant ones, hastened to her funeral.

I do not know how many people attended.

§ 176
Burial and fame of holiness.

Ad 35: She was buried first in our common sepulcher at Campo Verano, and then was transferred to the Chapel of another tomb of our Institute, which was built afterward. I could not determine the place, because since that time I have not gone out of the house, except once only to see the Holy Door of St. Mary Major.

Ad 36: I do not know that any sign of cult was ever made toward the Servant of God. However, out of private devotion I, and, as I know, other Consisters, wear some relics of hers upon us, and commend ourselves to her prayers.

Ad 37: Our Consisters, not only from here but also those passing through Rome, do not fail to visit the tomb of our Foundress. Of outsiders I know that the Princess of Fitalia and the Prince, when they come to Rome, go too, and that the said Princess, in the month of the dead, has several Masses celebrated there, as the Institute also has others celebrated in suffrage for that blessed soul.

Ad 38: In her lifetime the Servant of God was generally esteemed by the

§ 177
Held as a saint in life and after death.

Sisters, as a saint, and among outsiders I know the Princess of Fitalia, who likewise esteemed her as such.

As I have already mentioned, in our needs we had recourse to the Servant of God with confidence, and if we felt ill we ran to her, that she might make the sign of the Cross over us.

As I said, this esteem as a saint continued after her death, and various graces are attributed to her, and some important miracle is awaited.

p. 99

The esteem as a saint has not only been preserved, but is growing, and still spreads among those outside the Institute.

Ad 39: I know that a Priest said to a Monk (who reported it to me without telling me the name) «that much more is needed to beatify the Servant of God, because there are tangles and intrigues with Cardinal Verga». I do not know, however, that others have been or are contrary to the fame of holiness of the Servant of God and to her Process of Canonization.

Ad 40: Sr. A. Brigida (I do not recall the surname) told me that, she herself being, I believe, at Patti in Sicily, this fact happened.

§ 178
Healings attributed to the Servant of God.

In our House in that City a little girl of about three years had been taken in without the permission of the President of the Orphanage (for such was our House). This girl fell gravely ill, I do not know well whether with enteritis or dysentery, and she had been reduced to a skeleton. The Superior was embarrassed, since she could not report the matter to the President of the Orphanage, and one day when the girl was very gravely ill, not knowing any more what to do, she sent for the girl's father and an aunt to hand the girl over to them, although in a most alarming state, to such a point as to make one believe she would without doubt die that day. But when the intention of taking her away from there, to hand her back to her father, came to be made known to the girl, she became agitated and fell into fits of despair, absolutely unwilling to leave the Superior, whom she loved so much. Then the Superior, so as not to agitate further that poor girl already in a pitiable state, told the father to send the servant in the evening to take away the corpse, so that the President should not come to discover anything. Meanwhile, however, they applied, I do not know whether an image or a relic of the Servant of God to that girl's body, and she, I do not know well whether after a little sleep, but certainly a little after the application of the said relic or image, asked for food, giving sign of immediate improvement, after which she slowly recovered. I do not recall when this fact happened, but it is not long ago.

Et prosequendo examen super articulis, Proc. fol. 357v., testis respondit:

p. 100

To Art. 70: It is true that our Consisters were from the beginning called to Hospitals, Schools, Orphanages, etc., and so many were the requests at the beginning that the Servant of God, finding no other way to satisfy them, clothed the Postulants and after a few days sent them here and there.

To Art. 74: I confirm that the Servant of God was regarded by her daughters as a loving mother, and into her bosom we poured our anguish and anxieties, and that one word from her or a look sufficed to restore serenity and calm, and that her arrival at the houses was for all in general an object of consolation.

I confirm in everything Art. 75: Although it is not its place, since I recall it at the moment I add here that Cardinal Protector Alimonda also esteemed the Servant of God greatly, and when he came to Piacenza he stayed with us, remaining several days.

To Art. 88: I recall that once, on the occasion of Corpus Domini, in this our Church the Servant of God herself placed herself before the Procession and made it turn aside onto Via Merulana, showing afterward her great joy at having made Our Lord pass also through the street.

To Art. 142: I know that the Servant of God prayed much and often, by day and by night, and her action was not only preceded but also accompanied by prayer.

I confirm Art. 150: I confirm that she did not blindly accept the offer to open new houses, but went or sent to learn the place, usages and customs, and the conditions necessary for the support of the Sisters, as is related in Art. 154.

To Art. 158: I recall that the Servant of God once declared that the ingratitude and betrayal of Judas made a very great impression on her.

I confirm that she renounced all the possessions of the house in favor of her children, before embracing the life of the Cloister, as is related in Art. 166.

To Art. 172: I know that she prayed long at the bedside of her son

p. 101

Alessandro; that she did not shed a tear, because I never saw her weep, except once at Piacenza, on the occasion of those tangles, which I do not know and for which the veil was about to be taken from Sr. Anna del Salvatore.

WITNESS IV
Sr. ANNA VITTORIA ARCHETTI

Scope in the process: From Sess. 448 of 6 November 1913 (fol. 372) to Sess. 498 of 21 November 1913 (fol. 416).

Name, surname, date and place of birth: Antonia Archetti, born about 1857, at Gandino (Bergamo).

State and profession: Religious in the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, Superior.

Quality of the witness: Eyewitness.

Age of the witness when she knew the Servant of God: 26 years.

Age of the Servant of God when the witness knew her: 52 years.

Age of the witness at the time of the deposition: 56 years.

Duration of the acquaintance and its grounds: The witness knew the Servant of God in 1883, the year of her entry into the novitiate at Piacenza; afterward the relations remained constant until 1900, although they were generally of an epistolary character, since the witness was Superior in several houses of the Institute, also in Brazil.

Observations on the witness, the scope and the content of the deposition: The information on the steps taken in view of the foundation of the Institute, and on how it, through the wise and enlightened guidance of Gattorno, soon knew an extraordinary growth, is interesting. As regards the heroic exercise of the virtues, the witness shows a wide and detailed knowledge and an appreciable capacity to grasp the elements of each virtue. We have, finally, good elements of proof concerning a solid and well-founded fame of holiness.

Ad 2 interr., Proc. fol. 376v., testis respondit:

§ 179
General particulars of the witness.

My name is Sr. Anna Vittoria Archetti, in the world Antonia, daughter of the late Matteo and Margherita Signini. I was born at Gandino (Province of Bergamo). I am about 56 years old. I entered among the Daughters of St. Anne on 30 May 1883. I made Religious Profession after one year, that is, in 1884. In that year I was made Superior of the house of Putignano, which was then opening. In 1885 I was assigned Superior of the house of Pará in Brazil, where I remained until the death of the Foundress. I was then recalled to Italy, where I have exercised the office of Superior in various houses, and now for three years I am Superior in a House of our institute at the Vicolo del Piombo.

Ad 6: I come to depose because invited by the Tribunal. I have not been instructed by anyone on the depositions to make. In my deposition I am not moved by secondary ends, but will depose for the truth and for the glory of God and of St. Anne. I shall not hold in my depositions to what I may have read in the articles of the Postulator, nor in biographies, but solely to what I myself witnessed and to what I heard from trustworthy persons.

§ 180
Scope of knowledge.

Ad 7: I knew the Servant of God Rosa Gattorno only when I was received by her at Piacenza in her Novitiate; to embrace the rule of this Institute (feeling myself already called to religious life) I was induced by a certain Carmelite Father of the ancient observance, Superior in the convent of Piacenza, who spoke to me very favorably of the Servant of God and of her Institute. With great enthusiasm spoke to me of the Servant of God, as a woman of great virtue and worker of miracles, the Superior I had during my Novitiate, which I made in the Hospital of Borgo San Donnino, Sr. Anna Camilla Valentini, and then Sr. A. Serafina Foglia with equal enthusiasm; then other Consisters and persons outside the Institute spoke of her to me with great favor.

I read the articles of the Postulator and the funeral eulogies after her death, but in my depositions I shall set these aside, as I have already said.

Ad 10, Proc. fol. 383: I heard from the consisters that, as a young girl, she was placed in education, but I do not know where; that she showed from childhood a good and pious disposition, and that she was not vain. Intelligent, she had much knowledge, among others of the French language, and was also of very attractive appearance.

§ 181
Model of wife and mother.

Ad 13: I know she was a model of a wife, that she had several children, of whom I recall only Carlotta, deaf and mute, who was educated in Milan in a good and Christian Institute. Of the other children I do not know where the Servant of God had them educated, but I am certain that she educated them and had them educated in a Christian way. I know that one of the sons, after having lived a life a little too free, died as a Christian through the assistance of the Servant of God. Carlotta is still living, united in marriage with a Count whose name I do not recall precisely.

It seems to me that the Servant of God was left a widow at twenty-seven. She strove that her husband die as a Christian as he had lived, and had funeral and burial made for him befitting his state, and Christian. She showed herself in that circumstance a strong woman, and then gave herself to works of piety and mercy.

Ad 16: The Servant of God occupied herself in her widowhood with the Congregation of the Daughters of Mary, it seems to me, by commission of the Archbishop of Genoa, who, if I remember well, entrusted to her other offices in various works of charity. She also gave herself to the care of the sick in their homes with much zeal and charity, preferring the most wretched and abandoned hovels.

§ 182
Apostolate in widowhood and foundation of the Institute. Beginning of the foundation in Piacenza.

Ad 17: Feeling herself then called by God to the foundation of an Institute of Sisters, she not only took counsel with her Confessor, but also with the Archbishop, and came even to Rome to Pope Pius IX, who, having received her very well, greatly encouraged her in the foundation to which she felt inspired. Although she felt a most lively affection for her relatives and for her parents still living, she did not hesitate to leave them, and even went so far as to step over the body of her mother, who had lain down on the threshold of the door to prevent her from going out.

Now I remember having heard that on that occasion she handed her sons over to a Priest, that he might take charge of their education, while the daughter, as I have already said, she had already sent to be educated in Milan.

Ad 19: She began her Institute at Piacenza, I do not know why not at Genoa. It seems to me that some ecclesiastics were not strangers to this determination and the Bishop of Piacenza approved.

I know in general that she had to overcome not slight difficulties at the beginning of her work, and that she overcame them courageously.

Ad 20: I do not know the year of the foundation of the Institute. At the beginning she called her Sisters Daughters of Mary Immaculate, but then, as I have heard, I do not recall well from which consister, through an apparition of Our Lady herself she called them Daughters of St. Anne. In the said apparition the habit was also determined, as we now wear it, although before, being also black, it differed especially in the cap and the veil. Likewise after this apparition she had her Sisters' hair cut, whereas before they wore it long.

I do not know with how many (it seems to me, however, four or five) companions she began her Institute.

For what reasons I do not know, but the Servant of God did not take the habit with the first companions (which I have heard was given by the Bishop); and only took it some short time afterward.

§ 184
Pius IX and the foundation of the Institute.

Ad 21: I do not know particulars concerning the Rules. I only recall that Pius IX told her to write it herself, assuring her that God would help her.
