Apropos of Pius IX, I recall further that when the Servant of God went to him for counsel on the foundation of the Institute, he, encouraging her to set to work, said to her: «Go, for the Lord calls you, and your Institute will flourish and spread throughout the whole world».

On the approval of the Rules by the Holy See I recall only that it came when Cardinal Verga was Protector.

The principal purpose of the Institute is the glory of God by means of works of charity, caring for the sick in their homes, in hospitals, taking care of orphanages, kindergartens, homes for the aged, etc., and attending to the instruction and education of girls in danger, the most lost and poor.

We have in our Constitutions the three usual temporary Vows, which are renewed annually for ten years, after which, if the candidates and the Superiors wish, they may be made perpetual.

§ 185
Strict in the admission of postulants: loving government.

Ad 22: The office of Superior General was held by the Servant of God from the beginning of the foundation until her own death, fulfilling it always with much zeal and great sacrifice. From the beginning of her Institute she showed herself strict in the admission of Postulants, taking all the most opportune information. I have heard, however, also that she was not so rigid as she was in the last years, in which she wanted, so to speak, every security in admission, and even those admitted to the Postulancy she could not resign herself to, so to speak, closing an eye on the weaknesses of those admitted.

I have heard that to Religious Profession she did not admit without the counsel of their mistress and of her own assistants. She watched most attentively over regular observance throughout the Institute, and for this visited her houses frequently, sending Visitors where she could not go herself, as in America, where she could not go because of her frail health, and sending also frequent exhortations.

As far as I know, she always sent as Superiors to the houses the most observant, prudent and most suitable Religious. Toward her Sisters she showed herself truly a loving mother, and wished also that all the Superiors show themselves such toward their subjects. And I recall that in the letters addressed to me she not only exhorted me to firm maintenance of discipline, but further to show myself good toward the Sisters of my house, and to watch continually. She did not let herself in any decision be guided by sympathies or antipathies; she was no respecter of persons.

§ 186
Strong in the difficulties of the foundation.

Ad 23: As I have heard, at the beginning of the foundation of the Institute bitter war was waged on the Servant of God at Piacenza, especially by Freemasonry, and the more she busied herself in works of charity, the bitterer the war became. She was accused of being a bigot, an impostor, a deceiver, but I do not know particulars. Notwithstanding this war the Institute progressed rapidly and is now spread in Italy, in France, in Spain, in Portugal, in Brazil, in Bolivia, in Argentina, in Peru, in Chile, in the United States, in Africa, and perhaps in other places which I do not recall. And I have also heard that at the mother's death we Sisters were five thousand. The Servant of God required of the Superiors the moral and financial accounting of their houses, and did not compromise on this. The Servant of God, however, without at all requiring it, asked the Superiors whether they had anything superfluous to send in aid of the generalate house, but, I repeat, she was not demanding.

Ad 24, Proc. fol. 392: I know that while I was in America an Apostolic visitation took place made by a Benedictine Father, a certain Serafini. The reason, from what I have heard, seems to have been certain complaints made by the Sisters of Piacenza against the local Superior; but I do not know, however, why, besides the house of Piacenza, the Visitor visited others also, such as that of Rome and that of Genoa, and I do not know particulars.

§ 187
Difficulties arising from the family.

Ad 25: The grandchildren, children of Carlotta the deaf-mute, were educated by our Sisters, in particular Sr. Giuseppina Tornatore. This fact aroused some remarks, especially against the son-in-law, who abused his kinship with the mother, perhaps to save money on the education of his children; and he even ventured to ask the sisters for gifts. As for the Servant of God, they sympathized with her because they knew she was a mother. The son-in-law, having the little villa adjoining this our generalate house, and having also a key to the gate, which allowed entry without going out onto the street, entered freely every day, when he wished; he went to the Servant of God and sometimes also to the kitchen to get something to eat. This frequent presence of the said Gentleman in the house annoyed the Servant of God, and I can attest it, having noticed it myself, those times when I stopped in Rome on my return from Brazil. I recall, however, that at that time there were elderly Sisters as portresses.

I know in no way that the education given to her grandchildren by our Sisters, and the frequent presence of the son-in-law of the Servant of God in the house, here and at Piacenza, where he did as in Rome, caused the slightest disorder in the Community. I must declare further that the said son-in-law was disliked by all the sisters, because they knew that he annoyed the Servant of God.

§ 188
She practiced virtue in an uncommon manner.

Ad 26: It seems to me I can affirm with all certainty that the Servant of God in all the time of her life, from youth, always observed the commandments of God, the precepts of the Church and the

obligations of her own state, the vows and the constitutions of her Institute (having become a religious) even in the smallest things. The constitutions, moreover, she took great care to have observed by her Sisters.

Ad 27: The Servant of God practiced the Theological and the Cardinal virtues and the others, humility, mortification, etc., and inculcated their practice also in her Sisters.

§ 189
Heroic exercise of faith.

As to faith, she believed firmly all the truths revealed by God and proposed by the Church, and for any article she would have been (I believe) ready for any sacrifice, even of life. She busied herself with the instruction of poor girls and took care that her daughters too should apply themselves to it with zeal, and she stimulated them in her conferences and in her frequent letters, as me, who was in America.

Ardent was her desire for the conversion of unbelievers and sinners. She prayed and inculcated in us that we pray for this purpose. She sent for this same purpose her Sisters to America and to Africa. Before they left for these places she had them make the Spiritual Exercises and in taking leave of them exhorted them so warmly to the work and to sacrifice that it was clearly seen how much faith and zeal lodged in her heart.

I myself heard how grateful and thankful she showed herself to God for having caused her to be born in the Catholic faith. She watched that in her daughters faith be kept alive, and that anything be avoided that could weaken it in the least, forbidding us among other things the reading of any newspaper, so that our spirit should not be distracted by things even merely worldly. Much more she watched and sent to inspect, that no book be introduced into our houses, I do not say perverse, but not even worldly.

§ 191
She practiced and greatly recommended prayer.

She held prayer in the highest esteem, and by example and word urged us to its practice. When she prayed, she was seen wholly absorbed in God; and faith and fervor shone great from her bearing.

I have heard it said, from Sr. Camilla Valentini, and it seems to me also from another Sister, that when the Servant of God prayed she seemed rapt in ecstasy, and that sometimes she did not answer when questioned. She was always seen recollected within herself, and showed her spirit ever ready for prayer, as I myself saw in the various months of my stays in Rome.

Sr. Serafina Foglia declared to me that she had seen her many times at night on her knees praying.

Once the Servant of God said to me myself: «Do not think, Sr. Vittoria, that when I retire I go to bed, but either I work or I pray».

§ 192
Frequency of the sacraments.

She confessed every eight days, and never omitted Communion any day, not even when traveling or if she felt weak. Before and after Communion, for which she prepared with great fervor, following it with equally fervent and very long thanksgiving (she left the Chapel half an hour after us), she did not want to be disturbed in any way.

§ 193
Characteristic devotions: Eucharist, Passion, Sacred Heart, Our Lady.

I have heard that at times during thanksgiving she was so absorbed in God that, called and even shaken by the habit, she gave no heed. She exhorted not only her Sisters to receive Communion often, but also the girls, when the occasion arose. She often visited the Most Holy Sacrament, and as soon as she had finished her urgent work, she went to the Chapel, where she was often found by the Sisters who were looking for her. Every Sunday she had the Most Holy Sacrament exposed from nine to twelve o'clock, before which she wanted the Sisters to go in adoration. To the Most Holy Trinity, and of it to the First Person, she had a most special devotion, which she also wanted transfused into us, as was shown by the prayers she had us say. And by her will we consecrate the month of January to the Eternal Father. She showed great devotion to the Child Jesus in the preparation for Christmas and inculcated in us that in each house the Mass be celebrated at night.

Immense was her devotion to the Passion of the Lord, which she had always present to her thought: and for this she loved with all her heart the Crucifix, which she called hers, and closed her letters saying: «I leave you in my Crucifix». In tribulations she turned to him, and he she presented to us as a model of resignation in our anguish, and as an object of comfort and hope.

A sister of mine by blood, who died in America, a religious in our house at Pernambuco, told me: «Do you know, Sr. Vittoria? I asked the Mother General to have my portrait made. And she answered me: You have the portrait: look at the Crucifix».

Her love of the Crucifix, I was told, she showed especially in Holy Week, doubling her penances and mortifications. I have heard also that the Crucifix spoke to her several times; and that that Crucifix is now in our Chapel here on the first floor of this house.

She was most devout also to the Most Sacred Heart of Jesus, whose devotion she inculcated in us, and she wished that we consecrate to him the month of June and for him she invited us to make sacrifices as well. When occasion offered, to the people and to the girls too she inculcated such devotion (as also that of the Passion of Our Lord) and in a special way the devotion of the first Fridays of the month.

She was most fond of meditation and woe to that Sister who showed herself sluggish in rising and late to meditation; she was sure to get a good reprimand from the Servant of God. I believe, moreover, that she began meditation before the Sisters went to the Chapel. The book which she wished adopted by her daughters for meditation is «L'anno doloroso» [The Sorrowful Year]. But on Monday she wished us to make it on the eternal Maxims, and on Saturday on Our Lady.

The care she took in having us celebrate the month of May, with the choice of good preachers, with a well-adorned altar, and all the novenas of Mary Most Holy, inculcating that the same be done in all houses, show how great was the love of the Servant of God for Our Lady. Before beginning the Institute, as I said, she took care of the daughters of Mary, and the first name given to her Sisters was that of Daughters of Mary Immaculate. I know she nourished special devotion to Our Lady under the title of Mary Sorrowful.

§ 194
Fervent devotion to the saints.

Proc. fol. 401: The Servant of God having great devotion to St. Michael the Archangel, she recommended to us Sisters to make his novena with devotion and to celebrate his feast.

She loved St. Francis of Assisi greatly for his poverty, which she sought to imitate, and to this Saint, as to St. Michael, she had an altar erected in our Church of this House, as she also had another erected in honor of St. Francis of Paola, on account of his humility, and likewise inculcated in us devotion to him.

I remember that in the first times when I was a religious she exhorted us to enroll in the third order of St. Francis of Assisi; I do not know whether afterward she continued this exhortation.

In a most special way she was most devout to St. Anne, Mother of the Virgin Most Holy, and inculcated in us devotion to her and the example of her virtues. For this she wished it inserted in the rules that we Sisters invoke her at every hour with an ejaculation, as she herself gave us the example. To her she wished the Church of this generalate House dedicated, and wished also that in each of our Houses there be an altar dedicated to St. Anne, and finally her devotion appears evident from the name her Institute bears.

p. 110

She was solicitous to acquire Indulgences, and exhorted us also to acquire them.

She took pains that in the Holy Year all the Sisters should gain the Jubilee.

§ 195
Veneration for the Word of God, the Bishops, the priests.

She had great reverence for the word of God, and wished that we sisters too hold it in high esteem; and when she exhorted us to this, she did so with great fervor.

Profound was her veneration for the Supreme Pontiff; she exhorted us to pray much for Holy Church, for the Supreme Pontiff. She wanted him always spoken of with profound respect, and demanded blind obedience not only to his commands, but also to his wishes. Likewise great was her veneration for the Cardinal Protectors, the other Cardinals, the Bishops in whose dioceses we have houses, and any Ecclesiastical authority, and she had great respect and wished that we have it for all Ecclesiastics, and pray for them.

I know that once in a House in Calabria, I think Rossano, some gossip having arisen about a Priest, I believe Chaplain of the said house of ours, on account of his relations with a Sister, the Servant of God changed all the personnel, and the Chaplain too, but using every prudence, that no rumor dishonoring to anyone should arise.

Her first care for the foundation of houses was prior agreement with the Bishops, and she wished the Superiors always to proceed united with their will.

She also tried to go along with the civil authority, and that any reason or pretext for complaint on its part be avoided.

Very great was her zeal for the decorum of the House of God;

§ 196
Zeal for the house of God.

she wanted it not only clean, but well adorned. She required the Sacristans to treat the things of the House of God with great respect and did not permit that through continual contact with them they become overfamiliar and pass before the Sacrament with a negligent genuflection, and this I myself heard noted by the Servant of God. She required also that on entering and leaving the Chapel, passing before the Most Holy Sacrament, the ground be kissed. From her manner of speaking it was clearly seen that the Servant of God had great hope of reaching Paradise.

p. 111

§ 197
Trust in God in tribulations.

Her hope, even for earthly things, for the affairs of her Institute, was placed in God, and she said to us: «Let us trust in God, and with this take courage, even in the greatest tribulations», as she wrote to me, when we were on the point of being driven out of Brazil through party hatred.

She had in her life many long and grave tribulations, moral and economic, but, resigned, always trusted in the Lord, as I myself was able to see. Notwithstanding, however, her great trust in God, she on her part employed all means to escape from difficulties, and in the beginnings of her Institute did not hesitate to go begging herself, although she knew she exposed herself, as happened, also to humiliations and refusals.

To the needy and afflicted, while giving counsels of hope in God, she sometimes also gave aid with money.

§ 198
Manifestations of divine love.

The charity toward God of this her servant is made manifest not only by her scrupulous exactness in observing the commandments, those of the Church and the constitutions of her Institute, as I have already said, but also by the exhortations made to us her Sisters, that we be faithful to God, even in the most minute things, exhortations which she also made, when occasion was given, to the sick and to other outside persons. When she learned of some grave offense to the Lord, she showed, as I myself saw, profound sadness. I have heard it said that, on hearing some blasphemy, she sought to make reparation with some ejaculation.

To the love of God she exhorted us all with great fervor.

§ 199
Love of neighbor manifested in many ways.

How great was her love of neighbor appears from her having given herself from girlhood to the instruction of girls, then to the care of poor sick women in her widowhood, from having assigned to her Institute as its purpose the instruction of girls, especially poor ones, and the relief of every misery.

I have heard it said that many, even distinguished persons, had recourse to her for counsel, which she did not refuse. She had prayer made for the conversion of sinners and to succeed in drawing them to God. Toward adversaries or enemies her charity remained unaltered, and she prayed and had prayer made for them. When someone spoke of the faults of others, her charitable word was always ready to excuse or soften them.

I have heard it said that she was most fond of peace, which she sought to maintain and to restore when it had vanished between some persons. I have heard told of a certain Sr. Anna Eletta (I do not recall the surname) resident in our House at Piacenza, who was very contrary to the Servant of God, who prejudiced her greatly by speaking ill of her, but the Servant of God bore everything long in peace, until that poor woman, having entirely lost the spirit of her vocation, left the Institute, and is now dead.

She recommended to us that we offer suffrages in a special way for our deceased sisters, and she had Masses celebrated for them, as she wrote also to me.

§ 200
Generous in the exercise of charity.

I saw with my own eyes that she helped the needy with clothing, food and money; and in free times, as for example in recreation time, she worked on clothing for the poor. In the exercise of this charity she was generous, and wanted us too, Superiors of the various houses, to be generous. Every day poor people came to this House and by her order a meal was prepared for them.

I have heard it said that she also helped, in the most delicate and secret way, persons fallen on hard times, who were in need of help.

I do not know until what time the Servant of God went personally to care for the sick. (When I entered the Institute she still went to care personally.) I know, however, that as long as she did so, she did it with great love, refusing no service however lowly, such as washing, sweeping, cleaning, emptying chamber pots, etc., and she exhorted us also to lend ourselves with love to all the humblest services for the sick.

§ 201
Most tender toward sick sisters.

Most tender was her charity toward sick sisters, as can be seen from the recommendations she made to us by letter; and I know that she herself, wherever she was at home, went personally to see them, consoled and blessed them. She had no difficulty at all in going to care also for persons affected by contagious diseases; she exhorted, as I have heard, her Sisters to care for the sick on occasions of epidemics, not to be afraid of anything, and to trust in God, showing herself very glad that her sisters listened to her and showed themselves disdainful of life for love of neighbor.

§ 202
Endowed with much prudence.

Proc. fol. 409v.: The Servant of God was endowed with much prudence, and I would have in mind no act of hers that could be charged with lightness; she reflected on and matured things before putting them into execution, and when it was a matter of important things, as for example the foundation of her Institute, she preceded them with long prayers. She had recourse to others for counsel, while she herself was a woman of much counsel, and many persons had recourse to her to consult her, as I have heard from trustworthy persons.

I believe that the Servant of God practiced the virtue of justice not only by defrauding no one of what was due to him, but also in the distribution of offices to her Sisters.

§ 203
Serene in the practice of justice and fortitude.

She did not fail to punish her Religious when she judged it necessary; but before coming to this she reflected, and preceded it with repeated admonitions. To whoever had done her some service or kindness, she showed her delicate gratitude.

The fortitude of her soul was never broken either by the weakness of her health or by the excessive work imposed on her by the spread of the Institute, showing herself very glad when she was overloaded with work, or by any adversity or tribulation. Her habitual illnesses she bore always with the most complete resignation.

She showed always a calm and gentle character; she always showed herself smiling in the same way, nor were varying moods seen alternating on her face.

§ 204
Constant spirit of mortification.

Temperance: As far as I know, the diet of the Servant of God was always strictly meatless, except in the last times of her life by order of the doctor; and I have heard it said that she could not even bear the smell of fatty foods.

In the morning I myself saw that she was accustomed to take a little cup of coffee without bread. At noon and in the evening the quantity of her food was very small. Her rest was very moderate, but I do not know particulars. Her bed was without mattress, with only a palliasse of leaves. The furnishing of her room was most simple: a little table, a Crucifix, and one or two chairs, and this little was of ordinary wood. I have heard it said that she wore hair shirts, little chains, and that a little chain was removed from her waist after she was dead.

Her most reserved bearing breathed great love of purity, and in her talks she greatly recommended to us reserve and propriety, especially with men. She did not permit, as indeed she prescribed in the Constitutions, that a Sister be alone with outside persons, and recommended to us Superiors to be well advised in the choice of sisters for those offices in which they would have to have contact with people of the world; and she insisted that we always watch.

In consequence of this love of purity she did not want us to be distracted by frivolous reading, such as novels or newspapers, even good ones, and this she recommended also to us Superiors, that we watch.

Poverty: Her dress had nothing singular; and I know she preferred old garments to new ones; and when her religious presented her with a new habit, she did not show herself at all pleased, and at times went on wearing her old patched garments.

This her love of poverty was shown further in the exhortations she made to us, that we take care of the most abandoned poor.

§ 206
Model of obedience and of humility.

Of her obedience I know only that she kept to the medical prescriptions, and to those of her Religious who attended her, and that she recommended this virtue of obedience to all of us.

From the whole of her acts it was very well seen that the Servant of God was very humble. She did not want to be called Mother General or Foundress, and abhorred signs of honor that might be paid her.

In the exercise of all the above virtues I believe, as the other sisters also think, that the Servant of God practiced them constantly, until death, without relaxation.

§ 207
She practiced the virtues in a heroic degree.

Ad 28: I believe that the exercise of the same said virtues reached, in the Servant of God, an extraordinary degree, and truly that of a Saint, that is, as is told of the saints who are venerated on the Altars. As to the concept of the heroism of the virtues, I cannot determine myself.

§ 208
Enriched with extraordinary gifts.

Ad 30: I have heard it said, I do not recall from which Sisters, that the Servant of God was at times rapt in ecstasy, that at times she penetrated the interior of hearts, and Sr. Anna Camilla Valentini told me that, when the Servant of God was in this House, she saw a fact that was taking place in a House in America, and the truth of her vision was afterward shown by the reports that came from there, but I do not know particulars.

Ad 32: I know that the Servant of God wrote a book, which I too read, but of which I do not even remember the title. This book was afterward withdrawn and I have not seen it again. She wrote also some little prayers, for example to Jesus Crucified, to the Most Holy Trinity, to the Eternal Father, which are printed.

The Servant of God wrote me very many letters, while I was in America, which were a comfort and edification to me; however, not foreseeing the future, I destroyed them all.

Ad 33: The Servant of God died in May of the year 1900.

§ 209
Holy death of the Servant of God.

While I was in America, I learned there that her death was very edifying and that, most resigned to the will of God, she herself asked for the Sacraments.

Ad 34: I heard it said that many people took part in her funeral, and that they said: «A Saint has died».

Ad 35: The body of the Servant of God was transported to Campo Verano and rests there in the tomb of the Institute, whose location I could not indicate, although I have been there three times.

Ad 37: Our Sisters go from time to time to visit her tomb and to commend themselves to her intercession; and I know that none of the Sisters who come to Rome omits this act of veneration to our Foundress.

§ 210
Esteemed in life as a saint and also after death.

Ad 38: In life the Servant of God was esteemed as a true Saint by her Religious and also by outside persons, and this esteem has been preserved also after death; and our Religious commend themselves to her in their needs. The outside persons who had and have so much esteem are in general those who have contact with our Institute by reason of the administration of the pious Institutions entrusted to our consisters. I absolutely exclude that any artifice was or is made to bring about and maintain the said esteem as a saint.

Ad 39: I have heard only from Sr. Anna of the Holy Spirit that she did not hold the Servant of God to be a Saint. This Religious, however, I regret to say, is certainly not exemplary, and is prone to speak a little ill of everyone. I recall in particular that she accused the Servant of God of being too demanding in obtaining money from the houses, a thing which I absolutely deny as far as I know. I note that she was a Superior, I do not recall in which House, from which she was removed on account of her stubborn and imprudent character. I do not recall who dismissed her as Superior. She is still living and I believe she is in a house in Piedmont.

WITNESS V
Sr. ANNA SERAFINA FOGLIA

Scope in the process: From Sess. 502 of 22 November 1913 (fol. 422) to Sess. 1022 of 25 November 1914 (fol. 857 v.), from Sess. 106[...] of 7.XII.1914 (fol. 995 v.) to Sess. 1122 of 12.1.1915 (fol. 1048); from Sess. 116[...] of 30.1.1915 (fol. 1081) to Sess. 1212 of 3.III.1915 (fol. 1120 v.).

Name, surname, date and place of birth: Serafina Foglia, born 12 March 1861 at Pieve San Giacomo (Cremona).

State and profession: Religious in the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, sacristan.

Quality of the witness: Eyewitness.

Age of the witness when she knew the Servant of God: 27 years.

Age of the Servant of God when the witness knew her: 57 years.

Age of the witness at the time of the deposition: 53 years.

Duration of the acquaintance and its grounds: The witness knew the Servant of God on a visit which the latter made to the house of Prato in 1888; afterward she met her again at Florence and, from 1895, lived always with the Foundress until her death (1900), acting as her nurse in the last year. Notwithstanding the shared life not very extensive in time (1895-1900), the witness knew the Servant of God intimately.

Observations on the witness, the scope and the content of the deposition: Given the imposing length of the testimony, the parts of lesser importance, not always well indicated, have been omitted.

These are the most important moments of the deposition: reconstruction of the family environment of the Gattorno House and of her life in the family as a young woman; the period of married life, with rich information concerning the spouse, the children and the Servant of God. The witness then devotes wide space to the foundation of the Institute and to the difficulties she had to face as Superior General.

The proof concerning each single virtue is particularly rich, as is that concerning the demonstration of supernatural gifts, the last illness and death, the spontaneous concourse of the faithful to pay homage to the body. To the fame of holiness and of miracles ample importance is finally attributed.

Ad 2 interr., Proc. fol. 424v., testis respondit:

§ 211
General particulars of the witness.

My name is Sr. Anna Serafina Foglia, daughter of the late Giovanna and Stella Ceresini. I was born at Pieve San Giacomo, Prov. of Cremona, on 12 March of the year 1861. I entered Religion at the age of 24 completed, at Piacenza. I professed after two years in our house of Prato in Tuscany. I have not had important offices; they sent me to beg, and entrusted to me the office of Sacristan at Prato and here, in which office I still am. After having been 8 years at Prato I was called to this generalate house in Rome, where I have always remained.

§ 212
Scope of knowledge.

Ad 7: After three years of my stay at Prato, I knew the Servant of God for the first time, of whom I had already heard speak in the Community as of a very good woman; and it is because of this talk that I had asked the Lord to let me know her before I died. The Servant of God had come on that occasion for the regular visitation of her house, and like all the others she called me too to listen to me. Having asked me what I did, and I having answered her that at times I went begging, and sometimes to care for the sick in their homes, she asked me further whether, on journey for the collection, I made Holy Communion every day; and I having answered that when we were far from the Church I did not, she replied: «This displeases me; you must try each evening to take lodging near some church, in order to be able to hear Holy Mass the next morning and make Communion». And having asked me further whether it vexed me, in the collection, to end some day without having been able to gather anything, and I having answered her: «Yes, Mother, what do you expect, one walks and walks, one grows tired, and on seeing ourselves in the evening without any fruit, naturally it vexes us». To which the Servant of God replied smiling: «See, daughter, when you remain at the day's end with empty hands, you have gained everything for yourself, whereas when you gather something, the fruit of your labors is already given you, and this goes to the Community». From this conversation, from the words of the Servant of God, from her bearing and her appearance, there remained in me the impression of the Servant of God as of a Saint. Two years later I saw the Servant of God again at Florence.

Coming then to Rome, called by the Servant of God in 1895, I had occasion to know her well, because although assigned to the office of Sacristan, she wanted me much of the time near her; she spoke to me of the things of God, especially in the evening after the Rosary; she often had me pray for her intentions, which at times she revealed to me, at times not; for example, when she was to open a house, she sent a new Superior, when she feared something for a Religious, etc. In the last year of the life of the Servant of God, since by the doctor's order a vigil had to be kept for her at night, it was I who always kept the night watches, the Servant of God sending me to sleep by day, and I acted as her nurse as I had done in the four preceding years, and attended her until death.

§ 213
Sincere veneration toward the Servant of God.

Ad 8: Toward the Servant of God I felt much affection while she was alive and feel it still, having esteemed her and esteeming her as a Saint; I often have recourse to her, that she may help me. I pray for her Canonization, but do nothing else for her; and in my deposition the affection I feel for her will not blind me, and I shall not say things read either in her obituaries or in any other book, including the articles of the Postulator of the Cause, but shall hold solely to what I saw, or heard from her herself, or from trustworthy persons.

§ 214
Family and childhood of the Servant of God.

Ad 9: The Servant of God was born I do not know when, at Genoa, of a well-to-do family. I heard from the Sisters who knew her at Piacenza, where she sometimes went, that her mother was very pious. I learned from the Servant of God herself that she had two sisters and two brothers; and that the sisters were pious and good, but that the brothers did not even go to Church. (One of them died this year.) She herself told me that, notwithstanding her mother's concern for the Christian education of the children (and to discipline them better she had placed them in boarding school, where the now deceased one would not stay because of his vivacity), they turned out not as the mother had wished and were a constant worry to the Servant of God for their eternal salvation. For them she prayed much and invited her Religious and me to pray. I recall still this particular: when the Preacher of the month of May came here, the Servant of God asked him to have the people recite every evening three Hail Marys for the conversion of a sinner, and I know from the Servant of God herself that the sinner whom the Servant of God recommended was her brother.

Ad 10 interr., Proc. fol. 432v.: From girlhood the Servant of God was exemplary. My consisters tell me that she was always obedient to her parents; and the Servant of God herself told me that from childhood she had from her mother the keeping of the wardrobe, of the pantry, and also the charge of directing the kitchen, of watching over her brothers and the servant women, which naturally could not have happened unless her mother had been fully pleased with her: further the Servant of God told me that her mamma loved her very much.

§ 215
Marriage and married life.

Ad 11: Her brothers pressing, and the mother also being content, she united herself in marriage to a Gentleman who, I believe, was her relative, of a well-to-do and Christian family. I recall that the Servant of God spoke to me of this marriage of hers always with much pain. Seeing this I said to her: «But do not think of it any more, my mother».

Ad 13: She told me that her husband was very good, and that it would have been a sin to wrong him in any way, and therefore they lived in peace and love together. She had three children whom, as soon as they were born, she took care to have baptized. One of them died at about 6 years of age, some years after the death of the husband, to the immense grief of the mother who, as she told me, felt she would go mad. The second died at Piacenza between 23 and 30 years. And there remained to her one daughter only who then, as I have said, became mute. When the husband died she placed her sons in a boarding school at Genoa, and kept her daughter with her, until she took the resolution to found the Institute. Then she placed her daughter also to be educated in a School for the Deaf-Mute. After a certain time she had to take her from there, because the daughter absolutely would not stay, and always looked for her mamma, and she had to take her back with her.

The son who remained to her after the death of the first, notwithstanding the many cares the Servant of God had taken that her offspring should grow up Christian, strayed from the right path and was the cause of many sorrows to her. I know that the Servant of God prayed much for the conversion of her son, and was heard by good God, because at the end of his life he returned to God, and was attended in his last illness by our Sisters and by his mother, who procured for him all the religious comforts.

§ 216
A widow after seven years of marriage.

Ad 14: After seven years of marriage the Servant of God remained a widow. The husband died after having endured an illness of three months, during which the Servant of God never abandoned him, neither day nor night. I recall that the Servant of God told me that the husband, not even when he felt ill, would omit saying the Rosary every evening, and they spoke together of spiritual things, as indeed had been done also in the preceding years, when the husband was in health. Such a loss cost the heart of the Servant of God much, and, as soon as the death was ascertained, she fell into a swoon; yet her soul was always resigned to the will of God, as she herself told me. She had the soul of her husband helped with very many Masses, and every year, on the anniversary of his death, had others celebrated. She told me further that after the death, having gone to her husband's tomb, she made him a promise to love him always, as she had loved him in life, and to give herself wholly to God. I said a moment ago that the Servant of God, at the death of the first son, seemed to go mad. This is easily explained, because to the grief of the loss of the husband there succeeded, at the short distance of three months, this other grief.

§ 217
Foundation. Apostolic visitation.

Ad 22, Proc. fol. 458: First Superior of the one house of Piacenza was the Servant of God, and she exercised the office of General when other houses were opened, and this she held until death. She was always, however, reluctant, the Servant of God, toward this office, and several times she had resolved to resign, and the Consisters told me, and among others M. Carrega, the present General, that once the Holy Father, Pius IX, intervened with an injunction to prevent her resignation, and this Pope intervened also from the beginning to determine the Servant of God to assume the office of General. I know further from the Servant of God that when a certain Serafini, a Benedictine I think, and later Bishop, was named Visitor of our Institute, he, having our Foundress before him, told her that it was necessary she give her resignation. (I note that this injunction the Visitor made to her from the first interview with our Mother.) The Servant of God then felt lively joy and answered the Visitor: «I am ready to do as Your Excellency wishes; choose whom you think better suited for this office». Then the Visitor: «Well then, remain still until October (we were then in the month of August) and when you return to Rome (for he had gone to see her at Piacenza) it will be discussed. Meanwhile do not open any other house without my order, nor without my order (but of this last I am not altogether sure) accept other Postulants». To which the Servant of God: «I am disposed to do as Your Excellency wishes».

From my Superior of Prato and from that of Florence, who took part in the first General Chapter presided over by Cardinal Alimonda, Protector of the Institute, I learned that in that Chapter the Servant of God presented her resignation as Superior General, but that all the Superiors (about 50 present) declared that they wanted her as their Mother General. The Cardinal, President, confirmed this decision of the Superiors, and she had to take it upon herself to continue in that office.

Speaking afterward with me, the Servant of God seemed rather preoccupied by this office, but then she added resigned: «It is the will of God». I heard her also exclaim: «Lord, where I cannot reach, You reach».

§ 218
She discharged the office of superior well.

As far as I know, and have heard myself, the Servant of God always discharged the office of General very well. From the beginning she showed herself most prudent in the acceptance of Postulants, not neglecting the most precise and sure information concerning them and their family; and if they had no family, because of the difficulties that would then arise in case of an unsuccessful outcome of the Postulant, she did not receive them, not knowing then to whom she could hand them back. She was also very difficult for the acceptance of Sisters into the Institute. The one point in which the Servant of God at times closed her eyes was if they were poor and had no dowry. In this case it sufficed for her that they had good moral qualities and gave good hope of a happy outcome. Although at the beginning of the Institute she had need of religious, the Servant of God never concerned herself, as far as I know, with making numbers.

§ 219
Prudent in the government of communities.

She visited frequently, every one or two years, the houses of the Institute in Italy, and where she did not go, as in America, she sent Visitors, and required from the Superiors a report on the economic and disciplinary course of the houses. Following the visitations she took the measures judged most opportune and necessary without regard to anyone. In the visitations, as I myself was able to see once, accompanying her on one of these at Genoa, she received first the subjects and then the Superiors. Once the Servant of God was ill and the Secretary and the Assistants tried to dissuade her from the visit she wanted to make to our houses in Sicily; and availing themselves of the familiarity which the Servant of God granted me with her, they said to me: «You too must try to dissuade the mother from this visit to Sicily, and persuade her to have the Superior come to Rome». Then I went to the Servant of God, pointing out to her that the purpose of the visit would be obtained equally, sparing herself ill as she was and having the Superior come to Rome. And the Servant of God: «You are right, my daughter, that I should spare myself, but if I go there I can hear both subjects and Superiors and know the true state of things. If I call the Superiors to Rome, they will tell me what I already know», and she went away with fever.

§ 220
She watched over the observance of the rules.

Ad 22, Proc. fol. 464: The Servant of God told me, and as several Consisters afterward confirmed to me, that in the visitations to the houses of the Institute, asking whether they had enough providence for temporal things, and being answered sometimes that they were in great difficulty, she was persuaded that the Rules were not observed enough, and in fact in her careful inquiry she found that it was really so. She therefore exhorted the Superiors and the subjects to the most exact observance of the Rules, telling them that if they observed these, providence would not fail. And it happened precisely as it resulted to her in the subsequent information, that from the scrupulous observance of the Rules, Providence followed more abundant. From some Superiors and Consisters I have heard it confirmed to me that really non-observance of the Rules is accompanied by lack of necessities and the forced recourse to the Mother General who in straits met their needs, and that with the Rules observed there was no longer need of recourse to the Mother General, who said: «See, now that you observe the Rules, you no longer need to have recourse to me for help».

§ 221
She took care of the good administration of the communities. Prudent in requiring administrative accounts.

Difficulties sometimes arose between the administrative commissions of the institutions directed by our Sisters, and then the Servant of God often ran personally to smooth over those difficulties.

Once Sr. Anna del Salvatore, Provincial of Sicily, telegraphed the Servant of God to hasten promptly to Palermo to avoid the Sisters being removed from a hospital through the opposition of the administrative Commission. The Servant of God said to her Assistants as soon as she received the telegram: «Tomorrow I leave for Palermo» and, seeing her Sisters struck by this sudden resolution, added: «Whoever wishes to come, follow me; if not, I shall go alone». She left the next day, hurried to Palermo, where she smoothed over the difficulties that had arisen, and the Sisters remained in that hospital. In the choice for offices the Servant of God never let herself be guided by ulterior motives, sympathies or antipathies, and on this point I never heard any criticism. When someone showed herself reluctant to accept charges or offices, she availed herself of her authority and imposed it by obedience.

She watched that her Religious should not lack necessities, and most tender was her care for the suffering and ill. Before founding the new houses the Servant of God informed herself that the means of subsistence be assured to the Sisters. This does not exclude that in the first days of the various foundations they had to suffer some discomfort or privation; but these were very passing things. If then she found that, notwithstanding the observance of the Rules, the sisters could not support themselves in a house, she withdrew them.

Ad 23: The Institute from the beginning began to spread with great rapidity. I recall that twenty-six years ago, when I entered the Institute, there already existed many houses in Sicily, that of Naples, and some in Rome (I believe at least two), at Prato, at Florence, at Bassano Veneto, at Pistoia, at Siena and in America. In the semiannual report, since an account must also be given regarding finances, the surplus of money must at the same time be sent to the Mother General, who then provides for the subsequent eventual needs of the same house or of others. It could happen, and I know it has happened, that some Superior, to cut a good figure with the Servant of God, skimped a little too much on the expenses of the house, leaving her subjects ill at ease. But if this fact came to the knowledge of the Servant of God, as in the long run it could not be avoided, she demanded an account from the Superior, at times even going so far as to remove her from office.

Proc. fol. 472v.: I absolutely exclude that the Servant of God made any pressure on the local Superiors to have as much as possible from their finances, and that she showed preference for those who sent to the generalate house a larger sum of money. She watched, however, that in the various Houses money not be wasted on useless or superfluous things.

§ 223
Economic relations with her family.

Ad 24: Before answering this Interrogatory, I shall say further that the Servant of God, withdrawing from the world, left her goods in administration to her brothers and her mother, to whom, however, she afterward gave aid also with other money which, however, was not the Institute's, but was given to her by her intimate friends, such as Princess Fitalia, the late Marchioness Cavalletti, that lady who gave the Institute the estate of Gargatano and whose name I do not now recall, Mother Benedetta Carrega, now General, and Sr. Anna Michelina Negri (these last naturally with money of which they could dispose without violating the vow of poverty), and Sr. Anna Maria Teresa Sorrentino, now resident in Palermo, and other persons. These offerings, of which the Servant of God then made use to aid her children, were determinately fixed by the donors for her children, as both the donors and the Mother herself told me. This did not prevent, however, the donors from showing themselves generous also toward the Institute.
